Topic: Topic 2.1.4: Bundle of His

Topic Description: Topic 2.1.4: Bundle of His

Heading: 2.1.4.H1 Learning Objective

2.1.4.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the Bundle of His and explain its function within the cardiac conduction system. ●       Describe the anatomical location and structural pathway of the Bundle of His. ●       Understand how the Bundle of His conducts impulses from the AV node to the ventricles. ●       Explain the relationship between the Bundle of His and bundle branches. ●       Recognize the clinical significance of His bundle conduction abnormalities and their role in device therapy. ●       Understand the relevance of His-bundle pacing in modern pacing therapy. 2.1.4.H2 Explanation 2.1.4.C2 The Bundle of His, also known simply as the His Bundle, is a specialized collection of cardiac conduction fibers that transmits electrical impulses from the AV node to the ventricles. It serves as the only normal electrical connection between the atria and ventricles under healthy physiological conditions. After the electrical impulse leaves the AV node, it enters the Bundle of His, which acts as the bridge carrying the impulse from the atrial conduction system into the ventricular conduction system. Without the Bundle of His, electrical activation of the ventricles would not occur in a coordinated or efficient manner. The Bundle of His is extremely important because it begins the process of rapid ventricular conduction, allowing the ventricles to contract in a synchronized pattern necessary for effective pumping. Subtopic 1: Anatomical Location of the Bundle of His The Bundle of His is located: ●       At the lower end of the AV node ●       Penetrating through the fibrous cardiac muscle ●       Into the upper part of the interventricular septum It lies in the membranous septum before dividing into the: ●       Right Bundle Branch ●       Left Bundle Branch The Bundle of His occupies a strategic position because it passes through the fibrous tissue barrier that electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. Subtopic 2: Why the Bundle of His Is Important The Bundle of His is critical because: ●       It is the only normal electrical bridge between atria and ventricles ●       It ensures impulses travel efficiently into ventricular tissue ●       It initiates synchronized ventricular activation Without it: ●       Electrical conduction to ventricles would fail ●       Ventricular escape rhythms would be needed ●       Severe bradycardia may result Subtopic 4: Electrical Conduction Through the Bundle of His After the AV node delays the impulse: ●       The Bundle of His rapidly conducts the signal downward The impulse then: 1.    Passes through the His Bundle 2.    Splits into bundle branches 3.    Activates Purkinje network 4.    Depolarizes ventricles This rapid conduction ensures: ●       Near simultaneous ventricular contraction ●       Efficient cardiac output   Subtopic 5: Intrinsic Pacemaker Ability of the Bundle of His Although not normally the primary pacemaker, the Bundle of His has backup pacemaker capability. Intrinsic firing rate: ●       20–40 bpm This rhythm may emerge if: ●       SA node fails ●       AV node fails However: ●       This rate is too slow for adequate perfusion in most patients Subtopic 6: Relationship to Bundle Branches The Bundle of His divides into: Right Bundle Branch (RBB) Conducts impulses to: ●       Right ventricle Left Bundle Branch (LBB) Conducts impulses to: ●       Left ventricle This branching system ensures: ●       Simultaneous biventricular activation Subtopic 8: His Bundle Dysfunction If conduction through the His Bundle is impaired: ●       Ventricular conduction slows/stops ●       Heart block may develop Common disorders: ●       Infra-Hisian block ●       Bifascicular block ●       Trifascicular block ●       Complete heart block Symptoms: ●       Bradycardia ●       Syncope ●       Fatigue ●       Sudden collapse Subtopic 10: His Bundle Pacing (Modern Device Therapy) One of the newest pacing strategies is: His Bundle Pacing (HBP) Instead of pacing RV apex: ●       Lead directly stimulates His Bundle Benefits: ●       Preserves natural conduction pathway ●       Produces physiologic ventricular activation ●       Reduces dyssynchrony Advantages: ●       Lower pacing-induced cardiomyopathy risk ●       Better synchrony than RV pacing ●       Mimics natural conduction

Heading: 2.1.4.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

2.1.4.C3 Term Definition Bundle of His Electrical bridge between AV node and ventricles His-Purkinje System Ventricular conduction network Infra-Hisian Block Block below AV node in His system His Bundle Pacing Physiologic pacing via His Bundle stimulation Bundle Branch Branches carrying impulse to ventricles Bundle of His Anatomy Diagram   Clinical Pearl The Bundle of His is one of the most critical conduction structures for ventricular activation. ●        It is the only normal electrical connection between atria and ventricles. ●        Damage can result in serious AV conduction abnormalities. ●        His-Purkinje disease often causes wide QRS bradycardia. ●        Infra-Hisian block usually requires pacing. ●        His Bundle pacing preserves physiologic conduction. ●        HBP reduces ventricular dyssynchrony compared with RV pacing. ●        His disease may progress unpredictably to complete heart block. ●        ECG conduction intervals help assess His function.   Device Relevance The Bundle of His is extremely important in pacing therapy because: Traditional RV Pacing May bypass normal His-Purkinje activation.

Topic: Topic 2.1.5: Bundle Branches and Purkinje Fibers

Topic Description: Topic 2.1.5: Bundle Branches and Purkinje Fibers

Heading: 2.1.5.H1 Learning Objective

2.1.5.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers and explain their role in ventricular conduction. ●       Describe the anatomical pathway of the right and left bundle branches. ●       Understand how the Purkinje network distributes impulses through the ventricles. ●       Explain the concept of synchronized ventricular activation and why it is clinically important. ●       Recognize conduction abnormalities such as bundle branch block and their significance in cardiac device therapy. ●       Relate bundle branch physiology to CRT and advanced pacing strategies. 2.1.5.H2 Explanation 2.1.5.C1 After the electrical impulse leaves the AV node and travels through the Bundle of His, it enters the next major part of the cardiac conduction system: the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. These structures form the terminal portion of the His-Purkinje conduction system, which is responsible for rapidly delivering electrical impulses throughout the ventricles. Their primary role is to ensure that the right and left ventricles contract quickly, efficiently, and simultaneously. This synchronized ventricular contraction is essential for maintaining optimal cardiac output and efficient blood ejection into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Without the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers: ●       Ventricular depolarization would be slow ●       Ventricles would contract asynchronously ●       Cardiac efficiency would decline significantly These fibers conduct impulses much faster than normal myocardial tissue, allowing nearly simultaneous activation of millions of ventricular myocardial cells. Subtopic 1: Right and Left Bundle Branches Once the Bundle of His enters the interventricular septum, it divides into two major pathways: Right Bundle Branch (RBB) The right bundle branch: ●       Travels down the right side of the interventricular septum ●       Conducts electrical impulses toward the right ventricle ●       Activates the RV myocardium Its primary function is to depolarize the: ●       Right ventricular septum ●       Right ventricular free wall Left Bundle Branch (LBB) The left bundle branch: ●       Travels down the left side of the interventricular septum ●       Conducts impulses toward the left ventricle ●       Activates the LV myocardium Because the left ventricle is larger and thicker, the left bundle branch has a more complex branching structure. Subtopic 2: Left Bundle Fascicles The Left Bundle Branch divides into smaller branches called fascicles. These include: Left Anterior Fascicle Conducts impulses to: ●       Anterior/superior LV wall Left Posterior Fascicle Conducts impulses to: ●       Posterior/inferior LV wall Some texts also describe: Septal Fascicle Supplies: ●       Septal myocardium This division helps ensure complete LV activation.     Subtopic 3: Purkinje Fibers The bundle branches terminate into an extensive network called the Purkinje fibers. Purkinje fibers are: ●       Specialized conduction fibers ●       Located beneath the endocardium ●       Distributed throughout ventricular myocardium Their role is to: ●       Deliver impulses rapidly to ventricular muscle ●       Ensure near-simultaneous contraction of ventricles This is the fastest conduction in the heart. Subtopic 4: Sequence of Ventricular Activation The normal ventricular activation sequence is: 1.    Septum depolarizes first (left → right) 2.    Apex depolarizes next 3.    Ventricular free walls activate 4.    Base activates last This organized sequence allows: ●       Apex-to-base contraction ●       Efficient upward blood ejection Subtopic 5: Why Rapid Ventricular Conduction Matters Rapid ventricular conduction ensures: Coordinated Contraction Both ventricles contract together. Maximal Stroke Volume Efficient blood ejection. Narrow QRS Complex Normal ventricular depolarization pattern. If ventricular activation becomes delayed: ●       QRS widens ●       Contraction becomes dyssynchronous ●       Pumping efficiency falls Subtopic 6: Bundle Branch Block (BBB) A Bundle Branch Block occurs when one of the bundle branches cannot conduct impulses properly. This causes: ●       Delayed activation of one ventricle ●       Dyssynchronous ventricular contraction Types: Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) Occurs when: ●       Right bundle branch fails Result: ●       LV activates first ●       RV activates late ECG: ●       Wide QRS ●       RSR' pattern in V1 Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) Occurs when: ●       Left bundle branch fails Result: ●       RV activates first ●       LV activates late ECG: ●       Wide QRS ●       Broad/notched R wave in lateral leads Subtopic 7: Clinical Significance of LBBB LBBB is particularly important because: ●       LV is main pumping chamber ●       Delayed LV activation reduces efficiency Effects: ●       Dyssynchrony ●       Lower EF ●       Reduced cardiac output ●       Worsened heart failure Subtopic 8: CRT Relevance in Bundle Branch Block Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT) is used when: Patients have: ●       Heart failure ●       Reduced EF ●       Wide QRS/LBBB CRT works by: ●       Pacing both ventricles simultaneously ●       Restoring synchrony Goal: ●       Improve coordinated contraction Subtopic 9: Fascicular Blocks Blockage of fascicles causes: Left Anterior Fascicular Block Produces: ●       Left axis deviation Left Posterior Fascicular Block Produces: ●       Right axis deviation May indicate: ●       Progressive conduction disease Subtopic 10: Purkinje Escape Rhythms If higher pacemakers fail: Purkinje fibers may generate escape rhythm. Rate: ●       20–40 bpm However: ●       Usually too slow to sustain perfusion

Heading: 2.1.5.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

2.1.5.C3 Term Definition Bundle Branch Conducts impulses to ventricles Fascicle Subdivision of left bundle branch Purkinje Fibers Terminal ventricular conduction fibers BBB Delay/block in ventricular conduction Dyssynchrony Uncoordinated ventricular contraction Bundle Branch / Purkinje Diagram       Clinical Pearl The His-Purkinje system is essential for efficient ventricular contraction. ●        Bundle branches rapidly deliver impulses to ventricles. ●        Purkinje fibers ensure synchronized ventricular activation. ●        BBB causes delayed ventricular activation and wide QRS. ●        LBBB commonly worsens heart failure symptoms. ●        LBBB is a major CRT indication. ●        Fascicular blocks may precede complete heart block. ●        Wide QRS often indicates distal conduction disease. ●        Purkinje rhythms may sustain life during complete block. Device Relevance Bundle branch conduction is critical in CRM because: CRT Therapy Corrects ventricular dyssynchrony from BBB. Pacemaker Therapy Treats infra-Hisian conduction disease. Conduction System Pacing Targets bundle branches physiologically. ICD Monitoring Detects ventricular conduction abnormalities. Chapter: Chapter 2.2: Electrical Activity

Topic: Topic 2.2.1: Depolarization vs Repolarization

Topic Description: Topic 2.2.1: Depolarization vs Repolarization

Heading: 2.2.1.H1 Learning Objective

2.2.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define depolarization and repolarization in cardiac electrophysiology. ●       Understand the relationship between electrical activity and myocardial contraction/relaxation. ●       Correlate depolarization and repolarization with ECG waveforms. ●       Relate these concepts to pacemaker sensing, pacing capture, and arrhythmia recognition. 2.2.1.H2 Explanation 2.2.1.C2 The heart’s ability to beat and pump blood depends entirely on electrical activity occurring at the cellular level. Every heartbeat begins when cardiac cells undergo changes in electrical charge across their membranes. These changes allow electrical impulses to form and spread throughout the myocardium, causing coordinated contraction and relaxation of the heart muscle. Two of the most fundamental electrical processes in the heart are: 1.    Depolarization 2.    Repolarization These processes occur continuously with every heartbeat and form the basis of all electrical rhythm generation, ECG interpretation, pacing, and arrhythmia management. To understand depolarization and repolarization, learners must first understand that every cardiac cell has an electrical charge difference across its membrane, called the membrane potential. Subtopic 1: Resting Membrane Potential- Polarization At rest, myocardial cells maintain a negative electrical charge inside the cell compared with outside compared to the outside, the cell is said to be in a polarized state. This polarized resting state prepares the cell for the next electrical impulse. Subtopic 2: What Is Depolarization? Depolarization is the process by which the inside of the cardiac cell becomes less negative and more positive, initiating electrical activation. It is the event that initiates contraction of cardiac muscle. Subtopic 3: Mechanism of Depolarization The steps of depolarization are: Step 1: Threshold Reached A stimulus raises membrane potential to threshold. Step 2: Sodium Channels Open Rapid influx of sodium ions occurs. Step 3: Positive Charge Increases Cell interior becomes positive. Step 4: Action Potential Generated Electrical impulse spreads across myocardium. This electrical activation then triggers: Muscle contraction Subtopic 4: Clinical Meaning of Depolarization Depolarization directly causes: Electrical Activation Myocardium becomes electrically stimulated. Mechanical Contraction Cardiac muscle contracts after depolarization. Without depolarization: ●       No contraction occurs ●       No heartbeat occurs This is why pacemakers function by artificially causing depolarization. Subtopic 5: What Is Repolarization? Repolarization is the process by which the cardiac cell returns to its resting negative electrical state after depolarization. it restores the cell’s readiness for the next heartbeat. Subtopic 6: Mechanism of Repolarization Steps include: Step 1: Sodium Channels Close No further sodium entry. Step 2: Potassium Channels Open Potassium leaves the cell. Step 3: Cell Interior Becomes Negative Again Returns toward resting potential. Step 4: Cell Ready for Next Beat Membrane restored to polarized state.   Subtopic 7: Relationship to Contraction and Relaxation Electrical and mechanical activity are linked: Depolarization → Contraction Electrical stimulation triggers contraction. Repolarization → Relaxation Electrical reset allows relaxation. This relationship is known as: Electromechanical Coupling Subtopic 8: ECG Correlation Depolarization and repolarization create ECG waveforms. P Wave Represents:  Atrial depolarization QRS Complex Represents: Ventricular depolarization T Wave Represents: Ventricular repolarization   Atrial repolarization is usually hidden within the QRS complex. Subtopic 9: Why Repolarization Is Important Without repolarization: ●       Cells cannot depolarize again ●       Rhythm would stop Proper repolarization ensures: ●       Rhythm regularity ●       Prevention of arrhythmias ●       Cellular recovery Abnormal repolarization may cause: ●       QT prolongation ●       Ventricular arrhythmias ●       Sudden cardiac death Subtopic 10: Refractory Period After depolarization: Cells temporarily cannot depolarize again. This period is called: Refractory Period Purpose: ●       Prevents premature reactivation ●       Prevents tetanic contraction ●       Maintains rhythm regularity   Subtopic 11: Relevance in Pacemaker Therapy Pacemakers rely on depolarization and repolarization principles: Pacing Pulse Artificially causes depolarization. Sensing: Detects natural depolarization. Capture: Occurs when pacing causes depolarization. Refractory Programming: Prevents oversensing inappropriate signals.

Heading: 2.2.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

2.2.1.C3 Term Definition Depolarization Electrical activation of cardiac cell Repolarization Return to resting electrical state Membrane Potential Voltage difference across cell membrane Polarized Resting negative electrical state Refractory Period Recovery time after depolarization Depolarization/Repolarization Diagram       Clinical Pearl Depolarization and repolarization are foundational concepts in rhythm management. ●        Depolarization initiates myocardial contraction. ●        Repolarization restores readiness for the next beat. ●        Abnormal depolarization may impair contraction. ●        Delayed repolarization may trigger dangerous arrhythmias. ●        Pacemakers artificially induce depolarization. ●        ICDs detect abnormal depolarization patterns. ●        ECG waveforms reflect depolarization/repolarization events. ●        Refractory periods prevent uncontrolled activation. Device Relevance These principles are central to CRM because: Pacemakers Stimulate depolarization electrically. ICDs Monitor abnormal depolarization/repolarization patterns. EP Studies Map depolarization pathways. Device Programming Uses refractory periods for sensing control. Topic: Topic 2.2.2: Impulse Propagation

Topic Description: Topic 2.2.2: Impulse Propagation

Heading: 2.2.2.H1 Learning Objective

2.2.2.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define impulse propagation and explain its role in cardiac electrophysiology. ●       Describe how electrical impulses travel from one cardiac cell to another. ●       Understand the mechanisms of cell-to-cell conduction and gap junction function. ●       Explain the concept of conduction velocity and why it varies in different cardiac tissues. ●       Recognize the importance of impulse propagation in maintaining synchronized heart rhythm. ●       Relate abnormalities in impulse propagation to arrhythmias and device therapy. 2.2.2.H2 Explanation 2.2.2.C2 Impulse propagation refers to the movement of electrical impulses through the heart’s conduction system and myocardial tissue. Once an electrical impulse is generated—typically by the SA node—it must travel rapidly and efficiently through cardiac tissue to stimulate the atria and ventricles in a coordinated manner. This organized spread of electrical activity allows the heart to contract sequentially and pump blood effectively. Without proper impulse propagation: ●       Cardiac contraction becomes uncoordinated ●       Blood flow becomes inefficient ●       Arrhythmias may develop ●       Cardiac output decreases Impulse propagation is one of the most important processes in cardiac electrophysiology because it links electrical impulse generation with mechanical pumping. Subtopic 1: How Electrical Impulses Travel Through the Heart Cardiac muscle cells are electrically connected to each other, allowing impulses to spread from one cell to the next. When one cardiac cell depolarizes: ●       Positive ions enter the cell ●       This changes the electrical charge of that cell ●       Adjacent cells detect this change ●       Electrical current spreads to neighboring cells ●       Neighboring cells depolarize in sequence This process continues until the electrical impulse has spread through the heart. Unlike nerve conduction, where impulses travel along isolated nerve fibers, cardiac conduction spreads: Cell-to-cell through interconnected myocardial tissue Subtopic 2: Role of Gap Junctions Cardiac cells are connected by specialized structures called gap junctions. Gap junctions are: ●       Tiny channels between adjacent cardiac cells ●       Located in intercalated discs ●       Allow ions and electrical current to pass directly between cells Function of gap junctions: ●       Facilitate rapid electrical communication ●       Allow myocardium to function as a single unit Because of gap junctions: The heart behaves like a functional syncytium, meaning many cells contract together as one coordinated muscle. Without gap junctions: ●       Electrical conduction would be interrupted ●       Myocardial contraction would be disorganized Subtopic 3: Functional Syncytium A syncytium refers to a group of cells that function together as a coordinated unit. The heart has two major syncytia: Atrial Syncytium Includes: ●       Right and left atrial myocardium Ventricular Syncytium Includes: ●       Right and left ventricular myocardium These are separated electrically by the fibrous cardiac skeleton, meaning: ●       Impulses cannot travel directly from atria to ventricles ●       They must pass through the AV node and Bundle of His Subtopic 4: Conduction Velocity Conduction velocity refers to the speed at which electrical impulses travel through cardiac tissue. Different cardiac tissues conduct at different speeds: Tissue Approximate Velocity SA Node Slow AV Node Very Slow Atrial Muscle Moderate Bundle Branches Fast Purkinje Fibers Very Fast Subtopic 5: Why Conduction Speed Varies Different conduction speeds serve different purposes. Slow Conduction in AV Node Purpose: ●       Creates AV delay ●       Allows ventricular filling before contraction Fast Conduction in Purkinje System Purpose: ●       Enables synchronized ventricular activation ●       Ensures efficient contraction Thus: Conduction speed is physiologically optimized for heart efficiency. Subtopic 6: Direction of Impulse Propagation The normal direction of impulse propagation is: 1.    SA Node 2.    Atria 3.    AV Node 4.    Bundle of His 5.    Bundle Branches 6.    Purkinje Fibers 7.    Ventricular Myocardium This organized sequence ensures: ●       Top-to-bottom activation ●       Sequential contraction ●       Efficient pumping Subtopic 7: Conduction Through Myocardium vs Specialized Tissue Impulse conduction differs between: Specialized Conduction Tissue Examples: ●       SA node ●       AV node ●       Purkinje system Characteristics: ●       Fast, organized conduction ●       Designed for electrical transmission   Myocardial Tissue Characteristics: ●       Slower conduction ●       Primarily contractile function Subtopic 8: Abnormal Impulse Propagation If impulse propagation is disrupted: ●       Conduction delays occur ●       Blocks may develop ●       Arrhythmias may result Causes include: ●       Ischemia ●       Scar tissue ●       Fibrosis ●       Electrolyte imbalance ●       Structural heart disease Subtopic 9: Reentry and Abnormal Propagation Abnormal propagation may lead to: Reentry Circuits Reentry occurs when: ●       Electrical impulse re-circulates abnormally ●       Continuously reactivates myocardium Can cause: ●       SVT ●       VT ●       AF This is one of the most common mechanisms of arrhythmia. Subtopic 10: Impulse Propagation and Device Therapy Cardiac devices depend heavily on understanding propagation. Pacemakers Deliver impulse to initiate propagation. CRT Devices Correct abnormal ventricular propagation. ICDs Detects abnormal conduction/arrhythmias. EP Mapping Systems Analyze impulse propagation pathways.

Topic: Topic 2.2.4: Refractory Periods and Excitability

Topic Description: Topic 2.2.4: Refractory Periods and Excitability

Heading: 2.2.4.H1 Learning Objective

2.2.4.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define refractory period and explain its role in cardiac electrophysiology. ●       Differentiate between absolute refractory period, relative refractory period, and effective refractory period. ●       Explain the concept of cardiac excitability and myocardial responsiveness to electrical stimulation. ●       Understand how refractory periods prevent abnormal repetitive contraction and arrhythmias. ●       Relate refractory period concepts to pacing, sensing, ICD therapy, and arrhythmia mechanisms. ●       Apply refractory period knowledge in device programming and troubleshooting. 2.2.4.H2 Explanation 2.2.4.C2 The heart is designed to contract in a rhythmic, organized pattern. After each electrical impulse and contraction, the cardiac cells need time to recover before they can respond to another electrical stimulus. This recovery time is known as the refractory period. The refractory period is one of the most important protective mechanisms in cardiac electrophysiology because it prevents the heart from being stimulated continuously or contracting in an uncontrolled manner. Without refractory periods, the myocardium could respond to repeated rapid impulses without relaxation, leading to ineffective pumping and life-threatening arrhythmias. Closely related to the refractory period is the concept of excitability, which refers to the ability of cardiac cells to respond to an electrical stimulus and generate an action potential. Excitability changes throughout the cardiac cycle depending on whether the cell is in a refractory or recovered state. Understanding refractory periods and excitability is essential in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, and electrophysiology studies all rely heavily on these principles for sensing, pacing, and arrhythmia detection. Subtopic 1: What Is a Refractory Period? A refractory period is the period of time after a cardiac cell has depolarized during which it is unable or less able to respond to another electrical stimulus. In simple terms: After a heart cell fires, it must “reset” before it can fire again. Purpose: ●       Allows proper recovery of ion channels ●       Prevents repeated immediate stimulation ●       Ensures organized rhythmic contraction Without refractory periods: ●       Cardiac cells could fire continuously ●       Heart would lose pumping efficiency Subtopic 2: Why Refractory Periods Are Necessary Refractory periods serve several critical functions: Prevent Tetanic Contraction Unlike skeletal muscle, the heart cannot remain continuously contracted. Maintain Rhythmic Pumping Allows relaxation between beats. Prevent Premature Reactivation Stops one impulse from immediately retriggering the myocardium. Protect Against Dangerous Arrhythmias Reduces likelihood of uncontrolled repetitive firing. Thus: Refractory periods are essential for normal heart rhythm and survival. Subtopic 3: Absolute Refractory Period (ARP) The Absolute Refractory Period is the period during which no new electrical stimulus—no matter how strong—can trigger another action potential. Occurs because: ●       Sodium channels are inactivated ●       Cell cannot depolarize again Timing: ●       Begins during depolarization ●       Continues through most of repolarization Clinical Importance: ●       Prevents immediate reactivation of myocardium ●       Maintains one contraction per beat Subtopic 4: Relative Refractory Period (RRP) The Relative Refractory Period occurs after the absolute refractory period. During this phase: ●       Some ion channels recover ●       A stronger-than-normal stimulus may trigger depolarization Characteristics: ●       Cell is partially excitable ●       Response threshold is elevated Clinical Significance: ●       Premature beats may occur here ●       Vulnerable period for arrhythmia initiation Subtopic 5: Effective Refractory Period (ERP) The Effective Refractory Period is the time during which a stimulus may depolarize the cell locally but cannot generate a propagated response. This means: ●       Electrical activity may begin ●       But cannot spread effectively to neighboring cells Importance: ●       Critical in arrhythmia prevention ●       Used in EP studies and antiarrhythmic drug evaluation Subtopic 6: Vulnerable Period A particularly dangerous time occurs late in repolarization: Vulnerable Period This is when: ●       Some cells are recovered ●       Others remain refractory If a premature impulse occurs here: ●       Dangerous arrhythmias may develop Examples: ●       Ventricular tachycardia ●       Ventricular fibrillation This corresponds to: Peak/downslope of T wave on ECG Subtopic 7: What Is Excitability? Excitability is the ability of cardiac cells to respond to an electrical stimulus. For a cell to be excitable: ●       Membrane must be recovered ●       Ion channels must be functional ●       Stimulus must exceed threshold Excitability varies depending on: ●       Phase of action potential ●       Refractory status ●       Electrolyte balance Subtopic 8: Factors Affecting Excitability Excitability may increase or decrease based on: Electrolyte Imbalance ●       Hyperkalemia ●       Hypokalemia Ischemia Damaged myocardium less excitable. Medications Antiarrhythmics alter excitability. Scar Tissue Reduces response capability. Fibrosis Disrupts electrical responsiveness. Subtopic 9: Refractory Period and Arrhythmias Abnormal refractory periods contribute to arrhythmia development. Too short: ●       Allows rapid reactivation ●       Promotes tachyarrhythmias Too long: ●       Causes conduction delay ●       May predispose to torsades/QT issues Uneven refractory periods: ●       Promote reentry circuits   Subtopic 10: Device Relevance of Refractory Periods Refractory periods are crucial in device programming. Pacemaker Refractory Periods Prevent oversensing of: ●       T waves ●       Retrograde P waves ●       Noise ICD Detection Algorithms Analyze refractory timing during tachyarrhythmias. EP Studies Measure refractory periods for arrhythmia assessment. ATP Therapy Times pacing based on refractory periods. Subtopic 11: Pacemaker Refractory Programming Pacemakers include programmable refractory periods: Examples: ●       Post-Ventricular Atrial Refractory Period (PVARP) ●       Ventricular Refractory Period (VRP) Purpose: ●       Prevent inappropriate sensing ●       Avoid pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

Heading: 2.2.4.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

2.2.4.C3 Term Definition Refractory Period Recovery time after depolarization Absolute Refractory Period No reactivation possible Relative Refractory Period Strong stimulus may reactivate Excitability Ability to respond to stimulus Vulnerable Period High-risk arrhythmogenic recovery phase Refractory Period Diagram 6     Clinical Pearl Refractory periods protect the heart from electrical chaos. ●        They prevent repeated uncontrolled stimulation. ●        Absolute refractory period ensures one contraction per beat. ●        Relative refractory period is vulnerable to ectopy. ●        T wave corresponds to ventricular repolarization/vulnerable period. ●        Premature beats during vulnerable period may trigger VT/VF. ●        Many antiarrhythmics prolong refractory periods. ●        Device refractory settings prevent inappropriate sensing. ●        EP studies assess refractory periods to induce arrhythmias safely. Device Relevance Understanding refractory periods is essential for: Pacemaker Programming Preventing oversensing and inappropriate inhibition. ICD Therapy Optimizing tachyarrhythmia detection. EP Lab Mapping Determining arrhythmia inducibility. Anti-Tachycardia Pacing Timing therapy delivery correctly.

Topic: Topic 3.1.1: ECG Basics

Topic Description: • Purpose of ECG • ECG as a recording of cardiac electrical activity • Use of ECG in rhythm interpretation • Relationship between ECG findings and heart rhythm

Heading: 3.1.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.1.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define an electrocardiogram (ECG). ●       Explain how ECG signals are generated. ●       Understand what an ECG measures and what it does not measure. ●       Identify common clinical uses of ECG. ●       Recognize why ECG interpretation is essential in pacemaker therapy.   3.1.1.H2 Explanation 3.1.1.C2 An electrocardiogram (ECG), also written as EKG, is a graphic recording of the heart’s electrical activity detected from the body surface using skin electrodes. It is one of the most widely used diagnostic tools in medicine because it is fast, non-invasive, inexpensive, and highly valuable in assessing rhythm and conduction abnormalities. In simple terms: ECG = A tracing that shows how electrical impulses move through the heart. Every heartbeat begins with an electrical signal. This signal starts in the sinoatrial (SA) node, spreads through the atria, pauses briefly in the atrioventricular (AV) node, then travels through the His-Purkinje system to activate the ventricles. As this wave of electrical activation moves through the myocardium, it creates small voltage differences that can be detected by electrodes placed on the skin. These signals are amplified and displayed as waveforms on ECG paper or a digital screen. Why the Heart Produces Electrical Signals The heart is a specialized muscular organ that contracts rhythmically. For contraction to occur in an organized way, the muscle cells must be activated electrically in the correct sequence. Normal sequence: SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → right/left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles This coordinated activation ensures: ●       Atria contract first to fill ventricles ●       Ventricles contract next to pump blood out ●       Heart rate adapts to body needs What an ECG Measures The ECG records electrical timing and direction, not direct mechanical pumping force. It helps evaluate: 1. Heart Rate ●       Bradycardia (slow) ●       Normal rate ●       Tachycardia (fast) 2. Rhythm ●       Sinus rhythm ●       Atrial fibrillation ●       Flutter ●       Paced rhythm ●       Ventricular arrhythmias 3. Conduction ●       AV block ●       Bundle branch block ●       Pre-excitation ●       Delayed intraventricular conduction 4. Chamber Activation Patterns May suggest hypertrophy or enlargement. 5. Ischemia / Injury Clues ST segment and T wave changes may indicate acute or chronic coronary syndromes. 6. Pacemaker Performance ●       Pacing spikes ●       Capture ●       Sensing issues ●       Mode behavior clues What an ECG Does NOT Measure Directly An ECG does not directly tell you: ●       Ejection fraction ●       Valve anatomy ●       Chamber pressures ●       Coronary blockage severity alone ●       Exact stroke volume ●       Mechanical contractile strength These require other tools such as echocardiography, imaging, or catheterization. Electrical vs Mechanical Function The ECG may show organized electrical rhythm, but the patient may still have poor circulation (e.g., shock or pulseless electrical activity). Therefore: Good ECG rhythm ≠ always good circulation. Always correlate ECG with: ●       Symptoms ●       Pulse ●       Blood pressure ●       Oxygenation ●       Clinical status Standard ECG Components A normal ECG waveform usually includes: ●       P wave = atrial depolarization ●       PR interval = AV conduction time ●       QRS complex = ventricular depolarization ●       T wave = ventricular repolarization Pictorial representation P wave -   PR Interval   QRS Complex     T Wave     Types of ECG Monitoring 12-Lead ECG Diagnostic standard used in clinics/hospitals. Rhythm Strip / Telemetry Continuous monitoring. Holter Monitor 24–48 hour ambulatory recording. Event Recorder Intermittent longer-term monitoring. Device Electrograms Signals stored by pacemakers/ICDs. Visual Hint    

Heading: 3.1.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

3.1.1.C3 Term Definition ECG Recording of heart electrical activity Electrode Skin sensor detecting voltage Depolarization Electrical activation of cells Repolarization Recovery to resting state Capture Successful paced depolarization Clinical Pearl ●       ECG is often the first cardiac test obtained. ●       A normal ECG does not exclude all heart disease. ●       Symptoms must guide urgency, not tracing alone. ●       ECG is central in bradycardia evaluation. ●       Device follow-up often begins with rhythm strip review. ●       Serial ECGs may reveal evolving disease. ●       Artifact can mimic arrhythmia. ●       Always check patient before trusting monitor alarms.

Topic: Topic 3.1.2: ECG Paper, Grid, Speed & Calibration

Topic Description: Topic 3.1.2: ECG Paper, Grid, Speed & Calibration

Heading: 3.1.2.H1 Learning Objective

3.1.2.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Describe the structure of ECG paper and grid lines. ●       Analysing an ECG strip for Rhythm diseases ●       Calculate heart rate and intervals from ECG strip. ●       Apply these principles to rhythm diagnosis and pacemaker analysis. 3.1.2.H2 Explanation 3.1.2.C2 The ECG tracing is displayed on a standardized graph paper or digital grid that allows clinicians to measure time, voltage, and rhythm intervals accurately. Understanding ECG paper is one of the first practical skills in ECG interpretation. In simple terms: ECG paper = A ruler for heart electricity. Without knowing paper speed and calibration, even experienced users can misinterpret: ●       Heart rate ●       PR interval ●       QRS duration ●       QT interval ●       Pacemaker timing ●       Rhythm regularity This topic is especially important for cardiac device specialists because pacing cycles, AV delays, escape rhythms, and sensing behavior often require precise measurement. Basic Layout of ECG Paper The ECG grid has: ●       Small boxes ●       Large boxes (5 small boxes together) ●       Horizontal axis = time ●       Vertical axis = voltage/amplitude The grid may be printed red or gray, but the scale remains standardized. Horizontal Axis = Time At the standard ECG recording speed of 25 mm/sec: One Small Box = 0.04 seconds = 40 milliseconds One Large Box (5 small boxes) = 0.20 seconds = 200 milliseconds Five Large Boxes = 1 second This is the basis for measuring intervals and heart rate.     Measuring Heart Rate Heart Rate refers to Ventricular Rate is the number of heartbeats or R-R cycles that occur in one minute e.g. if 60 R-R cycles occur in a minute, Rate=60bpm   •The period of each R-R Cycle is called an R-R interval and its duration is specified in milliseconds •There are 60 X 1000 milliseconds in a minute •Rate = No. of R-R cycles in 60000 ms •Rate = 60000/duration of each R-R cycle in ms   Method 1: Small Box Method HR=1500small boxes between R wavesHR = \frac{1500}{\text{small boxes between R waves}}HR=small boxes between R waves1500​ More precise for regular rhythms. Example R-R Interval = 5 boxes = 5 X 200 ms = 1000ms Rate = 60000/R-R Interval = 60000/1000 = 60 bpm     Method 2: Large Box Method (Regular Rhythm) HR=300large boxes between R wavesHR = \frac{300}{\text{large boxes between R waves}}HR=large boxes between R waves300​ Examples:   Method 3: 6-Second Method (Irregular Rhythm) Count QRS complexes in 30 large boxes (6 seconds), then multiply by 10. Useful in atrial fibrillation.     Measuring Common Intervals PR Interval Start of P wave to start of QRS. Normal: ●       120–200 ms ●       3 to 5 small boxes QRS Duration Beginning to end of QRS. Usually: ●       <120 ms QT Interval Start of QRS to end of T wave. Must be corrected for heart rate (QTc). Heart Rate measurement exercises     3.1.2.H3 Pacemaker Relevance 3.1.2.C3 Accurate grid interpretation helps identify: ●       Programmed lower pacing rate ●       AV delay timing ●       Atrial paced to ventricular paced intervals ●       Failure to capture ●       Undersensing pauses ●       Oversensing inhibition ●       Fusion beats Common Beginner Errors Error 1: Counting Wrong Boxes Confusing small with large boxes. Error 2: Ignoring Speed Intervals misread if speed unknown. Error 3: Ignoring Gain Low voltage may be machine setting, not pathology. Error 4: Measuring from Peak Instead of Onset Use waveform start/end, not tallest point. Digital Monitors Modern ECG monitors may use digital display instead of paper, but the same principles apply: ●       Sweep speed ●       Gain ●       Grid scale Practical Tip for Device Specialists When evaluating pacing spikes: ●       Increase sweep speed if available ●       Use multiple leads ●       Zoom digital strips when possible Memory Aid Horizontal = Time Vertical = Voltage 25 mm/sec = Standard 10 mm = 1 mV Visual Hint (Top 3 Best Images)

3.1.2.C4 Term Definition Gain Vertical signal amplification Sweep Speed Horizontal recording speed Calibration Standard signal marker Interval Time between ECG points RR Interval Distance between consecutive R waves   Clinical Pearl ●       Always check speed and gain first. ●       25 mm/sec is standard routine speed.  ●       Measure from waveform onset and offset. ●       Rate formulas work best in regular rhythm. ●       Irregular rhythms often need 6-second method. ●       Accurate intervals are vital in device clinics.

Topic: Topic 3.2.1: Overview of ECG Components

Topic Description: Topic 3.2.1: Overview of ECG Components

Heading: 3.2.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.2.1.C1 By the end of this section, learners will be able to: ●       Identify all major ECG components in one heartbeat. ●       Explain what each waveform, segment, and interval represents. ●       Relate ECG components to cardiac conduction physiology. ●       Recognize why component analysis is essential in rhythm and pacemaker interpretation. ●       Prepare for detailed subtopics that follow. 3.2.1.H2 Explanation 3.2.1.C2 Every heartbeat recorded on an ECG is made of distinct parts called components. These include waves, segments, and intervals that represent specific electrical events occurring in the atria, AV node, ventricles, and recovery phase. In simple terms: ECG components are the alphabet of ECG interpretation. If learners understand each component individually, they can later interpret: ●       Bradycardia ●       Tachycardia ●       AV block ●       Bundle branch block ●       Ischemia patterns ●       Pacemaker rhythms ●       Drug effects ●       Electrolyte abnormalities A normal heartbeat commonly follows this sequence: P wave → PR interval → QRS complex → ST segment → T wave → QT interval Sometimes a U wave may also be seen. Main ECG Components Overview 1. P Wave Represents atrial depolarization. Meaning: ●       Electrical activation of right and left atria ●       Usually first visible wave in normal sinus rhythm Clinical relevance: ●       Identifies sinus rhythm ●       Detects atrial enlargement ●       Helps diagnose AF/flutter ●       Important for atrial sensing/pacing 2. PR Interval Measured from start of P wave to start of QRS. Represents: ●       Atrial depolarization + AV nodal conduction delay + His conduction time Normal approx: ●       120–200 ms Clinical relevance: ●       Long PR = first-degree AV block ●       Variable PR = Wenckebach possibility ●       Short PR = pre-excitation possibility 3. QRS Complex Represents ventricular depolarization. Usually largest waveform. Normal width: ●       Typically <120 ms Clinical relevance: ●       Wide QRS = BBB / ventricular origin / pacing ●       Narrow QRS = supraventricular conduction usually 4. ST Segment Begins at end of QRS (J point) and ends at start of T wave. Represents early ventricular recovery phase. Normally near baseline. Clinical relevance: ●       ST elevation may suggest acute injury pattern ●       ST depression may suggest ischemia or demand mismatch 5. T Wave Represents ventricular repolarization. Usually upright in many leads. Clinical relevance: ●       Inversion may indicate ischemia or strain ●       Tall peaked T may suggest hyperkalemia 6. QT Interval Measured from start of QRS to end of T wave. Represents total ventricular electrical activation + recovery. Changes with heart rate. Clinical relevance: ●       Long QT increases risk of dangerous arrhythmia ●       Drug safety monitoring important 7. U Wave (Occasional) Small wave after T wave. May be normal or more visible in: ●       Bradycardia ●       Hypokalemia Waves vs Segments vs Intervals Waves Visible deflections. Examples: ●       P ●       QRS ●       T Segments Flat portions between waves. Examples: ●       PR segment ●       ST segment Intervals Include waves + segments. Examples: ●       PR interval ●       QT interval Why ECG Components Matter in Pacemaker Patients P Wave Needed for atrial sensing. PR Interval Relevant to AV synchrony. QRS Used to assess ventricular pacing morphology. ST/T Can be altered after pacing; interpret carefully. QT May be relevant in drugs and bradycardia patients.   Quick Memory Sequence P → PR → QRS → ST → T → QT Think: ●       Atria start ●       Delay ●       Ventricles activate ●       Plateau ●       Recover ●       Total ventricular time Common Beginner Errors ●       Confusing PR interval with PR segment ●       Calling T wave a P wave ●       Missing wide paced QRS ●       Measuring QT incorrectly ●       Ignoring hidden P waves Visual Hint (Top 3 Best Images) 5

Topic: Topic 3.3.1: P Wave

Topic Description: • Represents atrial depolarization • Used to assess atrial activity • Important for rhythm identification

Heading: 3.3.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.3.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the P wave and explain how it is generated. ●       Identify normal P-wave characteristics. ●       Recognize common abnormal P-wave patterns. ●       Use P-wave analysis for rhythm diagnosis. ●       Apply P-wave concepts in pacemaker patients. 3.3.1.H2 Explanation 3.3.1.C2 The P wave is the ECG waveform that represents atrial depolarization—the electrical activation of the right and left atria before they contract. In simple terms: P wave = The signal that tells the atria to beat. It is usually the first visible component of a normal heartbeat and provides important information about where the rhythm starts and how atrial activation is occurring. For beginners, the P wave is one of the most valuable rhythm clues. For cardiac device professionals, it is essential because many pacemakers sense or pace the atria. How the P Wave Is Generated Normal atrial activation begins in the sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the upper right atrium near the superior vena cava. The impulse spreads in sequence: 1.    Through the right atrium 2.    Across interatrial conduction pathways (including Bachmann’s bundle) 3.    Into the left atrium 4.    Toward the AV node This coordinated electrical movement creates the surface P wave seen on ECG. Because the right atrium activates slightly before the left atrium, the P wave reflects the combined depolarization of both atria. Why the P Wave Matters P-wave analysis helps determine: ●       Is rhythm sinus or non-sinus? ●       Is atrial activity present? ●       Is there AV association with QRS? ●       Is atrial enlargement possible? ●       Is atrial pacing occurring? ●       Is atrial fibrillation/flutter present? Normal P-Wave Characteristics In normal sinus rhythm, the P wave is commonly: ●       Present before each QRS complex ●       Uniform in shape beat-to-beat ●       Upright in Lead II ●       Upright in Leads I and aVF (commonly) ●       Negative in aVR ●       Smooth and rounded ●       Duration usually <120 ms ●       Amplitude often <2.5 mm in inferior leads Best Leads to Assess the P Wave Lead II Often the clearest lead for P-wave visibility. V1 Helpful for biphasic P-wave analysis and atrial abnormality clues. aVR Normally negative P wave in sinus rhythm. P Wave and Sinus Rhythm A rhythm is likely sinus when: ●       P wave before every QRS ●       Each P followed by QRS ●       Stable PR interval ●       Consistent P-wave morphology ●       Expected axis (upright in II, negative in aVR) Abnormal P-Wave Patterns 1. No Visible P Waves May occur in: ●       Atrial fibrillation ●       Junctional rhythm ●       Hidden P waves in tachycardia ●       Artifact obscuring signal 2. Inverted P Waves May suggest: ●       Low atrial rhythm ●       Junctional rhythm ●       Retrograde atrial activation If P waves are inverted in Lead II, think non-sinus origin. 3. Tall Peaked P Waves May suggest right atrial enlargement. Historically called P pulmonale. Possible causes: ●       Pulmonary hypertension ●       COPD ●       Tricuspid disease 4. Broad / Notched P Waves May suggest left atrial abnormality. Historically called P mitrale. Possible causes: ●       Mitral valve disease ●       Hypertension ●       Diastolic dysfunction 5. Changing P-Wave Shape May suggest: ●       Wandering atrial pacemaker ●       Multifocal atrial rhythm Different atrial foci produce different morphologies. Hidden or Difficult P Waves P waves may be concealed: ●       Inside preceding T wave ●       Within QRS complex ●       During rapid SVT ●       During ventricular pacing Use multiple leads and slower sweep speed if available. P Wave Relationship to PR Interval The P wave marks atrial depolarization, but the PR interval includes: ●       P-wave duration ●       AV nodal delay ●       His conduction time Thus P wave alone does not assess AV conduction fully. P Waves in Atrial Arrhythmias Atrial Fibrillation No organized P waves. Chaotic baseline. Atrial Flutter Sawtooth flutter waves instead of normal P waves. Atrial Tachycardia Abnormal but organized atrial waves. Pacemaker Relevance Atrial Sensing Pacemaker detects intrinsic P waves. Atrial Pacing Pacing spike before atrial depolarization. Dual-Chamber Tracking P waves may trigger ventricular pacing after AV delay in tracking modes. Atrial Undersensing Intrinsic P waves missed. Oversensing Noise mistaken as atrial activity. Clinical Examples Example 1 Rate 52 bpm, upright P before every QRS → Likely sinus bradycardia Example 2 Irregular rhythm, no organized P waves → Likely atrial fibrillation Example 3 Spike before P wave, then QRS later → Atrial paced rhythm Common Beginner Errors ●       Calling every baseline bump a P wave ●       Ignoring Lead II ●       Diagnosing AF without checking artifact ●       Missing retrograde P waves ●       Forgetting P-QRS relationship Practical 5-Step P-Wave Check 1.    Is a P wave present? 2.    Is it before each QRS? 3.    Is morphology consistent? 4.    Upright in Lead II? 5.    Is PR relationship logical? Memory Aid P = Precedes QRS in sinus rhythm P = Atrial Pacemaker clue Visual Hint

Heading: 3.3.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

3.3.1.C3 Term Definition P Wave Atrial depolarization Sinus Rhythm Rhythm originating from SA node Atrial Sensing Detection of intrinsic atrial signal Retrograde P Wave Atrial activation from below upward Flutter Wave Rapid organized atrial waveform Clinical Pearl ●       Lead II often best shows P waves. ●       No visible P wave does not always mean AF. ●       Inverted P in Lead II suggests non-sinus origin. ●       P-wave shape can hint at atrial enlargement. ●       Atrial pacing spikes may be subtle. ●       Hidden P waves are common in SVT. ●       P-QRS relationship is often more useful than P wave alone. ●       Accurate atrial sensing is key in dual-chamber pacing.

Topic: Topic 3.4.1: QRS Complex

Topic Description: o Represents ventricular depolarization o Used to assess ventricular activation o Important for identifying conduction abnormalities o QRS width: narrow vs wide QRS rhythm identification

Heading: 3.4.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.4.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the QRS complex and explain what it represents. ●       Identify normal QRS morphology and duration. ●       Differentiate narrow vs wide QRS complexes. ●       Recognize common causes of abnormal QRS patterns. ●       Apply QRS analysis in pacemaker patients. 3.4.1.H2 Explanation 3.4.1.C2 The QRS complex is the ECG waveform that represents ventricular depolarization, meaning the electrical activation of the right and left ventricles before they contract. In simple terms: QRS = Signal telling the ventricles to pump. Because the ventricles are larger muscle chambers than the atria, the QRS complex is usually the largest and most prominent waveform on the ECG. It is one of the most clinically valuable ECG components because it helps assess: ●       Ventricular conduction speed ●       Origin of rhythm ●       Bundle branch blocks ●       Ventricular arrhythmias ●       Pacemaker capture ●       Chamber activation synchrony How the QRS Complex Is Generated After the impulse passes through the AV node, it travels rapidly through: 1.    His bundle 2.    Right bundle branch 3.    Left bundle branch 4.    Purkinje network 5.    Ventricular myocardium Rapid organized activation produces a relatively narrow QRS in healthy conduction systems. Components of the QRS Complex Q Wave First negative deflection before any positive wave. R Wave First positive deflection. S Wave Negative deflection after an R wave. Not every QRS contains all three parts. Examples: ●       R only ●       RS ●       qR ●       rSr' ●       QS Normal QRS Duration At standard ECG speed: Normal: QRS<120 msQRS < 120\text{ ms}QRS<120 ms Equivalent: ●       Less than 3 small boxes A narrow QRS usually means ventricular activation is using the normal His-Purkinje system. Why QRS Width Matters Narrow QRS Usually indicates: ●       Supraventricular origin with normal ventricular conduction ●       Sinus rhythm ●       Atrial fibrillation with intact conduction ●       SVT (often narrow) Wide QRS May indicate: ●       Bundle branch block ●       Ventricular rhythm ●       Ventricular pacing ●       Hyperkalemia ●       Pre-excitation ●       Nonspecific intraventricular delay QRS Morphology Basics The shape of the QRS depends on: ●       Lead viewed ●       Conduction pathway used ●       Ventricular origin of beat ●       Presence of scar ●       Pacing site Thus the same beat looks different in V1 vs V6. R-Wave Progression (Chest Leads) Normally across V1 to V6: ●       Small R in V1 ●       Increasing R through V3/V4 ●       Larger R in V5/V6 Poor progression may occur in: ●       Prior anterior MI ●       Lead misplacement ●       LVH ●       RV pacing Pathologic Q Waves Deep or wide Q waves in certain leads may suggest prior myocardial infarction or scar. Clinical correlation required. Common Wide QRS Causes 1. Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) Delayed RV activation. Often rsR' in V1. 2. Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) Delayed LV activation. Broad QRS with characteristic lateral changes. 3. Ventricular Tachycardia Wide-complex tachycardia often presumed VT until proven otherwise. 4. Ventricular Pacing Pacing spike followed by wide QRS.   Pacemaker Relevance Ventricular Capture Spike followed by wide QRS indicates paced depolarization. RV Apical Pacing Often creates LBBB-like morphology. CRT / Biventricular Pacing May narrow QRS compared with intrinsic LBBB. Loss of Capture Spike without resulting QRS. Fusion Beats Part intrinsic, part paced QRS. QRS in Tachycardia Interpretation When fast rhythm occurs: Narrow Complex Tachycardia Usually supraventricular. Wide Complex Tachycardia Could be: ●       VT ●       SVT with aberrancy ●       Paced rhythm Clinical caution required. Common Beginner Errors ●       Thinking all wide QRS = VT ●       Missing pacing spike before wide QRS ●       Measuring from peak instead of onset/offset ●       Ignoring lead placement artifact ●       Calling BBB based on one lead only Practical QRS Review Method Ask: 1.    Is QRS narrow or wide? 2.    Is rhythm fast or slow? 3.    Is pacing spike present? 4.    Is morphology consistent? 5.    Is this new vs old ECG? Clinical Examples Example 1 Sinus rhythm, QRS 90 ms → Normal narrow complex conduction Example 2 Rate 160, wide regular QRS → Treat as VT until proven otherwise   Example 3 Pacing spike then wide QRS → Ventricular pacing capture Example 4 Intrinsic LBBB, CRT pacing narrows QRS → Improved synchrony clue Memory Aid P = Atria QRS = Ventricles Wide = Slow/Abnormal pathway Visual Hint  

Heading: 3.4.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

3.4.1.C3 Term Definition QRS Complex Ventricular depolarization Narrow QRS <120 ms ventricular activation Wide QRS ≥120 ms delayed/abnormal activation Bundle Branch Block Delay in right or left bundle conduction Capture Successful paced depolarization   Clinical Pearl ●       QRS width is one of the fastest ECG clues. ●       Narrow QRS often means supraventricular conduction. ●       Wide tachycardia should be treated cautiously as VT. ●       Ventricular pacing normally widens QRS. ●       RV pacing often mimics LBBB morphology. ●       Compare paced vs intrinsic QRS when possible. ●       Measure onset to end, not peak to peak. ●       New wide QRS may be clinically important.

Topic: Topic 3.5.1: T Wave

Topic Description: • Represents repolarization • Used to assess ventricular recovery phase • Important in rhythm and ECG interpretation

Heading: 3.5.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.5.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the T wave and explain what it represents. ●       Identify normal T-wave morphology. ●       Recognize common abnormal T-wave patterns. ●       Understand clinical causes of T-wave changes. ●       Apply T-wave interpretation in paced rhythms and device patients. 3.5.1.H2 Explanation 3.5.1.C2 The T wave is the ECG waveform that represents ventricular repolarization, meaning the electrical recovery of ventricular muscle cells after depolarization and contraction. In simple terms: T wave = The ventricles resetting for the next beat. After the QRS complex activates the ventricles, the ventricular myocardium must recover electrically before the next heartbeat can occur. This recovery process generates the T wave. Although often less dramatic than the QRS complex, the T wave can provide major clues regarding: ●       Ischemia ●       Electrolyte abnormalities ●       Drug effects ●       Conduction abnormalities ●       CNS stress responses ●       Secondary changes after pacing or bundle branch block Why the T Wave Appears Upright in Many Leads Depolarization and repolarization move through the ventricles differently. Because of these electrical properties, the T wave is often upright in many leads where the QRS is upright. This is normal physiology. Normal T-Wave Characteristics A normal T wave is commonly: ●       Smooth and asymmetric ●       Rounded contour ●       Concordant with QRS in many leads (same general direction) ●       Upright in Leads I, II, V3–V6 commonly ●       Variable in V1 ●       Negative in aVR commonly Amplitude varies by lead and individual. Why T Waves Matter Clinically T-wave abnormalities may be early or subtle markers of disease. They can reflect disturbances in repolarization caused by: ●       Reduced blood flow ●       Electrolyte imbalance ●       Structural heart disease ●       Medications ●       Wide QRS conduction patterns Common Abnormal T-Wave Patterns 1. T-Wave Inversion The T wave becomes negative in leads where upright is expected. Possible causes: ●       Ischemia ●       Prior infarction changes ●       Ventricular strain ●       CNS events ●       Post-tachycardia memory changes ●       Bundle branch block / pacing secondary changes 2. Tall Peaked T Waves Narrow, tented, prominent T waves may suggest: ●       Hyperkalemia This can be clinically urgent. 3. Flat T Waves Low-amplitude T waves may be seen with: ●       Hypokalemia ●       Nonspecific changes ●       Medications ●       Ischemia 4. Biphasic T Waves Part positive and part negative. May occur in: ●       Ischemia patterns ●       Electrolyte disorders ●       Nonspecific repolarization changes 5. Hyperacute T Waves Broad, large T waves may appear early in acute coronary occlusion before obvious ST elevation. Clinical context important. T-Wave Changes in Ischemia T-wave abnormalities may precede or accompany ST changes. Examples: ●       Symmetric inversion ●       Hyperacute broad T waves ●       Dynamic changes over time Serial ECG comparison is valuable. T Waves and Electrolytes Hyperkalemia ●       Tall peaked T waves ●       Widening QRS later if severe Hypokalemia ●       Flattened T waves ●       Prominent U waves ●       Arrhythmia risk T Waves in Bundle Branch Block and Pacing Wide QRS rhythms often produce secondary repolarization changes. Example: RV Pacing Wide paced QRS may show T wave opposite the major QRS direction. Example: LBBB Discordant ST-T patterns can be expected. Therefore not every abnormal T wave means ischemia. Pacemaker Relevance Device professionals should know: ●       Ventricular pacing commonly alters T-wave appearance. ●       Compare paced ECG to prior paced ECG. ●       Sudden major new changes with symptoms require escalation. ●       Electrolyte disturbances can affect paced and intrinsic rhythms alike. T-Wave Memory After periods of pacing or tachycardia, T waves may remain altered temporarily even after normal conduction resumes. This is sometimes called cardiac memory. Common Beginner Errors ●       Calling all inverted T waves ischemia ●       Ignoring pacing/BBB context ●       Missing hyperkalemic peaked T waves ●       Overreading isolated minor flattening ●       Ignoring dynamic changes over time Practical T-Wave Review Method Ask: 1.    Upright where expected? 2.    Peaked, flat, or inverted? 3.    Symmetric or nonspecific? 4.    Wide QRS / pacing present? 5.    Symptoms or electrolyte issue? Clinical Examples Example 1 Tall peaked T waves in multiple leads → Hyperkalemia concern Example 2 New deep anterior T inversion + chest pain → Ischemic concern Example 3 RV paced rhythm with discordant T waves → May be expected secondary change Memory Aid QRS = Activate T = Recover Visual Hint  

Heading: 3.5.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

3.5.1.C3s Term Definition T Wave Ventricular repolarization T-Wave Inversion Negative T wave where upright expected Hyperacute T Wave Early broad prominent ischemic T wave Secondary Repolarization Change T-wave change due to abnormal depolarization Cardiac Memory Persistent T-wave changes after altered activation Clinical Pearl ●       T-wave changes are common but not always dangerous. ●       Dynamic T-wave changes are more important than static mild abnormalities. ●       Hyperkalemic peaked T waves may be urgent. ●       Pacing and LBBB often distort T waves. ●       Compare with previous ECGs. ●       Symptoms guide significance. ●       Isolated nonspecific flattening is common. ●       Electrolytes can strongly affect repolarization.

Chapter: Chapter 3.6: ECG Measurements

Topic: Topic 3.6.1: PR Interval

Topic Description: • Measurement from atrial depolarization to ventricular activation • Used to assess AV conduction • Important in identifying AV blocks

Heading: 3.6.1.H1 Learning Objective

3.6.1.H1 Learning Objective 3.6.1.C1 By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: ●       Define the PR interval and explain what it represents. ●       Measure the PR interval accurately on ECG. ●       Identify normal and abnormal PR intervals. ●       Recognize common conduction disorders involving the PR interval. ●       Apply PR interval concepts in pacemaker patients. 3.6.1.H2 Explanation 3.6.1.C2s The PR interval is the time measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex. It represents the time taken for the electrical impulse to travel from the atria to the ventricles. In simple terms: PR interval = Time from atrial activation to ventricular activation. This includes: ●       Atrial depolarization ●       Conduction through the AV node ●       Delay in the AV node ●       His bundle conduction ●       Arrival of impulse to ventricular conduction system The PR interval is one of the most clinically important ECG measurements because it reflects atrioventricular (AV) conduction. Why the PR Interval Matters The AV node normally slows conduction briefly. This delay allows: ●       Atria to contract first ●       Ventricles to fill adequately before systole ●       Efficient cardiac output ●       Coordinated timing between chambers Without this delay, filling efficiency may decrease. Where to Measure the PR Interval Measure: ●       From the first visible deflection of the P wave ●       To the first deflection of the QRS complex This could be: ●       Beginning of Q wave ●       Beginning of R wave if no Q wave present Normal PR Interval At standard speed (25 mm/sec): Normal Range: 120 ms  to  200 ms120\text{ ms} \; to \; 200\text{ ms}120 msto200 ms Equivalent to: ●       3 to 5 small boxes What Happens Physiologically During the PR Interval? The impulse travels through: 1.    SA node discharge (already occurred before P wave seen) 2.    Right and left atria 3.    AV node delay 4.    His bundle 5.    Bundle branches (early portion before QRS onset) The AV node contributes the major delay. Short PR Interval A PR interval <120 ms may suggest: 1. Pre-excitation Syndrome Example: accessory pathway conduction (e.g., WPW pattern). 2. Junctional Rhythm Impulse starts near AV junction. 3. Ectopic Atrial Rhythm Near AV Node Shorter distance to ventricles. Prolonged PR Interval PR interval >200 ms suggests delayed AV conduction. Most common cause: First-Degree AV Block Every atrial impulse reaches ventricles, but slowly. Example: P before every QRS, but PR is long. Progressive PR Changes Second-Degree AV Block Type I (Wenckebach) PR progressively lengthens until a QRS is dropped. Variable PR with Conduction Disease Can indicate more advanced pathology. Fixed vs Changing PR Interval Fixed PR Interval Often sinus rhythm or first-degree AV block. Changing PR Interval May suggest: ●       AV block ●       Ectopic rhythms ●       AV dissociation ●       Pacemaker timing behavior PR Interval in Bradycardia A slow rate may mildly lengthen PR in some individuals, especially with increased vagal tone. Seen in: ●       Athletes ●       Sleep ●       Young healthy adults Clinical context matters. PR Interval in Tachycardia At faster heart rates, PR may shorten slightly due to autonomic changes, but persistent abnormalities still need evaluation. Pacemaker Relevance The PR interval is highly relevant in pacing therapy. 1. AV Synchrony Proper atrial-to-ventricular timing improves filling. 2. Dual-Chamber Devices Often track atrial activity and pace ventricles after programmed AV delay. 3. Long Native PR Some symptomatic patients with very prolonged PR may lose hemodynamic efficiency. 4. Device Diagnostics Surface ECG can help assess paced AV timing. Clinical Symptoms of PR Problems Many patients with isolated first-degree AV block are asymptomatic. However, markedly prolonged PR may contribute to: ●       Fatigue ●       Reduced exercise tolerance ●       Palpitations ●       “Pseudo pacemaker syndrome” in some cases Common Beginner Errors ●       Measuring from peak of P wave instead of start ●       Measuring to peak of R wave instead of QRS onset ●       Confusing PR interval with PR segment ●       Ignoring variable PR changes ●       Not checking paper speed Practical Reading Method Ask: 1.    Is there a P before every QRS? 2.    Is PR between 120–200 ms? 3.    Is PR fixed or changing? 4.    Any dropped beats? 5.    Is pacing involved? Clinical Examples Example 1 Regular rhythm, PR = 160 ms → Normal AV conduction Example 2 PR = 260 ms, every P conducts → First-degree AV block Example 3 Progressive PR prolongation then dropped QRS → Wenckebach pattern Example 4 Atrial sensed event followed by paced QRS after delay → Dual-chamber pacing behavior Memory Aid P starts it R receives it PR = Travel time between them Visual Hint  

Heading: 3.6.1.H3 Vocabulary & Key Definitions

3.6.1.C3s Term Definition PR Interval Time from atrial activation to ventricular activation AV Node Electrical gateway between atria and ventricles First-Degree AV Block PR >200 ms with all beats conducted Wenckebach Progressive PR prolongation with dropped beat AV Delay Programmed paced atrial-to-ventricular timing Clinical Pearl ●       PR interval reflects AV conduction, not just AV node alone. ●       First-degree AV block is often benign but context matters. ●       Markedly long PR can reduce AV synchrony. ●       Progressive PR prolongation suggests Wenckebach. ●       Short PR may indicate accessory pathway conduction. ●       Always measure from onset to onset. ●       Check PR in paced rhythms too. ●       Symptoms matter more than numbers alone.

Chapter: Chapter 4.1: Bradyarrhythmia

Topic: Topic 4.1.1: Bradyarrhythmia

Topic Description: • Sinus arrest/ Pause Sinus Bradycardia • Sinus Block • Wandering atrial pacemaker • Premature atrial contraction (PAC) • AV block (First degree, Second degree type 1, Second degree • Type 2 – Mobitz), Third degree – Complete heart block

Heading: Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter introduction, learners will be able to: ● Define cardiac arrhythmia in simple clinical terms. ● Explain how abnormal electrical impulse formation or conduction can disturb normal heartbeat rhythm. ● Differentiate between tachycardia and bradycardia based on heart rate. ● Recognize the main categories of cardiac arrhythmias. ● Explain why arrhythmias may reduce cardiac output. ● Identify common symptoms associated with abnormal heart rhythms. ● Understand why bradyarrhythmias are important in pacemaker and cardiac rhythm management practice. ● Recognize the difference between intrinsic arrhythmia and device-related rhythm behavior. ● Apply a basic rhythm interpretation sequence using rate, regularity, P waves, QRS width, and symptoms. ● Avoid common beginner errors during ECG rhythm interpretation. Chapter Overview Cardiac Arrhythmias Cardiac arrhythmias refer to a group of conditions characterized by an irregular, too fast, or too slow heartbeat. These occur when the electrical impulses that coordinate heartbeats do not function properly, causing the heart to pump blood inefficiently.       1. Classification by Speed Tachycardia: A resting heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm). Bradycardia: A resting heart rate slower than 60 beats per minute. The heart depends on a precise electrical system to maintain an effective pumping rhythm. Under normal conditions, electrical impulses begin in the sinoatrial (SA) node, travel through the atria, pause briefly in the atrioventricular (AV) node, and then spread rapidly through the ventricles. When this electrical system becomes abnormal, the result is called an arrhythmia. In simple terms: Arrhythmia = Any abnormal heart rhythm, abnormal rate, irregular timing, or abnormal impulse conduction. Arrhythmias can be: ●      Too slow (bradyarrhythmias) ●      Too fast (tachyarrhythmias) ●      Irregular ●      Intermittent ●      Life-threatening or benign This chapter is highly relevant in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, CRT systems, and monitoring technologies are all designed to detect or treat rhythm disorders.  Arrhythmias can be: ● Too slow, known as bradyarrhythmias ● Too fast, known as tachyarrhythmias ● Irregular ● Intermittent ● Life-threatening or benign ● Symptomatic or asymptomatic ● Temporary or persistent ● Related to impulse formation or impulse conduction This chapter is highly relevant in cardiac rhythm management because pacemakers, ICDs, CRT systems, and monitoring technologies are all designed to detect or treat rhythm disorders. For pacemaker learners, bradyarrhythmias are especially important because pacemakers are commonly used to support slow or unreliable intrinsic heart rhythms. Why Arrhythmias Matter Abnormal rhythm may reduce cardiac output and cause symptoms such as: ●      Palpitations ●      Dizziness ●      Fatigue ●      Chest discomfort ●      Syncope ●      Shortness of breath ●      Sudden cardiac arrest (certain rhythms) Some arrhythmias are discovered incidentally, while others require urgent treatment. Main Categories of Cardiac Arrhythmias 1. Bradyarrhythmias Slow heart rhythms (heart rate less than 60 bpm) due to: ●      Sinus node dysfunction ●      AV block ●      Escape rhythm failure 2. Tachyarrhythmias Fast heart rhythms (heart rate more than 100 bpm)  such as: ●      Sinus tachycardia ●      SVT ●      Atrial flutter ●      Atrial fibrillation with RVR ●      Ventricular tachycardia   3. Ectopic Rhythms Extra beats from abnormal focus: ●      PACs ●      PVCs 4. Conduction Disorders ●      Bundle branch block ●      Fascicular block ●      AV delay/block Why This Chapter Matters for MedTech / Pacemaker Learners Professionals in cardiac rhythm management must quickly recognize: ●      Symptomatic bradycardia needing pacing ●      AF burden in implanted device patients ●      VT/VF risk rhythms ●      Pacemaker malfunction vs intrinsic arrhythmia ●      Device response to rhythm disorder Core Principle First identify rate, then regularity, then P waves, then QRS width, then symptoms. This is the foundation of rhythm interpretation.   Common Beginner Errors ●      Calling every irregular rhythm AF ●      Missing symptomatic bradycardia ●      Confusing paced rhythm with ventricular tachycardia ●      Ignoring medication causes ●      Focusing on ECG without symptoms

Heading: Vocabulary & Key Definitions

Term Meaning Arrhythmia Abnormal heart rhythm Bradycardia Slow heart rate Tachycardia Fast heart rate Ectopy Premature abnormal beats Conduction Block Delayed or blocked electrical signal     Clinical Pearls: Cardiac Arrhythmia Fundamentals Always treat the patient, not the monitor, because a slow rate is only dangerous if symptomatic. ● Never assume every irregular rhythm is atrial fibrillation without first ruling out hidden P waves. ● P waves are your most critical diagnostic tool for determining rhythm origin and AV relationship. ● Always review the patient’s medication list, as beta-blockers or digoxin frequently cause bradycardia. ● Remember that a wide QRS complex is not always ventricular tachycardia; check for pacing spikes. ● Understand that tachyarrhythmias reduce cardiac output primarily by shortening ventricular filling time. ● Prevent diagnostic errors by strictly using a step-by-step rate, rhythm, P wave, and QRS analysis. ● Recognize that intrinsic ectopic beats directly influence pacemaker sensing, tracking, and mode switching. ● Note that the clinical danger of a sinus pause is heavily influenced by the patient's posture at onset.
