Heading: Battery, Circuitry and Can Design • RF Shielding and Hermetic Seals

Battery, Circuitry and Can Design • RF Shielding and Hermetic Seals 6.2.H1C1 Chapter Learning Objectives By the end of Chapter 6.2, learners will be able to: Define a pacemaker pulse generator. Identify the major external and internal components of a pulse generator. Explain the purpose of the battery, electronic circuitry, connector block and metallic case. Describe how battery energy is converted into controlled pacing pulses. Explain how the pulse generator senses and analyses intrinsic cardiac activity. Identify the major circuits involved in sensing, timing, pacing and telemetry. Explain the relationship between pacing output and battery longevity. Describe the meaning of battery status, recommended replacement time and end of service. Explain the design and functions of the pacemaker can. Differentiate the metallic can from the polymer connector block. Explain how the can may function as part of a unipolar pacing or sensing circuit. Describe the purpose of radiofrequency and electromagnetic shielding. Explain how filters reduce unwanted electromagnetic interference. Describe the function of hermetic seals. Explain how electrical conductors pass through a sealed pulse-generator enclosure. Recognize possible effects of electromagnetic interference on pacemaker operation. Relate pulse-generator design to device reliability, patient safety and follow-up.   6.2.H1C2 Chapter Overview The pulse generator is the central operating unit of a conventional pacemaker system. It contains the energy source and electronic components required to: Sense the heart’s intrinsic electrical activity Analyse cardiac timing Decide whether pacing is required Generate controlled pacing pulses Deliver the pulses through the leads Store diagnostic information Communicate with an external programmer or remote-monitoring system Monitor battery and lead-system performance The pulse generator is implanted under the skin, usually in the pectoral region, and is connected to one or more pacing leads through a connector block. Its internal components must function for many years while remaining protected from: Blood Tissue fluid Moisture Mechanical stress Radiofrequency energy Electromagnetic fields Temperature variation Internal electrical interference This chapter examines two main areas: Topic 6.2.1: Battery, Circuitry and Can Design This topic explains the power source, electronic control systems, pulse generation, sensing circuits, memory, telemetry components and physical construction of the pulse generator. Topic 6.2.2: RF Shielding and Hermetic Seals This topic explains how the pulse generator limits unwanted electromagnetic interference while still permitting intentional telemetry communication. It also explains how the internal electronics are sealed from body fluids. 6.2.H1C3 Core Concept The pulse generator can be understood as a miniature implantable computer with a specialised power source. It performs a continuous sequence: 1.      Receive electrical signals from the heart. 2.      Filter and amplify those signals. 3.      Measure cardiac timing. 4.      Compare the rhythm with programmed criteria. 5.      Decide whether a pacing pulse is required. 6.      Generate the programmed electrical output. 7.      Deliver the output through the appropriate lead. 8.      Confirm and record system behaviour. 9.      Store diagnostic and performance information. 10.                              Communicate with external clinical equipment when interrogated. In simple terms: Battery = provides energy Circuitry = senses, analyses and controls Can = protects the internal components Connector block = connects the pulse generator to the leads Telemetry system = communicates with external equipment IMAGE 6.2-1

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.2.1: BATTERY, CIRCUITRY AND CAN DESIGN

Heading: 6.2.1.H1C1 Learning Objectives

6.2.1.H1C1 Learning Objectives By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: Define the pacemaker pulse generator. Identify the battery, circuitry, connector block and can. Explain the basic operating sequence of a pulse generator. Describe the role of a pacemaker battery. Explain why conventional pacemaker batteries are designed for long-term, low-current operation. Recognize that battery chemistry varies by device model. Identify factors that influence projected battery longevity. Explain how pacing amplitude, pulse width and pacing percentage affect energy use. Describe battery-status monitoring and replacement indicators. Identify the major functional circuits inside a pulse generator. Explain sensing amplification and filtering. Explain timing and decision logic. Describe pacing-output circuitry. Explain the role of memory, diagnostics and stored electrograms. Describe telemetry and remote-monitoring functions. Explain rate-response sensor processing. Describe the purpose of safety and backup circuitry. Define the pacemaker can. Explain why titanium is commonly used for the metallic enclosure. Differentiate the can from the connector block or header. Explain the purpose of feedthrough conductors. Describe how the can may be used as an electrode in unipolar pacing. Relate pulse-generator construction to implantation, replacement and follow-up. 6.2.1.H1C2 Topic Overview The pulse generator contains all the electronic systems needed to monitor and support the patient’s cardiac rhythm. The major components are: Battery Sensing circuitry Timing circuitry Control processor Pacing-output circuitry Memory Diagnostic circuitry Telemetry system Activity or physiologic sensors Safety circuits Connector block Hermetically sealed metallic can The pulse generator must satisfy two competing engineering needs. It must be: Small enough for comfortable implantation Large enough to contain an adequate battery and reliable electronics Powerful enough to deliver pacing therapy Energy-efficient enough to function for years Sensitive enough to detect small cardiac signals Resistant to electrical noise Sealed against body fluids Capable of communicating through the skin   6.2.1.H1C3 Concept and Fundamentals of the Pulse Generator A pulse generator is an implantable device containing a battery and electronic circuitry that controls cardiac pacing and monitoring. The pulse generator does not continuously stimulate the heart without analysing the rhythm. In most programmed pacing modes, it first observes the intrinsic cardiac activity. If the device detects an appropriate natural heartbeat within the programmed timing interval, pacing output may be inhibited. If the expected intrinsic event does not occur, the device may deliver a pacing pulse. The exact response depends on: Programmed pacing mode Lower rate Chamber configuration AV timing Sensing settings Refractory periods Rate-response programming Special algorithms Patient rhythm The pulse generator therefore performs both monitoring and treatment. 6.2.1.H1C4 External Components of a Pulse Generator The major externally visible components include: Metallic can The can is the main metal enclosure that contains the battery and internal electronics. Connector block or header The connector block is usually located on the upper portion of the device and contains the ports into which the lead connector pins are inserted. Connector ports The number and type of ports depend on whether the device is: Single chamber Dual chamber Biventricular Designed for specialised lead configurations Set screws Set screws mechanically and electrically secure the lead connector within the header. Sealing grommets Grommets permit access to the set screws while limiting fluid entry into the connector area. Suture hole A suture hole may be used to secure the pulse generator within the surgical pocket and reduce device migration or rotation. Radiopaque identification Many pulse generators contain radiopaque markings that help identify the manufacturer, model family or device type on imaging. IMAGE 6.2.1-1 6.2.1.H1C5 Internal Components of a Pulse Generator Inside the sealed enclosure are several interconnected systems. These may include: Primary battery cell Voltage-regulation components Sensing amplifiers Band-pass filters Timing circuits Microprocessor or custom integrated circuits Pacing-output circuits Capacitors Memory Telemetry electronics Antenna or communication coil Sensor-processing circuits Protection components Clock or timing reference Safety and reset circuits Feedthrough connections to the header The exact internal design varies between manufacturers and device models. IMAGE 6.2.1-2

Heading: PACEMAKER

  PACEMAKER BATTERY 6.2.1.H2C1 Purpose of the Battery The battery provides the electrical energy required for all pacemaker operations. It supplies power for: Continuous rhythm sensing Signal amplification Timing calculations Microprocessor operation Pacing-pulse generation Memory storage Diagnostic functions Telemetry communication Activity sensing Automatic measurements Device-status monitoring Only a portion of the battery energy is used for pacing pulses. The internal electronics also require continuous low-level energy. 6.2.1.H2C2 Battery Design Requirements A pacemaker battery should provide: Long service life Stable voltage Predictable depletion Low self-discharge Reliable operation at body temperature Low internal current leakage Ability to support brief pacing-output demands Biocompatibility through secure containment Resistance to internal corrosion Accurate monitoring of remaining service capacity The battery must perform reliably for years without external charging in most conventional pacemakers. 6.2.1.H2C3 Pacemaker Battery Chemistry Conventional pacemakers generally use primary, non-rechargeable lithium-based battery systems. The exact chemistry depends on the device design and manufacturer. Examples historically or currently used in cardiac implantable devices include: Lithium–iodine systems Lithium silver-vanadium-oxide-based systems Hybrid lithium chemistries Other specialised lithium primary-cell designs The learner should not assume that every pacemaker uses the same chemistry. Battery chemistry is selected according to: Required current profile Device size Desired longevity Output capability Voltage characteristics Safety and reliability requirements 6.2.1.H2C4 Primary Versus Rechargeable Battery A conventional transvenous pacemaker normally uses a primary battery. Primary battery A primary battery: Is not recharged after implantation Supplies energy until replacement is required Is designed for predictable long-term depletion Allows the complete generator to be replaced when the battery approaches end of service Rechargeable battery Rechargeable batteries are used in some other implantable therapeutic devices but are not the standard energy source for conventional permanent transvenous pacemakers. A rechargeable system requires: Transcutaneous energy transfer Charging hardware Patient participation Additional charging-control systems 6.2.1.H2C5 Battery Voltage The battery produces an internal voltage that powers the circuitry and pacing-output system. Battery voltage is not identical to the pacing amplitude programmed for the patient. The device may use electronic circuits to: Regulate voltage Store energy temporarily Shape the pacing pulse Generate an output higher or lower than the instantaneous battery voltage Maintain output as battery conditions change The clinician therefore programs pacing output, while the internal circuitry manages how the battery energy is converted into that output. 6.2.1.H2C6 Battery Capacity Battery capacity represents the total electrical charge available from the battery under specified conditions. Capacity alone does not determine device longevity. Longevity also depends on: Device current consumption Pacing burden Pacing amplitude Pulse width Lead impedance Number of paced chambers Sensor use Diagnostic storage Telemetry use Automatic algorithms Frequency of high-output pacing Battery chemistry Circuit efficiency Two devices with similar battery size may have different projected longevity because their internal power requirements differ. IMAGE 6.2.1-3 . 6.2.1.H2C7 Current Drain Current drain is the rate at which the pulse generator uses battery energy. There are two broad categories. Background current drain This supports continuous functions such as: Clock operation Sensing Timing Memory maintenance Basic processor operation Internal monitoring Therapy-related current drain This includes energy used for: Atrial pacing Ventricular pacing High-output pacing Rate-responsive pacing Automatic threshold testing Telemetry sessions Diagnostic electrogram storage Higher total current drain generally shortens device longevity. 6.2.1.H2C8 Effect of Pacing Amplitude Pacing amplitude is the voltage or current strength of the delivered pulse, depending on device design. Increasing pacing amplitude increases energy consumption. In a simplified voltage-regulated pacing system, energy use rises markedly as voltage is increased. For example, increasing output from a moderate value to a much higher value may consume substantially more energy than the numerical change alone suggests. Therefore, chronic pacing output is generally programmed to: Remain safely above the capture threshold Provide an appropriate safety margin Avoid unnecessary excess output Patient safety always takes priority over battery conservation. 6.2.1.H2C9 Effect of Pulse Width Pulse width is the duration of the pacing pulse. A longer pulse width delivers energy for a longer period and generally increases battery consumption. Pacing output must therefore be considered as a combination of: Amplitude Pulse width Lead impedance Pacing frequency A low amplitude with a very long pulse width may still consume significant energy. 6.2.1.H2C10 Effect of Pacing Percentage Pacing percentage describes how often the device delivers pacing pulses. A patient paced 5% of the time generally uses less therapy energy than a patient paced 100% of the time, assuming other conditions are similar. High pacing percentages may occur in: Complete heart block Severe sinus-node dysfunction Pacemaker-dependent patients Certain programmed pacing strategies Cardiac resynchronization therapy Pacing percentage is therefore an important factor in projected longevity. 6.2.1.H2C11 Effect of Lead Impedance Lead impedance affects current flow. With voltage-regulated pacing: Lower impedance allows greater current flow. Greater current flow may increase battery drain. Higher impedance reduces current flow, although very high impedance may indicate a circuit problem. The most energy-efficient impedance is not simply the highest possible value. The lead must remain within the expected operating range and provide reliable sensing and capture. 6.2.1.H2C12 Number of Pacing Chambers A single-chamber device supports one pacing channel. A dual-chamber device may support: Atrial sensing and pacing Ventricular sensing and pacing AV timing Additional diagnostics A CRT pacemaker may support: Right atrial channel Right ventricular channel Left ventricular channel Multiple left ventricular pacing vectors Resynchronization algorithms Additional active channels and higher pacing burdens can increase energy use. 6.2.1.H2C13 Diagnostic and Memory Energy Use Modern pulse generators may store: Heart-rate trends Pacing percentages Atrial arrhythmia episodes Ventricular high-rate episodes Intracardiac electrograms Lead measurements Activity trends Rate histograms Mode-switch episodes Device alerts Co

Topic: Topic 6.2.3: Single-Chamber Pacemaker Timing Cycles

Topic Description: Topic 6.2.3: Single-Chamber Pacemaker Timing Cycles

Heading: How it works in single-chamber pacing: lower rate, upper rate, upper tracking rate context, refractory period, and blanking period

H1C1  Learning Objectives By the end of Chapter, the learner should be able to explain how a single-chamber pacemaker uses timing intervals to decide whether to pace, inhibit pacing, ignore signals, or protect the sensing circuit from repeated detection. ·        Define lower rate interval and calculate the escape interval from a programmed lower rate. ·        Differentiate blanking from refractory sensing in single-chamber timing. ·        Explain VOO asynchronous timing and why intrinsic events do not affect it. ·        Explain VVI inhibited timing and how a valid ventricular sensed event resets the escape interval. ·        Identify what happens when a signal is sensed during the refractory period. ·        Describe noise reversion and why repeated refractory sensed events do not reset the lower-rate timer. ·        Explain the upper sensor rate/upper rate interval in VVIR or AAIR single-chamber rate-responsive pacing. ·        Correctly state that upper tracking rate is not a true VVI/VOO/VVIR/AAI/AAIR single-chamber tracking function; it belongs to atrial-tracking modes such as VDD/DDD or specialized AV-synchronous leadless systems. Describe hysteresis and why it promotes intrinsic rhythm when appropriate. H1C2  How to Read Single-Chamber Timing Diagrams Before learners review the animated source slides, they should know how to read the timing diagrams. The horizontal line represents time. Each paced or sensed event starts, resets, or continues a timing cycle depending on the programmed mode and on whether the sensed event occurs inside or outside the refractory period.   Marker / Term Learner meaning Timing effect in this chapter VP Ventricular paced event Starts a new lower-rate timing cycle and initiates blanking followed by refractory timing. VS Ventricular sensed event outside refractory In VVI/VVIR, inhibits the scheduled pace and restarts the timing cycle from the sensed event. VR or SR Ventricular refractory sensed event / sensed event during refractory The signal is recorded, but it does not produce the usual inhibited-mode response and does not reset the lower-rate escape interval. AP / AS Atrial paced or sensed event Used only when the chapter compares AAIR atrial-based rate-responsive timing. Lower-rate interval The maximum escape interval before pacing occurs if no valid intrinsic event is sensed Example: 60 ppm equals about 1000 ms. Blanking period Immediate post-event period when the device is blind to electrical activity Prevents sensing the pacing artifact or the same depolarization twice. Refractory period Post-event nonresponsive period after the event; after blanking, signals may be detected but not used to reset timing Protects against inappropriate timing reset due to T waves, far-field signals, or noise.   H1C3  Core Timing Formula Most timing-cycle questions can be solved by converting a programmed rate into an interval. Use the formula below whenever the learner needs to compare lower rate, hysteresis rate, or upper sensor rate. Formula / Example Calculation Teaching point Interval in ms 60,000 / rate in ppm Pacemaker timing is often interval-based even when the programmed value is shown as ppm. 60 ppm 60,000 / 60 = 1000 ms Common lower-rate example in the source deck. 50 ppm 60,000 / 50 = 1200 ms Common hysteresis example in the source deck. 120 ppm 60,000 / 120 = 500 ms Common upper sensor-rate example in VVIR/AAIR teaching. Learner checkpoint calculate the interval before revealing the answer. This makes later VVI, VVIR, and hysteresis sequences easier to follow.   H1C4  Key Terminology and Marker Abbreviations Term Meaning in this chapter AP Atrial pace: output delivered in the atrium. AS Atrial sense: intrinsic atrial event sensed outside the refractory period. VP Ventricular pace: output delivered in the ventricle. VS Ventricular sense: intrinsic ventricular event sensed outside the refractory period. VR / SR Ventricular refractory sense or single-chamber refractory sense: a signal detected during refractory. The device records it but does not reset the lower-rate escape interval. Blanking The short period immediately after paced or sensed activity when the pacemaker is intentionally blind to electrical signals. Refractory period A protective interval after paced or sensed activity during which signals may be detected/marked but are not allowed to trigger the normal timing response. Lower rate interval The maximum allowed time between events before the pacemaker must pace. Interval in ms = 60,000 / programmed lower rate in ppm or bpm. Upper sensor rate The highest pacing rate allowed when the sensor indicates increased physiologic demand in a rate-responsive single-chamber mode. Upper tracking rate The highest rate at which atrial activity can be tracked to ventricular pacing in atrial-tracking modes; included here only as a comparison because it is often confused with upper sensor rate.   H1C5  Timing Components in a Single-Chamber Cycle   Learning objective Build the learner's mental model of the timing cycle before discussing each interval separately.   A single-chamber timing cycle starts with a paced event or a valid sensed event. From that event, the device starts a sequence of protective and decision intervals: blanking first, refractory next, and the remaining lower-rate interval until the next pace is due. In rate-responsive modes, the sensor can shorten the interval up to the upper sensor rate limit. H1C6  explanation Think of the pacemaker as running a clock. Each valid event either starts the clock or resets it. During the early part of the clock, the sensing circuit is protected from detecting its own output or the immediate depolarization. Later in the cycle, the pacemaker can sense intrinsic activity and either inhibit the next pace or continue timing toward the next pacing output. H1C7  Detailed  points The basic single-chamber timing components are lower rate interval, blanking period, and refractory period. Rate-responsive single-chamber modes add sensor-driven timing and an upper sensor rate/upper rate interval. Inhibited modes respond to valid intrinsic activity. Asynchronous modes do not respond to intrinsic activity. H1C8  Single-Chamber Timing Algorithm Use this algorithm as the mental model for the rest of the chapter. The exact interval names and device behaviors can vary by model, but the educational sequence is consistent for basic single-chamber timing. A paced event or a valid non-refractory sensed event occurs. The blanking period starts immediately; during this earliest period, the device is intentionally blind to electrical signals. The refractory period continues after the event. After blanking ends, the device may detect signals, but refractory signals do not trigger the normal timing response. After refractory ends, the device is able to respond to valid sensed events according to the programmed mode. If no valid intrinsic event occurs before the relevant escape interval expires, the pacemaker delivers a pace. If a valid sensed event occurs in an inhibited mode, the scheduled pace is inhibited and a new cycle starts from the sensed event.   Figure 1: Single-chamber timing terms: lower rate, refractory period, blanking period, and upper rate.    

Heading: Section 2 - Section 4

H2C1  Section 2 - Lower Rate Interval Learning objective Explain how the pacemaker prevents the rate from falling below the programmed lower rate. H2C2  On-screen learner content The lower rate interval is the escape interval. It defines the slowest rate at which the pacemaker will deliver pacing when no valid intrinsic event is sensed. H2C3  explanation If the lower rate is programmed to 60 ppm, the pacemaker should not allow more than about 1000 ms to pass without a valid event. A ventricular pace or a valid ventricular sense starts a new timing interval in VVI. If no valid ventricular sense occurs before the interval expires, the pacemaker delivers a ventricular pace. H2C4  Detailed  points Formula: lower rate interval in milliseconds = 60,000 / lower rate in ppm. Example: 60 ppm = 1000 ms; 50 ppm = 1200 ms; 120 ppm = 500 ms. A paced event starts the programmed lower-rate interval. A non-refractory sensed event in an inhibited mode resets/restarts the lower-rate interval. A refractory sensed event is recorded but does not reset the lower-rate escape interval. H2C5  Lower Rate - Learner Explanation The lower rate is best understood as the longest allowed waiting time between a valid event and the next paced event when the patient does not provide an acceptable intrinsic rhythm. It is not the same as saying the pacemaker must pace every interval. In demand modes such as VVI, a valid intrinsic ventricular sensed event can satisfy the timing requirement and prevent an unnecessary paced beat. If the patient is slower than the programmed lower rate, the device paces to prevent bradycardia. If the patient produces a valid intrinsic beat before the interval expires, the device inhibits the scheduled pace and restarts timing. If the detected signal occurs during refractory, it is marked but does not count as the valid event that resets the lower-rate timer . Figure 2: Lower rate interval example in VVI at 60 ppm: the escape interval defines the slowest pacing rate H3C1  Section 3 - Blanking Period Learning objective Differentiate true blindness during blanking from refractory sensing after blanking.   Blanking is the period immediately after a paced or sensed event when the pacemaker cannot detect electrical activity. It is designed to prevent oversensing of the pacing artifact or the immediate depolarization associated with the event. H3C2  explanation During blanking, the pacemaker is intentionally blind. This prevents the sense amplifier from detecting the pacing stimulus or the same depolarization more than once. Blanking is typically short and device-specific. The key teaching point is that blanking is not the same as refractory: during blanking the event is not seen; during refractory after blanking, the event may be seen but should not produce the usual timing response. H3C3  Detailed  points Blanking begins immediately after a paced or sensed event. During blanking, the device is blind to electrical activity. Blanking prevents sensing of pacing artifact, afterpotentials, or the immediate intrinsic depolarization. Blanking is usually contained within the longer refractory period. If blanking is too short, the device may oversense its own output or depolarization; if too long, it may miss true early intrinsic signals. H3C4  Blanking - Learner Explanation Expansion Blanking is the most protective part of the post-event timing sequence. During blanking, the device is not asking, “Should I respond to this signal?” Instead, it is not sensing signals for timing purposes at all. This prevents the device from detecting the pacing spike, lead afterpotential, or the same depolarization as if it were a new cardiac event. Question Blanking answer Can the device sense electrical activity during blanking? For teaching purposes, no. The device is considered blind during blanking. Does a signal during blanking reset the lower-rate timer? No. It is not treated as a valid sensed event for timing reset. Why is blanking needed? To avoid double counting the paced/sensed event or sensing the device output itself.     Figure 3: Blanking period example: the device is temporarily blind immediately after a paced or sensed event. Topic: TOPIC 6.3.1: PACING SPIKES AND CAPTURE

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.3.1: PACING SPIKES AND CAPTURE

Heading: Pacing Spikes & Capture • Sensing Behaviour • Interactive Paced ECG Labelling

Pacing Spikes & Capture • Sensing Behaviour • Interactive Paced ECG Labelling      Pacing spikes, capture, and loss of capture.   INTENDED AUDIENCE Sales executives, service engineers, field application specialists, clinical support personnel, biomedical engineers, and learners who require a structured foundation in recognising paced rhythms on surface ECG.   EDUCATIONAL USE AND SAFETY NOTE This chapter supports training and pattern recognition. A surface ECG alone does not replace device interrogation, intracardiac electrograms, lead measurements, clinical assessment, or emergency protocols. Any suspected loss of capture or dangerous sensing failure—especially in a pacing-dependent patient—requires prompt clinical escalation.   6.3.H1C1  Pacemaker – ECG Interpretation 6.3.H1C2  Learning Objectives By the end of Chapter 6.3, learners will be able to: · Define pacing output, pacing spike, electrical capture, mechanical capture, sensing, inhibition, triggering, fusion, pseudofusion, undersensing, and oversensing. · Identify atrial, ventricular, and dual-chamber pacing spikes on a surface ECG, including circumstances in which modern bipolar pacing spikes may be small or difficult to see. · Confirm atrial capture by demonstrating an appropriate atrial depolarization after an atrial stimulus and confirm ventricular capture by demonstrating an appropriate QRS complex after a ventricular stimulus. · Differentiate consistent capture, intermittent capture, complete loss of capture, fusion, and pseudofusion. · Explain how pacing site, lead configuration, tissue activation sequence, filter settings, and display gain influence the apparent paced ECG morphology. · Interpret normal sensing behaviour in inhibited, triggered, and dual-chamber tracking responses. · Differentiate undersensing from oversensing using surface ECG timing, device markers, stored electrograms, and lead trends. · Explain the inverse relationship between the programmed sensitivity value in millivolts and the sensitivity of the sensing circuit. · Recognise the purpose of blanking and refractory intervals and distinguish these from true sensing failure. · Apply a systematic eight-step method to interpret paced ECGs without jumping directly to a device-malfunction conclusion. · Prioritise urgent escalation when loss of capture, prolonged inhibition, symptoms, or pacing dependency creates immediate risk. · Complete an interactive labelling exercise and justify every label using timing and morphology rather than visual guesswork. 6.3.H1C3  Chapter Overview Pacemaker ECG interpretation is the process of connecting three different layers of information: the electrical command delivered by the pulse generator, the response of the myocardium to that command, and the device response to intrinsic cardiac activity. A pacing spike shows that output was delivered or at least appeared on the surface ECG. It does not, by itself, prove that myocardial depolarization occurred. Capture is confirmed only when the appropriate cardiac chamber depolarizes after the stimulus. Sensing is evaluated by determining whether the pacemaker correctly recognises native atrial or ventricular events and then inhibits, triggers, tracks, or resets its timing cycles in the expected manner. A disciplined interpreter therefore asks three questions in sequence: What event occurred first? What did the device do in response? What did the heart do in response? This sequence prevents common errors such as calling a small bipolar spike “absent output,” calling pseudofusion “loss of capture,” or calling a refractory event “undersensing.” The chapter progresses from visible pacing artefacts to capture, sensing, timing interactions, malfunction patterns, and an interactive paced-ECG labelling exercise. Throughout the chapter, the surface ECG is treated as one part of a complete assessment. Device interrogation and clinical correlation remain essential whenever malfunction is suspected. IMAGE 6.3-1 Learning purpose: Establishes that the visible pacing spike and the myocardial response arise from different parts of the system and must be evaluated separately.  

Heading: 6.3.H1C4  Fundamentals and Core Concepts

6.3.H1C4.1  The Three-Layer Model Layer Question Evidence Device output Did the pacemaker deliver a stimulus? Pacing spike, device marker such as AP/VP, output telemetry, pulse amplitude and width. Myocardial response Did the intended chamber depolarize? P wave after atrial output, QRS after ventricular output, intracardiac evoked response, pulse or hemodynamic response. Device sensing response Did the pacemaker detect intrinsic activity correctly? Appropriate inhibition, tracking, timing reset, sensed marker such as AS/VS, stored electrogram.   Errors arise when one layer is used as proof of another. A device marker can confirm that the device classified an event, but the classification may be incorrect. A pacing spike can confirm visible electrical output, but capture may fail. A QRS may follow a spike by coincidence, especially when intrinsic conduction is present. Interpretation therefore depends on repeatable timing relationships across multiple beats. 6.3.H1C4.2  Pacing Output A pacing pulse is a brief electrical stimulus defined primarily by amplitude, commonly expressed in volts, and pulse width, commonly expressed in milliseconds. The pulse must create an adequate electric field at the electrode–tissue interface to depolarize excitable myocardium. The output programmed above the measured threshold provides a safety margin against physiologic variation, lead maturation, changes in contact, metabolic disturbances, medications, and measurement uncertainty. The pacing spike on the surface ECG is an artefact produced by the pacing pulse and the recording system. Its apparent size is influenced by the lead polarity, distance from the ECG electrode, vector orientation, pulse amplitude and width, ECG filter settings, gain, sampling, and display resolution. Unipolar pacing often creates a larger visible spike than bipolar pacing because the current pathway is larger. Modern bipolar or leadless pacing stimuli may be very small on standard ECG displays. 6.3.H1C4.3  Capture Capture is successful depolarization of the intended chamber following a pacing stimulus. Atrial electrical capture is demonstrated by an atrial depolarization—usually a P wave—after the atrial spike. Ventricular electrical capture is demonstrated by a QRS complex after the ventricular spike. In a dual-chamber sequence, atrial output may capture the atrium and be followed by intrinsic ventricular conduction or by a ventricular pacing stimulus after the programmed AV interval. Electrical capture and mechanical capture are related but not identical. Electrical capture confirms depolarization on ECG or intracardiac electrogram. Mechanical capture confirms effective myocardial contraction and perfusion, assessed by a pulse, blood pressure waveform, plethysmography, arterial line, echocardiography, or clinical signs. In an unstable patient, both must be checked. 6.3.H1C4.4  Sensing Sensing is the device’s recognition of intrinsic cardiac electrical activity through an implanted electrode. The device compares the incoming signal with its programmed sensing threshold and timing rules. A correctly sensed event can inhibit an unnecessary pacing pulse, start an AV delay, trigger a paced event, reset an escape interval, contribute to rate calculations, or be stored as diagnostic information. The sensitivity setting is expressed in millivolts and is counterintuitive: a lower numerical value is more sensitive because a smaller signal can cross the detection threshold. A higher numerical value is less sensitive because a larger signal is required. Sensitivity must be adequate to detect true cardiac signals while rejecting far-field signals, repolarization waves, muscle activity, electromagnetic interference, and lead noise. 6.3.H1C4.5  Timing Cycles, Blanking, and Refractory Intervals A pacemaker is a timing system as well as a pulse generator. Lower-rate intervals, AV delays, upper-rate limits, refractory periods, and blanking periods determine when an event can be sensed and how the device responds. During a blanking interval, the sensing amplifier is intentionally unable to register events to protect against detection of the device’s own output or immediate after-potentials. During a refractory interval, signals may be detected or marked but do not produce the normal timing response. The exact behaviour is manufacturer- and mode-specific. IMPORTANT INTERPRETATION RULE An event occurring inside a programmed blanking or refractory window may appear “not sensed” on the surface ECG even though the device is functioning exactly as programmed. Always place the event in the timing cycle before diagnosing undersensing.          

Heading: 6.3.H1C5  Systematic Eight-Step Paced ECG Interpretation

6.3.H1C5  Systematic Eight-Step Paced ECG Interpretation   1 Confirm patient status and urgency. Assess symptoms, hemodynamics, pacing dependency, and whether the strip represents a stable teaching example or a possible emergency.   2 Confirm ECG quality. Verify paper speed, gain, lead selection, baseline stability, filter settings, and whether pacing artefacts may have been attenuated.   3 Identify the underlying atrial and ventricular rhythm. Look for intrinsic P waves, QRS complexes, atrial fibrillation, AV block, pauses, and ectopy before assigning a paced rhythm.   4 Locate every visible pacing spike and classify its likely chamber: atrial, ventricular, or both. Use the event that follows, not spike size alone.   5 Assess capture after each stimulus. Atrial output should be followed by atrial depolarization; ventricular output should be followed by a QRS. Evaluate consistency across the entire strip.   6 Assess sensing. Determine whether intrinsic events appropriately inhibit, trigger, track, or reset device timing. Look for premature output suggesting undersensing and unexplained pauses suggesting oversensing.   7 Assess timing and mode behaviour. Measure paced cycle length, AV interval, upper-rate behaviour, refractory interactions, and the relationship between atrial and ventricular events.   8 Synthesize and escalate. State the rhythm, pacing pattern, capture status, sensing status, likely mechanism, alternative explanations, and the need for interrogation or urgent support.   IMAGE  6.3-2 Learning purpose: Provides a repeatable visual algorithm that learners can apply to every paced ECG.     CHAPTER ORIENTATION CHECK Before continuing, the learner should be able to explain why a pacing spike is evidence of output but not proof of capture, and why a pause in pacing may represent either correct inhibition or dangerous oversensing.  

Heading: Pacing Spikes & Capture:

Learning Objectives · Identify visible atrial, ventricular, and dual-chamber pacing stimuli. · Explain why pacing spikes may be large, small, distorted, or apparently absent. · Confirm chamber-specific electrical capture and distinguish it from mechanical capture. · Recognise intermittent and complete loss of capture. · Differentiate fusion and pseudofusion from true capture failure. · Explain the role of pacing threshold, output amplitude, pulse width, and safety margin. · Recognise ECG morphology associated with common ventricular pacing sites while avoiding overconfident localisation. · Apply a structured troubleshooting process for suspected capture failure. 6.3.1.H2C2  Concept and Fundamentals The ECG

Topic: TOPIC 6.2.2: RF SHIELDING AND HERMETIC SEALS

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.2.2: RF SHIELDING AND HERMETIC SEALS

Heading: 6.2.2.H1C1 Learning Objectives

6.2.2.H1C1 Learning Objectives By the end of this topic, learners will be able to: Define radiofrequency energy and electromagnetic interference. Explain why an implanted pacemaker requires electromagnetic protection. Describe the shielding role of the metallic can. Explain why shielding cannot completely isolate the pulse generator from all electromagnetic fields. Describe how input filters reduce unwanted electrical signals. Explain the purpose of feedthrough filters. Describe the relationship between shielding and intentional telemetry. Differentiate inductive communication from radiofrequency communication. Identify common sources of electromagnetic interference. Explain how EMI may affect sensing, pacing, telemetry and stored diagnostics. Describe possible device responses to noise or interference. Define a hermetic seal. Explain why body-fluid exclusion is essential. Describe the hermetic titanium enclosure. Explain the role of welded seams. Describe ceramic or glass-insulated electrical feedthroughs. Differentiate the hermetic can seal from connector-block seals. Explain possible consequences of a loss of hermetic integrity. Describe clinical evaluation after suspected electromagnetic or physical device damage. Recognize that procedure-related precautions are device- and manufacturer-specific.   6.2.2.H1C2 Topic Overview A pacemaker is an electronic implant operating inside an electrically active environment. It is exposed to: Cardiac electrical signals Skeletal-muscle signals Static magnetic fields Alternating magnetic fields Radiofrequency transmitters Medical equipment Electrosurgical systems Radiofrequency ablation systems MRI systems Security systems Industrial electrical equipment The pacemaker must detect tiny intracardiac signals while rejecting unwanted electrical noise. At the same time, it must intentionally communicate with an external programmer or remote-monitoring system. The design must therefore balance two opposing requirements: 1.      Block or reduce unwanted electromagnetic energy. 2.      Permit controlled communication with approved external equipment. The internal electronics must also remain isolated from body fluids throughout the life of the implant. RF shielding and hermetic sealing address these requirements. 6.2.2.H1C3 Concept and Fundamentals RF shielding RF shielding refers to design features that reduce the entry of unwanted radiofrequency or electromagnetic energy into sensitive electronic circuits. Hermetic sealing Hermetic sealing refers to the creation of an enclosure that prevents clinically significant entry of gases, moisture and body fluids into the protected electronic compartment. In simple terms: Shielding protects the electronics from unwanted electromagnetic energy. Hermetic sealing protects the electronics from moisture and body fluids. These protections work together but perform different functions. ELECTROMAGNETIC FUNDAMENTALS 6.2.2.H2C1 Meaning of Electromagnetic Interference Electromagnetic interference is unwanted electrical or magnetic energy that alters, or has the potential to alter, device operation. Interference may reach the pacemaker through: Radiated electromagnetic fields Magnetic-field coupling Capacitive coupling Conducted current through the body Lead-system antennas Direct contact with medical equipment High-energy transient events Not every electromagnetic field produces clinically significant interference. Risk depends on: Field strength Frequency Distance Duration Orientation Device design Lead configuration Sensitivity setting Pacing dependency Programmed mode 6.2.2.H2C2 Electric Fields An electric field develops around electrical voltage sources. Strong electric fields may couple with: Pacemaker leads Body tissue Device conductors Sensing circuits The resulting signal may be interpreted as noise if it reaches the sensing amplifier with sufficient amplitude. 6.2.2.H2C3 Magnetic Fields Magnetic fields may arise from: Permanent magnets Electrical motors Transformers MRI systems High-current conductors Magnetic tools or accessories Static magnetic fields may activate a device’s magnetic response. Alternating magnetic fields may induce electrical currents in leads or internal conductors. 6.2.2.H2C4 Radiofrequency Energy Radiofrequency energy refers to electromagnetic energy in frequency ranges used for: Wireless communication Mobile telephones Radio transmitters Telemetry RFID systems Medical ablation Security equipment Industrial applications The effects depend on power, frequency, distance and device design. 6.2.2.H2C5 Conducted Interference Conducted interference occurs when electrical current travels through tissue or connected equipment and reaches the implanted system. Examples may include: Electrosurgery Radiofrequency ablation External defibrillation Diathermy Electrical stimulation therapies Poorly grounded equipment The current pathway relative to the device and leads is clinically important. 6.2.2.H2C6 Radiated Interference Radiated interference reaches the device without direct electrical contact. Potential sources include: High-power transmitters Mobile communication equipment Radar Industrial radiofrequency systems Security systems Wireless power systems Distance from the source usually reduces field strength. IMAGE 6.2.2-1 .

Heading: RF AND EMI SHIELDING

RF AND EMI SHIELDING 6.2.2.H3C1 Purpose of RF Shielding RF shielding helps prevent unwanted electromagnetic energy from reaching sensitive internal circuits. The objectives are to reduce: False sensing Pacing inhibition Inappropriate pacing Telemetry interruption Data corruption Circuit reset Component damage Unintended mode change No shield provides absolute protection against all fields and energy levels.   6.2.2.H3C2 Metallic Can as a Shield The conductive metallic enclosure acts as an electromagnetic barrier around much of the internal circuitry. It can: Reflect part of an incident electromagnetic field Conduct induced currents around the enclosure Reduce field strength reaching internal circuits Provide a reference potential Protect the battery and electronic module The shielding effect depends on: Metal conductivity Wall thickness Frequency Seam integrity Openings Feedthrough design Antenna structure Device orientation 6.2.2.H3C3 Faraday-Enclosure Concept The can operates partly like a Faraday enclosure. A conductive enclosure causes external electrical energy to redistribute along the metal surface, reducing penetration into the internal space. However, a pacemaker is not a completely closed shield because it requires: Electrical feedthroughs Lead connections Telemetry communication Sensor operation Controlled magnetic response in some devices Therefore, protection depends on the complete system, not the metal case alone. 6.2.2.H3C4 Feedthrough Filters Lead conductors must enter the sealed enclosure through feedthroughs. These conductors can also provide a pathway for high-frequency interference. Filter components near the feedthrough may help: Attenuate unwanted high-frequency energy Shunt interference away from sensitive circuits Protect sensing amplifiers Reduce RF entry through lead connections Preserve normal low-frequency cardiac sensing Feedthrough filtering must allow the intended pacing and sensing signals to pass. 6.2.2.H3C5 Sensing-Circuit Filters The sensing pathway includes filters designed around the frequency characteristics of cardiac electrograms. These filters help reject: Very low-frequency baseline drift High-frequency RF noise Skeletal-muscle signals Pacing artefacts External electrical interference Filtering is combined with: Sensitivity settings Blanking periods Refractory periods Noise-detection algorithms Bipolar lead configurations 6.2.2.H3C6 Bipolar Lead Advantage in EMI Reduction A bipolar sensing circuit uses two closely spaced electrodes. Because the sensing loop is relatively small, it is generally less likely to detect distant electromagnetic signals than a large unipolar circuit. A unipolar sensing circuit includes: Lead-tip electrode Body tissue Pulse-generator can This creates a larger antenna-like loop and may increase susceptibility to some forms of interference. The actual response depends on the complete device and environment. 6.2.2.H3C7 Grounding and Internal Reference The internal circuitry uses defined electrical reference points. The can may serve as: Electrical reference Shielding enclosure Return electrode in unipolar configurations The internal circuit design controls how signals are referenced and processed while maintaining patient electrical safety. 6.2.2.H3C8 Transient-Protection Components Protection circuits may limit brief voltage spikes caused by: External defibrillation Electrosurgery Static discharge RF ablation Environmental transients Protective components may include: Voltage clamps Current-limiting elements Filter capacitors Protective diodes Input-isolation circuits These components reduce risk but do not make the device immune to high-energy exposure. IMAGE 6.2.2-2   INTENTIONAL TELEMETRY COMMUNICATION 6.2.2.H4C1 Need for Communication Through the Shield The pacemaker must communicate with external clinical equipment despite being inside a metal enclosure and beneath the skin. Telemetry is required to: Interrogate the device Retrieve stored data Display real-time electrograms Review battery and lead status Change programming Receive software-controlled commands Support remote monitoring Transmit device alerts The shielding design must therefore block unwanted signals while permitting approved communication. 6.2.2.H4C2 Inductive Telemetry Inductive telemetry uses magnetic coupling between: An external programming head An internal communication coil The programming head is placed close to the implanted device. Potential characteristics include: Short communication range Controlled coupling Reduced communication with distant systems Reliable in-clinic interrogation Older and some current systems may use inductive communication. 6.2.2.H4C3 Radiofrequency Telemetry Radiofrequency telemetry uses an implanted antenna and an approved external communication system. Potential advantages include: Communication without placing a wand directly over the device Greater patient comfort Faster transfer of diagnostic information Remote-monitoring capability Continuous or scheduled connectivity in selected systems The operating frequency and communication protocol are device-specific. 6.2.2.H4C4 Remote Monitoring Remote monitoring may transmit: Battery status Lead measurements Arrhythmia episodes Device alerts Pacing percentages Stored electrograms Therapy data The home transmitter or compatible mobile device relays information to a secure clinical network. Remote monitoring does not continuously replace the pacemaker’s internal control. The implanted generator performs its essential sensing and pacing functions independently. 6.2.2.H4C5 Telemetry Interruption Strong electromagnetic interference may temporarily disrupt communication between the implanted device and external programmer. Possible findings include: Inability to interrogate Interrupted programming session Delayed data transmission Telemetry error message Need to reposition the programmer Need to move away from an interference source Successful interrogation after the disturbance helps confirm restored communication. 6.2.2.H4C6 Communication Security Modern wireless medical systems may use: Device authentication Encrypted data Defined communication sessions Proximity controls Paired external systems Software access controls Network-security protections Security features vary by model and generation. Topic: Topic 6.3.2 – Sensing Behaviour:

Topic Description: Topic 6.3.2 – Sensing Behaviour:

Heading: Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives · Define normal sensing, undersensing, and oversensing. · Explain how intracardiac electrograms are filtered, amplified, and compared with a sensing threshold. · Apply the inverse millivolt relationship: lower programmed value means greater sensitivity. · Interpret appropriate inhibition, triggering, tracking, and timing reset. · Distinguish sensing failure from events occurring in blanking or refractory periods. · Recognise far-field sensing, T-wave sensing, myopotential sensing, electromagnetic interference, and lead noise. · Explain atrial crosstalk, ventricular safety pacing, and noise-response concepts at a foundational level. · Use surface ECG, marker channels, stored electrograms, sensing amplitudes, and impedance trends to troubleshoot sensing concerns. 6.3.2.H3C2  Concept and Fundamentals The sensing circuit allows the pacemaker to listen to the heart. An implanted electrode records a local intracardiac electrogram. The signal is filtered and amplified, then compared with a programmable detection threshold. The device also applies timing rules so that an electrical deflection is not only large enough to be detected but occurs at a time when the channel is permitted to respond. Normal sensing means the device detects the intended intrinsic event and responds appropriately for the programmed mode. Undersensing means a true intrinsic event is not recognised when it should be. Oversensing means the device classifies an unintended signal as a true cardiac event. Both can produce inappropriate pacing behaviour, but their surface ECG patterns are usually opposite: undersensing can cause unwanted pacing, while oversensing can suppress needed pacing.         Normal sensing, undersensing, and oversensing. IMAGE 6.3.2-1   Learning purpose: Shows that sensing depends on both signal amplitude and timing logic, not simply the presence of a wave on the surface ECG.     6.3.2.H3C3  Sensitivity in Millivolts The sensitivity setting defines the minimum signal amplitude required for detection. A setting of 0.5 mV is more sensitive than 2.0 mV because a smaller signal can be detected. This inverse relationship is a frequent source of programming and interpretation errors. Making the device more sensitive may correct undersensing but can increase susceptibility to oversensing. Making it less sensitive may reduce oversensing but can miss low-amplitude true events. Python-generated conceptual scale: lower mV setting equals greater sensing sensitivity. Programming change Electronic effect Potential benefit Potential risk Decrease mV value Device becomes more sensitive. May detect smaller true P or R waves. May oversense noise, T waves, myopotentials, or far-field events. Increase mV value Device becomes less sensitive. May reject unwanted signals. May undersense true low-amplitude cardiac events.   IMAGE 6.3.2-2   Learning purpose: Visually reinforces the inverse relationship and the trade-off between under- and oversensing.   6.3.2.H3C4  Normal Sensing Responses The effect of a sensed event depends on the pacing mode and the chamber in which the event is detected. In an inhibited mode, a sensed event suppresses the scheduled output in that chamber and resets an escape interval. In a triggered response, a sensed event produces an output, commonly used in specific timing or diagnostic behaviours. In dual-chamber tracking, a sensed atrial event starts an AV delay; if no ventricular event occurs, the pacemaker paces the ventricle at the end of that interval.   Sensed event Expected device response in common dual-chamber operation Surface ECG clue Atrial sensed (AS) Starts an AV delay and may be tracked to a ventricular event, subject to upper-rate and refractory rules. Intrinsic P wave followed by intrinsic QRS or ventricular pacing after a consistent AV interval. Ventricular sensed (VS) Inhibits ventricular output and resets ventricular timing. Intrinsic QRS occurs without an unnecessary ventricular pacing spike. Atrial paced and captured (AP) Starts a paced AV delay. Atrial spike and P wave followed by intrinsic or paced ventricular event. Ventricular paced (VP) Delivered when no qualifying VS occurs before ventricular timing expires. Ventricular spike followed by paced QRS.   Normal sensing, undersensing, and oversensing on surface ECG. IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.3.2-3 Learning purpose: Builds the learner’s ability to correlate surface events with intracardiac sensing and timing responses.    

Heading: 6.3.2.H3C5  Blanking and Refractory Behaviour

6.3.2.H3C5  Blanking and Refractory Behaviour Blanking intervals prevent the sensing amplifier from detecting high-amplitude signals caused by pacing output or immediate after-potentials. A post-atrial ventricular blanking interval helps prevent the ventricular channel from sensing the atrial pacing pulse. A post-ventricular atrial blanking period may protect the atrial channel from the ventricular pacing artefact. The exact durations and adaptive behaviours vary by device. Refractory intervals allow the device to recognise or annotate some signals without allowing them to trigger a normal timing response. A post-ventricular atrial refractory period helps prevent retrograde P waves or far-field R waves from being tracked as new atrial events. An event inside a refractory interval may appear on the ECG but may not reset or trigger pacing. This is programmed behaviour, not necessarily undersensing. Concept Can the amplifier detect the event? Does it trigger normal timing? Primary purpose Blanking interval Usually no; sensing is intentionally disabled. No. Protect against sensing of pacing artefact or immediate unwanted signals. Refractory interval May be detected or marked, depending on device. Generally no normal tracking/reset response. Prevent inappropriate response to physiologic or far-field signals. Normal sensing window Yes, if the signal crosses threshold. Yes, according to mode and timing rules. Detect intended intrinsic activity.   IMAGE 6.3.2-4   Learning purpose: Prevents learners from mislabelling correctly ignored events as device undersensing.   6.3.2.H3C6  Undersensing Undersensing occurs when the pacemaker fails to recognise a true intrinsic event that should be detected. Because the event does not reset or inhibit the timing cycle, a pacing stimulus may occur too soon after the intrinsic beat, may fall on a P wave, QRS, ST segment, or T wave, or may compete with the intrinsic rhythm. In a dual-chamber device, atrial undersensing can prevent appropriate tracking; ventricular undersensing can lead to unnecessary ventricular output. The key ECG clue is a pacing stimulus that appears despite a preceding intrinsic event that should have inhibited or reset the device. However, the interpreter must first exclude that the event occurred during a blanking or refractory period, was below the intracardiac signal amplitude despite being obvious on the surface ECG, or belonged to a chamber that the mode was not sensing. Cause category Examples Expected supporting evidence Programming Sensitivity set too insensitive; inappropriate timing windows; mode not sensing that chamber. Low or borderline sensed amplitude; event markers absent; problem may resolve with programming. Signal amplitude Small P or R wave, scar, changing rhythm morphology, lead position. Low measured electrogram amplitude; variable sensing with posture or rhythm. Lead / connection Dislodgement, fracture, insulation or connector problem. Change in sensing, impedance, threshold, noise, or imaging. Physiologic / rhythm Premature event inside refractory period, low-amplitude fibrillatory waves, ventricular ectopy with different vector. Timing-specific missed events; intracardiac electrogram clarifies classification.   UNDERSENSING SIGNATURE Intrinsic event is present, but the device behaves as though it did not occur. The next pacing output follows the device’s internal clock instead of being inhibited or reset.   IMAGE 6.3.2-5 Learning purpose: Separates true sensing failure from timing-related nonresponse and links mechanisms to surface ECG findings.     6.3.2.H3C7  Oversensing Oversensing occurs when the pacemaker detects an unintended signal as cardiac activity. Because the device believes an intrinsic event occurred, it may inhibit a needed output, reset a timing interval, create an inappropriate high-rate response, or store false arrhythmia episodes. In a pacing-dependent patient, ventricular oversensing can cause dangerous pauses or asystole. Oversensed signal Typical source Possible clue Lead noise Conductor fracture, insulation breach, connector problem, mechanical movement. High-frequency irregular electrogram; may be reproducible with movement; abnormal or variable impedance trend. Myopotential Pectoral or diaphragmatic skeletal muscle activity, more relevant in certain configurations. Noise associated with arm movement, deep inspiration, or muscle contraction. Electromagnetic interference External electrical field or equipment. Simultaneous noise across channels; temporal association with environment or procedure. T wave Ventricular repolarization detected after QRS. Double counting of QRS and T; apparent rapid sensing and pacing inhibition. Far-field R wave Ventricular depolarization detected by atrial channel. Atrial marker shortly after QRS, often affected by PVARP and atrial sensitivity. Atrial signal on ventricular channel / crosstalk Atrial pacing pulse or local signal detected in ventricular channel. Ventricular inhibition immediately after atrial output unless protected by blanking/safety pacing.   OVERSENSING SIGNATURE A pacing output is unexpectedly delayed or absent because the device has detected a signal that may not represent true intended chamber depolarization.   IMAGE 6.3.2-6   Learning purpose: Creates a visual differential diagnosis for oversensing and highlights that not all “sensed” events are cardiac.   6.3.2.H3C8  Atrial Crosstalk and Ventricular Safety Pacing Atrial crosstalk is detection of the atrial pacing stimulus by the ventricular sensing channel. If interpreted as a ventricular depolarization, it could inhibit ventricular output in a patient who needs it. Dual-chamber systems use ventricular blanking after atrial pacing to reduce this risk. Some systems also use ventricular safety pacing: if an event is sensed in a vulnerable crosstalk-detection window after atrial pacing, the device delivers a ventricular stimulus at a shortened, protected interval rather than completely inhibiting the ventricle. Safety pacing can produce closely spaced atrial and ventricular stimuli and may be mistaken for inappropriate timing. The exact algorithm, interval, and markers vary by manufacturer. The correct interpretation requires device-specific interrogation and knowledge of programmed features. IMAGE- 6.3.2-7 Learning purpose: Explains why a short AP-to-VP interval may represent a safety feature rather than malfunction.     6.3.2.H3C9  Marker Channels and Stored Electrograms Device marker channels label how the pacemaker classified events. Common generic abbreviations include AS for atrial sensed, AP for atrial paced, VS for ventricular sensed, and VP for ventricular paced. Additional markers may identify refractory events, noise, mode switch, safety pacing, premature ventricular events, or high-rate episodes. Marker names and conventions differ between manufacturers. Markers improve interpretation but are not infallible. A marker shows the device’s classification, not necessarily the true physiologic identity of the signal. For example, a VS marker may represent a true R wave, a T wave, lead noise, or cro

Chapter: CHAPTER 6.4 — TYPES OF PACEMAKERS

Topic: TOPIC 6.4.1: SINGLE-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.4.1: SINGLE-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Heading: Pacemaker – Types of Pacemakers

Single Chamber • Dual Chamber • Device Selection • Paced-Rhythm ECG     Hardware architecture of single- and dual-chamber pacing systems. Scope of this chapter This chapter explains conventional single- and dual-chamber pacemaker systems and their ECG behaviour. Device selection must be individualized by a qualified pacing specialist. Patients with reduced left ventricular function, high anticipated ventricular pacing burden, heart failure, congenital heart disease, or other complex conditions may require cardiac resynchronization therapy or conduction-system pacing rather than a routine single-versus-dual decision.     6.4.H1C1  Pacemaker – Types of Pacemakers 6.4.H1C2  Learning Objectives By the end of Chapter 6.4, learners will be able to: ·        Define single-chamber and dual-chamber pacemaker systems using both hardware configuration and programmed pacing mode. ·        Describe how an atrial single-chamber system differs from a ventricular single-chamber system. ·        Explain the roles of sensing, pacing, inhibition, triggering, tracking, AV delay, lower-rate limit, and rate response in common pacemaker modes. ·        Interpret the NBG pacing-code positions used in AAI, AAIR, VVI, VVIR, VDD, DDI, DDDR, and related modes. ·        Identify the major ECG patterns produced by single-chamber atrial pacing, single-chamber ventricular pacing, and dual-chamber pacing. ·        Differentiate AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, and AS-VS responses on a dual-chamber paced ECG. ·        Compare single- and dual-chamber systems across lead number, AV synchrony, hemodynamic benefit, procedural complexity, programming, follow-up, complications, and patient selection. ·        Use atrial rhythm, AV conduction, chronotropic competence, expected ventricular pacing burden, ventricular function, comorbidity, venous access, infection risk, and patient goals to explain the device-selection process. ·        Recognize situations in which a standard single- or dual-chamber pacemaker may be insufficient and CRT or conduction-system pacing should be considered. ·        Avoid common interpretive errors, including assuming that every single-chamber pacemaker is VVI, every dual-chamber system always paces both chambers, or every visible pacing spike indicates successful capture. ·        Communicate ECG observations accurately while remaining within the professional scope of a service engineer, sales professional, or clinical support team member. 6.4.H1C3  Chapter Overview A pacemaker is classified partly by the number of cardiac chambers it can sense and pace. A single-chamber system interacts primarily with one chamber—either the atrium or, much more commonly, the ventricle. A dual-chamber system interacts with both an atrium and a ventricle, allowing the device to coordinate atrial and ventricular timing when clinically appropriate. The classification is simple at the hardware level, but ECG interpretation and clinical selection require deeper reasoning. The central question is not merely “How many leads are present?” The more useful questions are: Which chamber needs support? Is organized atrial activity available? Is AV conduction reliable? Does the patient benefit from AV synchrony? How much ventricular pacing is expected? What is the ventricular function? Are there anatomical, infection, or frailty constraints? What future pacing strategy is most likely to preserve cardiac performance? A dual-chamber pacemaker can behave like a single-chamber system if programmed in a single-chamber mode, and a dual-chamber ECG may show no pacing spikes when intrinsic activity is faster than the programmed lower rate. Conversely, a ventricular single-chamber pacemaker may deliver life-sustaining pacing without producing atrial coordination. Therefore, the learner must separate hardware, mode, timing behavior, and clinical purpose. Core learning principle Device type, programmed mode, and moment-to-moment ECG response are related but not identical. Always identify all three before drawing a conclusion.   6.4.H1C4  Fundamentals and Core Concepts 6.4.H1C4.1  What “Chamber” Means in Pacemaker Classification In pacemaker terminology, “chamber” refers to a cardiac chamber in which the system can deliver pacing, sense intrinsic electrical activity, or both. The atrial chamber is usually the right atrium. The ventricular chamber is usually the right ventricle, although contemporary systems may use His-bundle pacing, left bundle branch area pacing, coronary sinus leads for resynchronization, or other specialized sites. In this chapter, the conventional terms atrial lead and ventricular lead are used unless otherwise stated. A single-chamber pulse generator generally connects to one pacing lead. A dual-chamber pulse generator generally connects to an atrial lead and a ventricular lead. However, hardware alone does not fully define behavior. A dual-chamber generator can be programmed to pace only the ventricle, and specialized VDD systems may sense atrial activity and pace the ventricle through a single lead without the ability to pace the atrium. 6.4.H1C4.2  Hardware Classification Versus Functional Mode Dimension Hardware question Functional question Single chamber Is there one intracardiac pacing lead or one leadless ventricular device? Which chamber is paced and sensed—atrium or ventricle? Dual chamber Are atrial and ventricular electrodes available? Is the device tracking, inhibiting, pacing, or mode-switching in each chamber? ECG behavior How many leads were implanted? Which events are intrinsic, sensed, paced, tracked, inhibited, or refractory at this moment?   6.4.H1C4.3  NBG Pacing-Code Essentials The standard pacing code describes device behavior. The first three positions are essential for ECG interpretation; the fourth commonly indicates rate modulation. A fifth position may describe multisite pacing. Position Meaning Common letters Interpretation I Chamber paced O, A, V, D None, atrium, ventricle, or dual II Chamber sensed O, A, V, D Where intrinsic activity is detected III Response to sensing O, I, T, D None, inhibited, triggered, or dual response IV Rate modulation O, R No rate response or rate-adaptive pacing V Multisite pacing O, A, V, D No multisite pacing or multisite chamber   Mode Plain-language meaning Typical learning context AAI / AAIR Atrium paced and sensed; atrial output inhibited by sensed atrial activity; R adds rate response. Selected sinus-node dysfunction with reliable AV conduction. VVI / VVIR Ventricle paced and sensed; ventricular output inhibited by sensed ventricular activity; R adds rate response. Permanent AF with bradycardia, ventricular backup, or selected leadless pacing. DDD / DDDR Both chambers paced and sensed; sensed events may inhibit or trigger timing responses; R adds rate response. Sinus rhythm with AV block, sinus-node dysfunction requiring atrial support, or combined disease. VDD Ventricle paced; atrium and ventricle sensed; atrial sensing can trigger ventricular pacing. AV block with reliable sinus activity when atrial pacing is not required; may be implemented with specialized lead systems. DDI / DDIR Both chambers can be paced and sensed, but atrial events do not track the ventricle in the same way as DDD. Selected atrial tachyarrhythmia-management or nontracking strategies.   6.4.H1C4.4  Demand Pacing and Timing Modern pacemakers commonly operate in demand modes. The device monitors the relevant chamber and withholds an output when an acceptable intrinsic event occurs within the timing interval. If no qualifying event is sensed before the escape interval expires, the pacemaker delivers a stimulus. In dual-chamber systems, the device also manages an AV delay between atrial activity and ventricular activation, upper tracking limits, refractory periods, blanking intervals, and mode-switch behavior. Rate-responsive modes add a sensor-driven pacing rate when the patient’s intrinsic rate does not rise adequately with activity. Rate response does not create AV synchrony by itself; it changes the pacing rate according to programmed sensor behavior. The letter “R” therefore describes rate adaptation, not an additional chamber. 6.4.H1C4.5  AV Synchrony and Its Clinical Importance AV synchrony means that atrial contraction occurs before ventricular contraction in a coordinated sequence. This sequence can support ventricular filling and cardiac output, particularly in patients who depend on atrial contribution. A dual-chamber system can preserve or reproduce this relationship by sensing or pacing the atrium and then allowing intrinsic ventricular conduction or delivering a ventricular stimulus after an AV delay. Loss of AV synchrony can produce symptoms in susceptible patients, including fatigue, dizziness, pulsations, dyspnea, hypotension, or the symptom complex historically described as pacemaker syndrome. Not every patient experiences a major hemodynamic difference, and procedural simplicity may appropriately outweigh AV coordination in selected situations. Device selection therefore balances physiologic benefit against lead-related and patient-specific risk. 6.4.H1C4.6  Ventricular Pacing Burden and Contemporary Pacing Strategy The percentage of ventricular beats paced over time is called ventricular pacing burden. Conventional right ventricular pacing can be appropriate and lifesaving, but a high pacing burden may create electrical and mechanical dyssynchrony in susceptible patients. The clinical significance depends on ventricular function, pacing site, substrate, duration, and individual response. When reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, heart failure, or a high anticipated ventricular pacing burden is present, the choice may extend beyond conventional single- versus dual-chamber pacing. Cardiac resynchronization therapy or conduction-system pacing may be considered according to specialist assessment and current guidance. This chapter therefore treats single versus dual as one branch of a broader pacing decision. Clinical boundary A non-prescribing learner may identify factors that influence device selection, but should not independently recommend a device for an individual patient. Escalate selection questions to the implanting electrophysiology or cardiology team.   IMAGE 6.4-1 LMS purpose: Establishes the meaning of chamber classification before mode codes are introduced.   IMAGE 6.4-2 LMS purpose: Interactive visual for code-decoding practice.   IMAGE  6.4-3 LMS purpose: Links pacing mode to hemodynamic physiology.   IMAGE 6.4-4 LMS purpose: Introduces why some patients need physiologic pacing or CRT evaluation.
