Topic: TOPIC 6.4.2: DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.4.2: DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Heading: TOPIC 6.4.2: DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

6.4.2.H2C1  Learning Objectives ·        Define a conventional dual-chamber pacemaker and describe its atrial and ventricular channels. ·        Explain DDD/DDDR pacing, AV delay, atrial tracking, inhibition, upper-rate behavior, and automatic mode switching. ·        Differentiate the four common moment-to-moment responses: AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, and AS-VS. ·        Identify common clinical situations in which preserving atrial support or AV synchrony is valuable. ·        Recognize advantages and trade-offs associated with a second lead and more complex programming. ·        Interpret dual-chamber paced ECGs systematically. ·        Distinguish dual-chamber hardware from VDD functional behavior and other mode variations. ·        Recognize when high ventricular pacing burden or ventricular dysfunction requires assessment for physiologic pacing or CRT. 6.4.2.H2C2  Definition and Fundamental Concept A dual-chamber pacemaker has the capacity to sense and/or pace both an atrium and a ventricle. In a conventional transvenous system, one lead is positioned in the right atrium and one lead is positioned in the right ventricle or a specialized ventricular conduction-system location. The pulse generator coordinates the two channels through programmed timing intervals. The major physiologic advantage is the ability to preserve or recreate AV synchrony. The device can pace the atrium when the sinus node is slow, allow intrinsic AV conduction when it occurs, pace the ventricle when conduction fails, and track sensed atrial activity up to programmed rate limits. Dual-chamber does not mean that every beat is paced in both chambers; the actual response depends on intrinsic rhythm and programming. 6.4.2.H2C3  DDD and DDDR Operation In DDD mode, both chambers can be paced and sensed. The “dual” response to sensing means that a sensed event may inhibit an output in the same chamber and may trigger a timing response in the other chamber. A sensed P wave can start an AV delay; if no intrinsic QRS is sensed before that delay ends, the device delivers a ventricular stimulus. A sensed ventricular event inhibits the scheduled ventricular output and resets relevant timing cycles. DDDR adds rate response. The atrial and ventricular pacing rate may increase according to sensor input when intrinsic chronotropic response is inadequate. The device must also respect the maximum tracking rate or upper sensor rate, depending on how the rate is generated. Figure 6.4.2-1. Dual-chamber AV-sequential pacing with atrial and ventricular capture.     6.4.2.H2C4  The Four Common Dual-Chamber Response Patterns A dual-chamber device may show any of four basic combinations on a surface ECG. Learning these combinations prevents the common error of expecting two pacing spikes on every beat.   Pattern Meaning Typical ECG appearance AP-VS Atrial paced, ventricular sensed Atrial spike followed by a paced P wave; native QRS occurs before the paced AV delay expires, so no ventricular spike is delivered. AS-VP Atrial sensed, ventricular paced Intrinsic P wave is detected; after the programmed AV delay, a ventricular spike and paced QRS occur because native conduction did not arrive in time. AP-VP Atrial paced, ventricular paced Atrial spike and captured P wave are followed by a ventricular spike and paced QRS after the paced AV delay. AS-VS Atrial sensed, ventricular sensed Intrinsic P wave and intrinsic QRS are both detected; the pacemaker may deliver no visible outputs while continuing to monitor and time events.   Figure 6.4.2-2. Four common dual-chamber ECG response patterns. 6.4.2.H2C5  AV Delay and Ventricular Pacing Minimization The AV delay is the programmed interval between an atrial event and the expected ventricular event. A paced AV delay begins after an atrial pacing stimulus; a sensed AV delay begins after a sensed atrial event. These values may differ because atrial sensing occurs after intrinsic atrial depolarization has already begun, whereas an atrial pacing stimulus initiates depolarization. When intrinsic AV conduction is reliable, programming strategies may allow the native QRS to occur and reduce unnecessary ventricular pacing. These strategies can use longer or dynamically managed AV intervals, search algorithms, or mode changes. Excessively long AV delays can also be hemodynamically unfavorable or create unexpected ECG appearances, so programming is individualized. 6.4.2.H2C6  Atrial Tracking and Upper-Rate Behavior Atrial tracking means that sensed atrial events initiate timing toward ventricular activation, allowing the ventricular rate to follow the atrial rate up to programmed limits. This supports physiologic rate response during sinus acceleration when AV conduction is absent or unreliable. Tracking is not unlimited. The maximum tracking rate and total atrial refractory period protect against excessively rapid ventricular pacing and shape upper-rate behavior. When atrial events occur too rapidly, the device may display Wenckebach-like upper-rate behavior, 2:1 block, or mode switching depending on the rhythm and programming. These patterns may be normal device responses rather than malfunction. Accurate interpretation requires the programmed upper-rate values and device markers. 6.4.2.H2C7  Automatic Mode Switching Automatic mode switching is designed to prevent rapid ventricular tracking of atrial tachyarrhythmias. When the device detects an atrial rate or pattern meeting programmed criteria, it changes from a tracking mode to a nontracking mode. After the atrial tachyarrhythmia ends and confirmation criteria are met, the device may return to the tracking mode. On the surface ECG, mode switching can produce an abrupt change in ventricular pacing behavior or rate. Atrial electrograms, marker channels, episode logs, detection duration, and programmed thresholds are used to confirm the mechanism. A regular ventricular paced rhythm during atrial fibrillation may therefore represent appropriate mode-switch operation. 6.4.2.H2C8  Common Clinical Contexts for Dual-Chamber Pacing Clinical context Why dual-chamber pacing may be valuable Programming/selection focus AV block with sinus rhythm Sensed atrial events can be followed by ventricular pacing, preserving atrial-ventricular sequence. Tracking rate, AV delay, ventricular pacing strategy, ventricular function. Sinus-node dysfunction with intermittent bradycardia The atrium can be paced while intrinsic ventricular conduction is preserved when available. Rate response, AV conduction, minimizing unnecessary ventricular pacing. Combined sinus-node and AV conduction disease Both atrial support and ventricular backup are available. DDDR timing, mode switching, pacing burden. Intermittent high-grade AV block Atrial rhythm can guide ventricular timing while reliable backup is maintained. Detection of conduction, AV delay, symptom correlation. Selected cardioinhibitory reflex syncope Dual-chamber pacing may be used in carefully selected patients with documented cardioinhibitory mechanisms. Strict indication criteria, age, documented rhythm, specialist assessment.   6.4.2.H2C9  Advantages of Dual-Chamber Systems ·        Ability to support the atrium and ventricle independently. ·        Preservation or recreation of AV synchrony when organized atrial activity is present. ·        Atrial tracking during sinus rhythm when ventricular conduction is absent or unreliable. ·        Atrial diagnostics that support recognition and burden assessment of atrial tachyarrhythmias. ·        Ventricular backup if AV conduction deteriorates in a patient with sinus-node dysfunction. ·        Flexible programming that can promote intrinsic conduction, provide rate response, and adapt during atrial tachyarrhythmias. ·        Potential reduction in pacemaker-syndrome symptoms compared with ventricular-only pacing in susceptible patients. 6.4.2.H2C10  Limitations and Trade-Offs ·        A second transvenous lead adds implant and long-term lead-management complexity. ·        Atrial lead dislodgement, insulation failure, conductor fracture, sensing problems, and threshold changes become possible. ·        More complex timing can create upper-rate, refractory, mode-switch, or far-field-sensing patterns that require careful interpretation. ·        Dual-chamber pacing does not eliminate the risk associated with a high conventional RV pacing burden. ·        An atrial lead may provide little benefit in permanent AF or atrial standstill. ·        More hardware may be undesirable in selected patients with infection risk, venous obstruction, frailty, or limited life expectancy. ·        A dual-chamber system must be programmed and followed appropriately; implanting two leads alone does not guarantee physiologic pacing. 6.4.2.H2C11  Dual-Chamber ECG Interpretation Sequence 1. Identify P waves, QRS complexes, atrial pacing spikes, and ventricular pacing spikes. 2. Classify each beat as AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, or AS-VS. 3. Confirm atrial capture after each atrial stimulus and ventricular capture after each ventricular stimulus. 4. Measure the paced or sensed AV interval where visible. 5. Determine whether intrinsic ventricular conduction appropriately inhibits ventricular output. 6. Check whether atrial events are being tracked, ignored in a refractory period, or managed by mode switching. 7. Assess upper-rate behavior when the atrial rate is elevated. 8. Compare QRS morphology across paced, intrinsic, fusion, and pseudofusion beats. 9. Use marker channels and intracardiac electrograms to distinguish true sensing failure from programmed blanking or refractory behavior.

Heading: 6.4.2.H2C12  Dual-Chamber Clinical Scenarios

6.4.2.H2C12  Dual-Chamber Clinical Scenarios Scenario Likely ECG response Interpretive point Sinus bradycardia with intact AV conduction AP-VS The atrium is paced; the QRS conducts intrinsically before ventricular pacing is required. Normal sinus rate with complete AV block AS-VP Each sensed P wave initiates an AV delay followed by ventricular pacing. Sinus-node dysfunction plus complete AV block AP-VP Both chambers require pacing support. Normal intrinsic sinus rhythm and AV conduction above lower rate AS-VS No pacing spike may be visible despite normal device operation. Atrial fibrillation detected during DDD operation Mode-switched nontracking ventricular support Rapid atrial activity should not be tracked to the ventricle once mode-switch criteria are met. Atrial rate exceeds maximum tracking capability Upper-rate behavior Wenckebach-like timing or 2:1 tracking can be programmed behavior, not failure.   6.4.2.H2C13  Clinical Pearls – Dual-Chamber Pacemakers ·        Dual-chamber hardware does not mean both chambers are paced on every beat. ·        AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, and AS-VS are the four basic response patterns to identify first. ·        A sensed P wave can trigger an AV delay without producing an atrial pacing spike. ·        A ventricular spike is inhibited when an intrinsic QRS is sensed before the AV delay ends. ·        Paced and sensed AV delays may be programmed differently. ·        Upper-rate behavior is a timing response and should not be labeled malfunction without programmed values. ·        Automatic mode switching protects against rapid tracking of atrial tachyarrhythmias. ·        Atrial lead information improves diagnostics but also creates additional sensing and lead-failure possibilities. ·

Topic: TOPIC 6.4.3: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SINGLE- AND DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.4.3: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SINGLE- AND DUAL-CHAMBER PACEMAKERS

Heading: Difference Between Single- and Dual-Chamber Pacemakers

The difference between single- and dual-chamber pacing is best understood across five domains: hardware, electrical behavior, hemodynamics, clinical use, and long-term management. No single domain should determine the choice in isolation.   Comparison factor Single chamber Dual chamber Primary chamber capability One chamber: atrium or ventricle. Both atrium and ventricle. Typical transvenous leads One. Two. Common modes AAI/AAIR or VVI/VVIR. DDD/DDDR, DDI/DDIR; other configurations possible. Atrial pacing Available only in an atrial single-chamber system. Available when an atrial lead and suitable programming are present. Ventricular pacing Available only in a ventricular single-chamber system. Available through the ventricular channel. AV synchrony Not actively maintained by VVI; AAI relies on native AV conduction. Can be preserved through sensing, pacing, and AV timing. Atrial tracking Not available in a ventricular single-chamber system. Available in tracking modes such as DDD or VDD. Protection if AV block develops Atrial-only pacing does not provide ventricular backup. Ventricular backup is available. Permanent AF VVI/VVIR often fits when atrial activity is not useful. Atrial lead may add little benefit unless rhythm strategy or future needs justify it. Sinus rhythm with AV block VVI can provide rate support but loses atrial coordination. Often favored to coordinate sensed atrial activity with ventricular support. Sinus-node dysfunction AAI may support atrium if AV conduction is reliable; VVI may cause AV dyssynchrony. Can pace atrium and provide ventricular backup, often while minimizing ventricular pacing. Atrial arrhythmia diagnostics Limited without atrial channel. More direct atrial electrogram and burden information. Implant complexity Generally fewer transvenous components. Additional lead placement and testing. Lead-related risk One lead can fail or become infected. Two leads create more potential lead-related failure points. Programming complexity Usually simpler timing. More complex AV, upper-rate, refractory, and mode-switch settings. ECG appearance Atrial-paced with native QRS or ventricular-paced wide QRS. May show AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, or AS-VS. Pacemaker syndrome risk May be greater with ventricular-only pacing in susceptible patients. AV coordination can reduce symptoms in appropriate patients. Ventricular pacing burden Can be high in VVI depending on indication and intrinsic rhythm. Can be minimized with suitable programming, but may still be high in AV block. Leadless option Established mainly as ventricular single-chamber pacing, with evolving coordination features. Fully leadless dual-chamber platforms are evolving and product-specific; conventional dual-chamber pacing uses two leads. Future upgrade considerations May require additional lead or system change if needs evolve. Broader capability initially, but future CRT/ICD needs can still require upgrade. Best choice Best when one chamber provides the needed therapy with acceptable trade-offs. Best when atrial support, AV synchrony, tracking, or ventricular backup provides meaningful benefit.   6.4.3.H2C2  What Single Chamber Does Better Single-chamber systems can be more appropriate when a second chamber adds little therapeutic value. This is especially relevant when organized atrial activity is permanently absent, when procedural or lead burd   en should be minimized, or when a leadless ventricular approach is selected. Simplicity is a clinical advantage only when it still meets the patient’s pacing requirements. 6.4.3.H2C3  What Dual Chamber Does Better Dual-chamber systems provide timing coordination between atrial and ventricular activity. They can support sinus-node dysfunction, track atrial activity during AV block, provide ventricular backup when conduction fails, and supply atrial diagnostics. These benefits are most meaningful when the atrium is organized and AV synchrony contributes to symptoms, exercise capacity, or hemodynamic stability.         6.4.3.H2C4  Common Misconceptions Misconception Correction Dual chamber is always superior. The best system is the least complex system that safely meets present and anticipated clinical needs. Single chamber always means ventricular pacing. A single-chamber system may be atrial or ventricular, although ventricular systems are more common. Two leads mean both chambers are always paced. A dual-chamber device may sense both chambers and deliver no pacing when intrinsic rhythm is adequate. A narrow QRS proves the ventricle was not paced. Pacing site and fusion can produce variable QRS width; timing and device information are required. A leadless pacemaker is automatically dual chamber because it can sense atrial motion. Atrial mechanical sensing can coordinate ventricular pacing but does not necessarily provide true atrial pacing or the full behavior of a two-lead system. A second lead only adds benefit. It adds capability and diagnostic information, but also adds procedural and long-term lead risk. Mode can be inferred from the implant card device type alone. The actual programmed mode and current response must be confirmed.   6.4.3.H2C5  Comparison Clinical Pearls ·       Compare therapeutic capability, not only lead count. ·       Organized atrial activity is a major branch point in the choice. ·       AV conduction reliability determines whether atrial-only pacing is safe and durable. ·       AV synchrony is valuable but must be weighed against added lead burden. ·       Permanent AF often favors ventricular-only support when pacing is required. ·       High expected ventricular pacing burden changes the discussion toward ventricular-function preservation. ·       Frailty, infection risk, venous access, anatomy, MRI needs, and future upgrades are legitimate selection factors. ·       A device selected for today should also anticipate likely progression of conduction disease. ·       Hardware capability and programmed mode must be documented separately. ·       No comparison table replaces individualized specialist assessment.     IMAGE 6.4.3-1 LMS purpose: Chapter anchor infographic for revision and LMS summary.   IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.4.3-2 LMS purpose: Interactive flip-card content.   IMAGE 6.4.3-3 . Topic: Topic 6.4.4 – Clinical Indication: Which Pacemaker to Choose?

Topic Description: Topic 6.4.4 – Clinical Indication: Which Pacemaker to Choose?

Heading: Clinical Indication: Which Pacemaker to Choose?

  Pacemaker selection begins only after the indication for permanent pacing has been established. The device type is then chosen by integrating rhythm diagnosis, conduction-system behavior, ventricular function, symptom mechanism, expected pacing burden, procedural risk, anatomy, comorbidity, patient goals, and the likely future course of disease. Important distinction “Does the patient need a pacemaker?” and “Which pacing system is most appropriate?” are two separate clinical decisions.   6.4.4.H2C2  Step 1 – Confirm the Clinical Problem ·       Identify the documented bradyarrhythmia or conduction disorder. ·       Establish whether symptoms correlate with the rhythm abnormality when correlation is required. ·       Exclude reversible causes such as medication effect, electrolyte disturbance, ischemia, infection, or temporary postoperative changes where appropriate. ·       Determine whether the need is intermittent backup, continuous pacing, rate support during activity, AV coordination, or resynchronization. ·       Assess urgency and pacing dependency. 6.4.4.H2C3  Step 2 – Evaluate Atrial Rhythm Organized atrial rhythm allows atrial sensing, atrial pacing, and atrial tracking to provide clinical value. Permanent AF, atrial standstill, or severely diseased atrial tissue may remove or reduce that value. Paroxysmal AF does not necessarily eliminate the value of a dual-chamber system because sinus rhythm may be present much of the time and mode switching can manage atrial tachyarrhythmias. Atrial status Selection implication Stable sinus rhythm Atrial support and AV synchrony can be considered. Sinus-node dysfunction Assess atrial pacing need, chronotropic response, and AV conduction. Paroxysmal AF Dual-chamber pacing may remain useful; mode-switch capability is important. Permanent AF Atrial pacing/tracking usually provides limited benefit; ventricular support may be sufficient. Atrial standstill or absent atrial capture Atrial lead benefit may be limited or absent. Frequent atrial tachyarrhythmia Assess mode switching, atrial sensing quality, symptom goals, and rhythm-management plan.   6.4.4.H2C4  Step 3 – Evaluate AV Conduction Reliable AV conduction allows an atrial-paced impulse to activate the ventricles intrinsically. Unreliable or absent AV conduction creates a need for ventricular backup. The evaluation considers resting conduction, conduction at higher atrial rates, documented AV block, bundle-branch disease, progression risk, medication effects, and the planned pacing rate. Atrial-only pacing should not be chosen simply because AV conduction appears normal on one resting ECG. The clinical team considers whether conduction remains dependable during activity and over the anticipated life of the device. 6.4.4.H2C5  Step 4 – Evaluate Chronotropic Competence Chronotropic competence is the ability to raise heart rate appropriately with exercise or metabolic demand. A patient with sinus-node dysfunction may need atrial pacing and rate response. A patient with permanent AF and slow ventricular response may need ventricular rate response. Rate-adaptive pacing is programmed only after considering activity level, sensor type, medications, pulmonary disease, and the desired rate profile. 6.4.4.H2C6  Step 5 – Estimate Ventricular Pacing Burden and Assess LV Function A patient with complete AV block may require ventricular pacing on nearly every beat. A patient with intermittent block may require only occasional backup. The expected burden influences the ventricular pacing strategy. Left ventricular ejection fraction, heart-failure symptoms, QRS pattern, existing dyssynchrony, and anticipated pacing percentage must be reviewed before choosing a conventional RV pacing strategy. When ventricular function is reduced or substantial pacing is anticipated, the specialist may consider cardiac resynchronization therapy or conduction-system pacing to reduce the risk of pacing-related heart failure. A standard dual-chamber pacemaker can preserve AV synchrony while still creating a high RV pacing burden; these are separate issues. 6.4.4.H2C7  Step 6 – Evaluate Procedure and Hardware Constraints ·        Venous patency and prior central venous devices. ·        Previous device infection or active infection risk. ·        Need for dialysis access preservation. ·        Congenital anatomy or prior cardiac surgery. ·        Tricuspid valve disease or intervention. ·        Anticoagulation and bleeding risk. ·        Expected ability to attend follow-up and remote monitoring. ·        MRI-conditional system requirements and compatibility of all implanted components. ·        Future likelihood of ICD, CRT, or additional pacing needs. ·        Patient preference after informed discussion of benefits and trade-offs.             6.4.4.H2C8  Simplified Selection Pathway   Figure 6.4.4-1. Simplified educational pathway for pacemaker type selection.           The pathway is intentionally simplified. It is designed to organize thinking, not to replace guideline tables, electrophysiology assessment, product-specific constraints, or shared decision-making   6.4.4.H2C9  Clinical Indication Matrix Clinical situation Common educational direction Critical modifiers Permanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia or AV block Single-chamber ventricular pacing commonly considered. Organized atrial activity absent; rate response and ventricular strategy remain important. Sinus-node dysfunction with intact AV conduction Dual-chamber pacing with minimized ventricular pacing often considered; atrial-only pacing is selective. Need for atrial support, progression risk of AV block, exercise conduction, reoperation risk. Complete AV block with sinus rhythm Dual-chamber pacing commonly considered to preserve atrial timing. Expected pacing burden, LV function, physiologic pacing/CRT assessment. Intermittent high-grade AV block with sinus rhythm Dual-chamber backup commonly considered. Atrial tracking and reliable ventricular protection. Combined sinus-node disease and AV block Dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing often considered. Both chambers require support; mode switch and pacing burden. Carotid sinus syndrome or reflex syncope with documented cardioinhibitory asystole Dual-chamber pacing may be used in carefully selected patients. Strict diagnostic criteria and specialist selection. High infection risk with permanent AF and ventricular pacing need Leadless ventricular pacing may be considered. Anatomy, access, future pacing needs, device-specific limitations. Reduced LVEF with high anticipated ventricular pacing Do not limit choice to standard single versus dual. Evaluate CRT or conduction-system pacing. Atrial standstill with AV block Atrial lead provides little functional benefit. Ventricular or advanced strategy based on ventricular function and pacing burden. Congenital heart disease or post-surgical anatomy Individualized system. Anatomy, surgical access, epicardial/transvenous options, long-term lead plan.   6.4.4.H2C10  Twelve Worked Selection Scenarios Scenario 1: Clinical reasoning A 78-year-old with permanent AF, dizziness, and ventricular rates of 30–35 bpm. Reasoned direction: A ventricular single-chamber strategy may meet the pacing need because organized atrial activity is absent. Evaluate rate response, ventricular function, access, and infection history.   Scenario 2: Clinical reasoning A 64-year-old with complete AV block, normal sinus node function, and preserved EF. Reasoned direction: Dual-chamber tracking can preserve atrial-ventricular sequence. Estimate pacing burden and consider the ventricular activation strategy.   Scenario 3: Clinical reasoning A 58-year-old with symptomatic sinus pauses and normal AV conduction. Reasoned direction: Atrial support is required. A dual-chamber system often provides ventricular backup and future flexibility; atrial-only pacing is a selective strategy.   Scenario 4: Clinical reasoning A 72-year-old with sinus-node dysfunction and intermittent Mobitz II block. Reasoned direction: Dual-chamber pacing is generally needed because both atrial support and ventricular backup are relevant.   Scenario 5: Clinical reasoning A 49-year-old with permanent AF, prior transvenous device infection, and no need for defibrillation. Reasoned direction: A leadless ventricular system may be considered after infection control and specialist evaluation.   Scenario 6: Clinical reasoning An 84-year-old with permanent AF, advanced frailty, and symptomatic slow ventricular response. Reasoned direction: A simpler ventricular system may align with goals of care, but the choice should follow shared decision-making rather than age alone.   Scenario 7: Clinical reasoning A 68-year-old with complete AV block, LVEF 35%, and anticipated near-100% ventricular pacing. Reasoned direction: The decision should include CRT or conduction-system pacing, not only standard dual-chamber RV pacing.   Scenario 8: Clinical reasoning A 55-year-old with isolated chronotropic incompetence and intact AV conduction. Reasoned direction: A rate-responsive atrial-support strategy is needed; dual-chamber pacing may offer backup and diagnostics.   Scenario 9: Clinical reasoning A patient with paroxysmal AF and symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction. Reasoned direction: Dual-chamber pacing can support sinus rhythm periods; mode switching reduces inappropriate tracking during AF.   Scenario 10: Clinical reasoning A patient with atrial standstill and complete AV block. Reasoned direction: Atrial pacing and tracking provide no useful function; choose ventricular/advanced pacing based on ventricular needs.   Scenario 11: Clinical reasoning A dialysis patient with limited upper-extremity venous access and permanent AF. Reasoned direction: Leadless ventricular pacing may reduce transvenous hardware, but access and long-term strategy require specialist review.   Scenario 12: Clinical reasoning A patient with DDD pacing and a high RV pacing percentage who develops falling EF. Reasoned direction: Reassess for pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and possible upgrade to CRT or conduction-system pacing.

Topic: Topic 6.4.5: ECG Showing Paced Rhythm

Topic Description: Topic 6.4.5: ECG Showing Paced Rhythm

Heading: 6.4.5.H2C1  Learning Objectives

6.4.5.H2C1  Learning Objectives ·        Identify atrial, ventricular, and AV-sequential pacing spikes. ·        Confirm atrial and ventricular capture. ·        Differentiate intrinsic, atrial-paced, ventricular-paced, and dual-chamber paced events. ·        Classify dual-chamber beats as AP-VS, AS-VP, AP-VP, or AS-VS. ·        Recognize demand inhibition, fusion, pseudofusion, and normal rate-related changes. ·        Distinguish a normal paced pattern from suspected failure to pace, failure to capture, undersensing, or oversensing. ·        Use a structured surface-ECG interpretation sequence and correlate it with device data. 6.4.5.H2C2  ECG Prerequisites Before analyzing a paced rhythm, confirm paper speed, calibration, lead selection, filtering, gain, and recording quality. Pacing spikes can be attenuated by display filters, bipolar lead configuration, low gain, or digital processing. A clean baseline and multiple leads improve confidence. The clinical state of the patient takes priority over perfect rhythm classification. 6.4.5.H2C3  Single-Chamber Atrial-Paced Rhythm The defining sequence is atrial stimulus → atrial depolarization → native AV conduction → QRS. The atrial pacing spike is usually narrow and immediately precedes the paced P wave. The PR interval reflects conduction from the paced atrial site through the AV node to the ventricles. The QRS is usually narrow unless baseline bundle-branch block, aberrancy, pre-excitation, or another conduction abnormality is present. Atrial spike without a P wave suggests atrial noncapture. A paced P wave without a subsequent QRS may reflect AV block. Atrial-only systems cannot directly rescue the ventricle, making this distinction clinically important.   Figure 6.4.5-1. ECG pattern: atrial-paced rhythm with ventricular sensing. 6.4.5.H2C4  Single-Chamber Ventricular-Paced Rhythm The defining sequence is ventricular stimulus → ventricular depolarization. A ventricular pacing spike is followed immediately by a paced QRS complex. The QRS is commonly wide because myocardial activation begins at the pacing site rather than using the entire native His–Purkinje system. Secondary ST–T changes are expected and are usually discordant to the major QRS direction. Intrinsic ventricular beats can inhibit pacing in VVI. The resulting strip may contain a mixture of intrinsic beats, paced beats, fusion beats, and pseudofusion spikes. A pacing interval longer than expected may be normal if an intrinsic event reset the escape interval or if hysteresis is programmed. Figure 6.4.5-2. ECG pattern: ventricular-paced rhythm in a single-chamber system. 6.4.5.H2C5  Dual-Chamber AV-Sequential Paced Rhythm In AP-VP rhythm, an atrial pacing spike is followed by a paced P wave. After the paced AV delay, a ventricular pacing spike is followed by a paced QRS. The interval between atrial and ventricular spikes reflects programmed timing, but the surface ECG may not show the exact intracardiac timing because stimulus artefact, chamber activation, and display processing influence measurements. Figure 6.4.5-3. ECG pattern: dual-chamber AV-sequential pacing. 6.4.5.H2C6  Atrial-Sensed, Ventricular-Paced Rhythm In AS-VP rhythm, an intrinsic P wave occurs without an atrial pacing spike. The pacemaker senses the P wave and starts the sensed AV delay. If an intrinsic QRS is not sensed before the delay expires, the device delivers a ventricular stimulus followed by a paced QRS. This pattern is typical when sinus-node function is intact but AV conduction is absent or too slow.   Figure 6.4.5-4. ECG pattern: atrial-sensed, ventricular-paced tracking rhythm. 6.4.5.H2C7  Atrial-Paced, Ventricular-Sensed Rhythm In AP-VS rhythm, an atrial stimulus and paced P wave are followed by an intrinsic QRS before the paced AV delay ends. The ventricular output is inhibited. This is common when sinus-node dysfunction requires atrial support but AV conduction remains intact. It can also be produced by algorithms designed to reduce unnecessary ventricular pacing. 6.4.5.H2C8  Atrial-Sensed, Ventricular-Sensed Rhythm In AS-VS rhythm, both chambers depolarize intrinsically above the lower-rate limit and within appropriate timing. No pacing spikes may be visible. The absence of pacing on a short ECG does not mean that the pacemaker is off or malfunctioning. The device may be monitoring, recording, and providing backup without delivering output. 6.4.5.H2C9  Fusion and Pseudofusion Fusion occurs when an intrinsic ventricular wavefront and a paced wavefront activate the ventricle at nearly the same time, producing a hybrid QRS morphology. Pseudofusion occurs when a pacing spike appears on an intrinsic QRS but does not materially contribute to ventricular activation because the myocardium is already depolarizing or refractory. Pseudofusion can look alarming but does not necessarily indicate inappropriate capture or malfunction. Figure 6.4.5-5. Topic: TOPIC 6.5.1: SENSING

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.5.1: SENSING

Heading: Electrical Concepts

Pacemaker sensing, EGM interpretation, impedance, threshold, safety margins and electromagnetic interference Figure 6.5-1. The pacemaker system is a closed electrical loop: sense, decide, pace and verify. Scope of this chapter This chapter explains the electrical measurements that make a pacemaker safe and clinically useful. It is written for service engineers, clinical support personnel, field application specialists and learners who must connect device data to ECG, EGM, lead integrity and patient risk. It is educational content and does not replace device-specific manuals, institutional protocols or physician judgment.   H1C1  Electrical Concepts H1C2  Learning Objectives At the end of this chapter, the learner should be able to: • Define pacemaker sensing and explain why demand pacing depends on reliable recognition of intrinsic cardiac activity. • Distinguish intrinsic signal amplitude from the programmed sensitivity threshold and correctly apply the inverse mV relationship. • Explain how atrial and ventricular electrograms are acquired, filtered, annotated and displayed with marker channels. • Identify normal sensing, undersensing and oversensing using surface ECG, intracardiac EGM, marker annotations and interval behaviour. • Describe common causes of undersensing, including low-amplitude signals, lead displacement, conductor or connection problems, inappropriate sensitivity programming and timing-window interactions. • Describe common causes of oversensing, including EMI, myopotentials, lead noise, far-field signals, crosstalk and T-wave sensing. • Define pacing lead impedance, explain its measurement using the voltage-current relationship and interpret stable, abrupt and gradual trends. • Define capture threshold and explain amplitude, pulse width, rheobase, chronaxie and the strength-duration relationship. • Explain a conceptual threshold test and identify the transition between consistent capture and loss of capture. • Explain the purpose of pacing safety margins and the trade-off between capture reliability and battery longevity. • Identify important sources of electromagnetic interference in hospitals and explain how MRI and electrocautery affect sensing and device behaviour. • Describe possible EMI outcomes including oversensing, pacing inhibition, noise response, magnet response, mode change and rare reset events. • Use a patient-first troubleshooting sequence integrating symptoms, rhythm, ECG, EGM, markers, impedance, threshold, programming and trends. • Recognize situations requiring immediate escalation, particularly in pacemaker-dependent patients or when capture is uncertain. H1C3  Chapter Overview A pacemaker is often described as a pulse generator that delivers an electrical impulse when the heart is too slow. That description is correct but incomplete. Modern pacing is possible because the device continuously performs four connected electrical tasks: it receives intracardiac signals, decides whether those signals represent real atrial or ventricular activation, delivers a programmed output when pacing is required, and stores measurements that allow the clinical team to judge system performance over time. Sensing, impedance and threshold are therefore not unrelated programmer values. Together they describe the functional electrical relationship among the pulse generator, lead, electrode, lead-tissue interface and myocardium. Sensing asks whether the device can hear the heart. Impedance asks whether the electrical pathway appears intact. Threshold asks how much energy is required to stimulate the heart. Safety margin asks how much reserve is needed above that minimum. EMI asks whether the device can be confused by an electrical or magnetic source outside the heart. Central interpretation principle A single value may be normal while the system is clinically abnormal, or abnormal while the patient is stable. Always combine the value with the trend, programmed configuration, ECG/EGM evidence, marker annotations, symptoms, lead age, procedure history and pacemaker dependence.   H1C4  Fundamentals: The Pacemaker as a Closed Electrical System An intrinsic myocardial depolarization creates a small electrical potential at the electrode. The signal travels through the lead conductor to the pulse generator, where the sensing amplifier and filters process it. The timing circuit classifies the event and decides whether pacing should be inhibited, tracked, triggered or allowed to occur. If pacing is delivered, current travels through the lead and across the lead-tissue interface. Capture occurs only when the delivered electrical field depolarizes enough excitable myocardium. Every stage can fail differently. A small intrinsic signal may remain below the sensitivity threshold. A damaged conductor may create intermittent high-frequency noise that is incorrectly sensed. An insulation defect may change the current path. Fibrosis or lead displacement may increase stimulation threshold. Strong EMI may enter the sensing channel and be classified as cardiac activity. The surface ECG may reveal the consequence, while the EGM and marker channel reveal what the device believed happened. Figure 6.5-2. Closed-loop view of pacemaker electrical function. IMAGE 6.5-01 Learning purpose: Establish the chapter’s mental model that sensing and pacing use the same implanted system but answer different electrical questions.       H1C5  The Core Electrical Measurements Measurement What it represents Unit Primary question Do not interpret without Intrinsic amplitude Size of the local atrial or ventricular signal presented to the sensing channel mV Is the signal large and stable enough to be recognized? EGM morphology, sensitivity, polarity, rate and trend Sensitivity setting Minimum signal amplitude or dynamic sensing criterion required for detection mV or algorithm How easily will the device classify an incoming signal as sensed? Device-specific sensing method, blanking and refractory periods Lead impedance Electrical opposition of the selected pacing circuit ohms Does the circuit appear intact and stable? Baseline, trend, polarity, lead model and context Capture threshold Minimum output that consistently depolarizes myocardium at a stated pulse width V at ms What energy is required to capture the chamber? Capture evidence, lead maturation, medications, electrolytes and trend Programmed output Amplitude and pulse width delivered during pacing V and ms Is reserve adequate above threshold? Threshold, automatic capture algorithm and dependence   Units matter Intrinsic signal amplitude and sensitivity are commonly shown in millivolts, but they are not interchangeable. Impedance is measured in ohms. Pacing output is described by amplitude and pulse width. A threshold result is incomplete unless the pulse width is stated.  

Heading: Sensing

Topic 6.5.1: Sensing What it is, how it is measured, why it matters and how EGMs make it visible H2C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define sensing as the detection and classification of intrinsic intracardiac electrical activity. • Explain the sensing pathway from myocardial depolarization to device marker annotation. • Interpret atrial and ventricular intrinsic amplitudes using programmer EGMs and test functions. • Correctly explain the inverse sensitivity scale. • Differentiate surface ECG, near-field EGM and far-field EGM. • Explain the role of filters, gain, polarity, blanking and refractory periods. • List the clinical and engineering advantages of reliable sensing. H2C2  What Is Pacemaker Sensing? Sensing is the pacemaker’s ability to detect electrical activity generated by the patient’s own heart. In a demand pacing mode, the device continuously monitors the atrial channel, ventricular channel or both. When a valid intrinsic event is detected, the device places a marker, resets one or more timing intervals and responds according to the programmed mode. The response may be inhibition of a scheduled pacing pulse, initiation of an AV delay, tracking of atrial activity, rate calculation, episode storage or activation of a diagnostic algorithm. The word detect has two layers. First, the electrical signal must physically reach the input amplifier with adequate amplitude and frequency content. Second, device logic must accept the signal as a valid event rather than blank it, classify it as refractory, reject it as noise or ignore it because it falls below the sensing criterion. Therefore, the presence of a visible P wave or QRS on the surface ECG does not guarantee that the pacemaker sensed it. In simple terms Sensing is the device listening to the heart. Pacing is the device speaking to the heart. A safe pacemaker must know when to listen, what to accept as a true beat and when to remain silent.   IMAGE  6.5-02     H2C3  How the Device Detects Intrinsic Signals 1. The myocardium depolarizes and creates a changing electrical potential near the electrode. 2. The selected electrode pair samples the local voltage difference, commonly tip-to-ring for bipolar sensing or tip-to-can for unipolar sensing. 3. The signal travels through lead conductors to the pulse-generator connector and input circuitry. 4. Input protection and filtering reduce frequencies or amplitudes unlikely to represent the intended cardiac signal. 5. The sensing amplifier compares the processed signal with a fixed or dynamically changing detection threshold. 6. If the signal crosses the criterion outside a blanking period, the device records a sensed event and assigns a marker such as AS or VS. 7. Timing logic uses the event to inhibit, trigger, track, count, store or classify subsequent activity according to the programmed mode and algorithms. The exact sensing architecture differs by manufacturer and device family. Some systems use a fixed programmed sensitivity, others use automatic gain or auto-adjusting thresholds, and many use a dynamic threshold that changes after paced or sensed events. Device-specific terms must therefore be interpreted using the relevant technical manual. H2C4  Detecting Intrinsic Atrial and Ventricular Signals Atrial sensing is designed primarily to recognize local atrial depolarization, represented by the P wave on the surface ECG and an atrial EGM on the device channel. Ventricular sensing is designed primarily to recognize ventricular depolarization, represented by the QRS or R wave. The device does not see the ECG exactly as an external monitor sees it. It sees the voltage difference between selected intracardiac electrodes after device-specific filtering and amplification.   Characteristic Atrial channel Ventricular channel Desired near-field signal Local atrial depolarization Local ventricular depolarization Common unwanted signals Far-field R wave, atrial myopotential, EMI, lead noise T wave, myopotential, EMI, lead noise Consequence of missed signal Loss of tracking, inappropriate atrial pacing or timing error Inappropriate ventricular pacing and competitive pacing risk Consequence of false signal False atrial high-rate detection or mode switch Pacing inhibition, pause or false rate detection Key review tools Atrial EGM, AS/AR/AP markers and P-wave trend Ventricular EGM, VS/VR/VP markers and R-wave trend   H2C5  How Sensing Is Measured Sensing is commonly assessed by measuring the device-defined amplitude of intrinsic atrial and ventricular electrograms. The programmer may display an instantaneous measurement, a test result, a histogram or a longitudinal trend. The value is expressed in millivolts. Larger intrinsic amplitudes generally provide more separation from the sensing threshold, but morphology, noise and stability are equally important. 1. E

Topic: Topic 6.5.2: Sensing Issues

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.2: Sensing Issues

Heading: Topic Learning Objectives

Undersensing, oversensing and a structured approach to ECG–EGM troubleshooting H3C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define undersensing and oversensing using device behaviour rather than surface appearance alone. • Identify the ECG, EGM and marker features of each sensing problem. • List programming, lead, tissue, rhythm and EMI causes. • Explain clinical consequences in dependent and non-dependent patients. • Apply a safe troubleshooting sequence and recognize red-flag findings. H3C2  Normal Sensing, Undersensing and Oversensing Figure 6.5-5. Conceptual comparison of appropriate sensing, undersensing and oversensing.         Behaviour Definition Device consequence Common ECG/EGM clue Appropriate sensing True intrinsic event is detected and correctly classified Pacing inhibited, tracked or timing reset appropriately Sensed marker aligns with intended P wave or QRS Undersensing True intrinsic event is not recognized Scheduled pacing may occur despite intrinsic activity; tracking may fail Intrinsic event present without expected marker or timing reset Oversensing Non-target or non-cardiac signal is classified as a true event Pacing may be inhibited; timing or diagnostics may be altered Markers appear without corresponding intended cardiac depolarization   H3C3  Undersensing: Failure to Detect a True Signal Undersensing occurs when a genuine intrinsic atrial or ventricular depolarization fails to meet the device detection or classification criteria. The heart has produced an event, but the pacemaker does not respond as though it occurred. In an inhibited pacing mode, a scheduled pacing pulse may therefore occur despite the presence of intrinsic activity. Undersensing may be continuous, intermittent, rate-dependent, posture-dependent or limited to a particular morphology. A missed P wave can prevent atrial tracking. A missed R wave can permit ventricular pacing near an intrinsic QRS or T wave. Absence of a normal marker because an event occurred during intentional blanking is not necessarily malfunction and must be distinguished from true undersensing. H3C4  Causes of Undersensing Cause group Examples Supporting evidence Typical response Signal too small Low P-wave or R-wave amplitude; changing rhythm morphology; scar Low measured amplitude or reduced EGM size Review polarity and sensitivity; assess rhythm and lead position Sensitivity too insensitive Programmed mV value too high for available signal Intrinsic signal remains below detection criterion Lower mV cautiously and verify that oversensing is not created Lead displacement or poor contact Acute or delayed movement Sensing and threshold changes; possible imaging or morphology change Urgent clinical and imaging review Conductor or connector problem Fracture, loose set screw, header issue Intermittent noise, high impedance or posture dependence Escalate and inspect trends; reproduce only with caution Lead-tissue interface change Inflammation, fibrosis or mineralization Threshold and sensing trend changes Correlate with lead age and clinical status Timing interaction Event falls inside blanking or refractory interval Signal visible but absent or marked refractory Review timing rather than automatically changing sensitivity Metabolic or clinical change Ischaemia, electrolyte disorder, drug effect or severe acidosis Concurrent clinical or threshold change Treat patient and reassess device Algorithm interaction Dynamic sensing behaviour at specific rates or sequences Problem linked to paced events or rate transitions Use device-specific technical documentation   IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.5-07   H3C5  ECG and EGM Pattern of Undersensing • An intrinsic P wave or QRS is present on the surface ECG. • The corresponding EGM may be small, distorted, absent from the selected channel or visible but not classified. • The expected AS or VS marker is absent, or the event is marked refractory or blanked. • The lower-rate or AV timing interval continues as if the intrinsic event did not occur. • A pacing output may follow at an inappropriate time and may capture, fail to capture, fuse or create pseudofusion. • Missed markers may occur only with low-amplitude ectopic beats, atrial fibrillation, rapid rates or posture changes. Do not diagnose from the pacing spike alone A pacing spike near a QRS may represent undersensing, fusion, pseudofusion, safety pacing or normal timing. The marker channel and EGM are required to determine what the device detected.   H3C6  Oversensing: Detecting Noise, T Waves or the Wrong Cardiac Signal Oversensing occurs when the pacemaker classifies an unwanted signal as an intrinsic event. The signal may be cardiac but inappropriate for the channel, such as a far-field R wave in the atrial channel or a T wave in the ventricular channel. It may be non-cardiac, such as skeletal myopotential, lead noise or EMI. Because the device believes a beat occurred, it may inhibit pacing or reset timing. Oversensing is particularly dangerous in a pacemaker-dependent patient when ventricular pacing is inhibited. The surface ECG may show pauses while the marker channel shows repeated ventricular sensed events that do not correspond to true QRS complexes. In other patients, oversensing may distort diagnostics, trigger false mode switching or reduce atrial tracking. H3C7  Major Oversensing Mechanisms Oversensed signal Typical source Clue Potential consequence T wave Ventricular repolarization detected as another ventricular event VS marker follows each QRS at T-wave timing Pacing inhibition, false rate calculation or diagnostic event Far-field R wave Ventricular signal seen on atrial channel Atrial marker consistently aligns with QRS False atrial high-rate detection or mode switch Myopotential Skeletal muscle electrical activity High-frequency signal related to movement or isometric effort Inhibition or false episode detection Lead fracture noise Intermittent conductor discontinuity Very rapid irregular EGM, posture or arm dependence, possible high impedance Pacing inhibition and urgent lead-integrity concern Insulation-related noise Current leakage or contact with tissue or fluid Low or variable impedance with nonphysiologic signals Oversensing and abnormal current drain Crosstalk Atrial pacing output detected by ventricular channel V event soon after AP; safety pacing may appear Inhibition or ventricular safety pacing EMI External electromagnetic field Noise begins and ends with exposure and may affect multiple channels Oversensing, inhibition, mode response or false stored episodes   IMAGE 6.5-08   H3C8  T-Wave Oversensing T-wave oversensing is classification of ventricular repolarization as an additional ventricular event. Although it is often emphasized in defibrillator sensing, it can also alter pacemaker timing. Likelihood depends on R-wave and T-wave amplitudes, filtering, dynamic sensitivity, pacing configuration and morphology. A clue is a ventricular marker that consistently occurs after the true QRS at the T-wave interval, often producing alternating short–long device intervals. • Confirm that the second marker aligns with the T wave and not with a premature ventricular complex. • Compare near-field EGM morphology and amplitude with the true R wave. • Determine whether the problem appears only during ventricular pacing, exercise, ischaemia, hyperkalaemia or a changed QRS/T morphology. • Any programming solution must preserve reliable detection of genuine ventricular activity.   H3C9  Undersensing versus Oversensing: Rapid Comparison Question Undersensing Oversensing What is wrong? A real cardiac signal is missed A false or inappropriate signal is counted Marker relationship Expected marker is absent Extra marker appears without the intended cardiac event Pacing response May pace despite intrinsic activity May inhibit pacing despite absence of a true beat Sensitivity direction Often consider greater sensitivity: lower mV, after evaluation Often consider less sensitivity: higher mV, after identifying the source Lead concern Low signal, dislodgement, conductor/connection or interface issue Fracture noise, insulation issue, myopotential or EMI Dependent-patient risk Competitive or inappropriately timed pacing Potential asystolic pause from inhibition Required evidence ECG + EGM + missing marker + timing ECG + EGM + extra marker + source   H3C10  Troubleshooting Workflow for a Suspected Sensing Problem 1. Protect the patient first. Assess symptoms, pulse, blood pressure and pacemaker dependence, and provide backup support when required. 2. Determine whether the problem is failure to pace, failure to capture, undersensing, oversensing or an expected timing response; these can coexist. 3. Freeze or print synchronized ECG, EGMs and marker channels during the event before changing settings whenever safely possible. 4. Identify whether the issue is atrial, ventricular or both and whether it is continuous or intermittent. 5. Check sensing amplitudes, lead impedance, pacing thresholds, battery status, lead configuration and trends. 6. Review stored episodes and alerts for high-rate noise, mode switch, lead integrity or abrupt changes. 7. Look for temporal triggers: surgery, MRI, electrocautery, trauma, pocket manipulation, arm movement, exercise or new equipment. 8. Use device-specific tests and cautious provocative manoeuvres only when appropriate. 9. Make a targeted programming change only after the likely mechanism is understood and verify that the opposite sensing problem is not created. 10. Redocument ECG/EGM behaviour and arrange imaging, lead review or closer follow-up when needed. IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.5-09 .   H3C11  Sensing Issues: Clinical Pearls • Undersensing means the device missed a true signal; oversensing means it counted the wrong signal. • An absent pacing pulse may be correct inhibition or dangerous oversensing—the markers help distinguish them. • A higher programmed sensitivity number is less sensitive in the common mV convention. • If greater sensitivity corrects undersensing, immediately check for newly created T-wave, far-field or noise oversensing. • Lead-fracture noise is often intermittent and may be movement-related. • T-wave oversensing usually has a consistent relationship to the preceding QRS. • Far-field R-wave sensing in the atrial channel aligns with ventricular depolarization. • Normal impedance does not exclude intermittent conductor noise. • Ventricular oversensing with inhibition is urgent in a pacemaker-dependent patient. • Never solve a sensing problem by programming without documenting the mechanism and confirming post-change safety.   H3C12  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Undersensing Failure to detect a genuine intrinsic cardiac event. Oversensing Detection of an unwanted cardiac or non-cardiac signal as a valid event. T-wave oversensing Classification of ventricular repolarization as another ventricular event. Far-field R-wave sensing Detection of ventricular depolarization by an atrial sensing channel. Myopotential Skeletal-muscle electrical activity entering a sensing channel. Lead noise Nonphysiologic signal related to a lead, connector or mechanical/electrical abnormality. Crosstalk Detection of pacing output from one channel by another channel. Noise reversion Protective response to sustained or repetitive signals interpreted as noise. Competitive pacing Pacing delivered in the presence of intrinsic activity. Pacing inhibition Withholding a scheduled output because a sensed event reset timing.

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.3: Impedance

Heading: Impedance

Topic 6.5.3: Impedance What it is, how it is measured, why trends matter and what abnormal changes may mean H4C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define electrical impedance in the pacing lead circuit and state its unit. • Explain the practical use of the voltage-current relationship in an implanted pacing system. • Describe how a pacemaker measures lead impedance. • Interpret stable, abrupt high, abrupt low and gradual trend changes. • Explain the advantages and limitations of impedance monitoring. • Integrate impedance with sensing, threshold, EGMs and clinical evidence. H4C2  What Is Pacing Lead Impedance? Impedance is the opposition that the complete pacing circuit presents to electrical current. In a simplified explanation, Ohm’s law relates voltage, current and resistance or impedance as Z = V/I. The implanted system is more complex than a pure resistor because tissue and electrode interfaces have capacitive and time-dependent properties, but the programmer reports an equivalent pacing impedance in ohms. The measured circuit includes the pulse-generator output pathway, connector, lead conductor, electrode, lead-tissue interface, body tissues and return electrode. In bipolar pacing, the return is usually the ring electrode. In unipolar pacing, the pulse-generator can is part of the return path. Changing polarity can therefore change measured impedance even when the lead is intact. Impedance is a circuit measurement It is not a direct lead-health score. A normal value cannot exclude every intermittent lead problem, and an outlying value may reflect configuration, timing, acute implant conditions or a non-lead cause.   IMAGE 6.5-10   H4C3  How Impedance Is Measured The pulse generator or programmer delivers a controlled test pulse or uses a pacing pulse and measures the resulting current. Because the applied voltage and pulse characteristics are known, the device calculates effective circuit impedance. Measurements may occur during a commanded test, automatically at scheduled intervals or with paced events depending on the system. 1. Confirm the chamber and lead configuration being measured. 2. The device applies a known test pulse or uses a pacing pulse. 3. Current through the selected circuit is sampled. 4. Impedance is calculated from the voltage-current relationship and displayed in ohms. 5. The value is compared with implant measurements, alert limits and longitudinal trends. 6. Any abnormal value is correlated with sensing, threshold, EGM noise, imaging and clinical history. Manufacturer examples illustrate why ranges are device-specific. Some systems use an automatic lead-detection window such as 200–2000 ohms, while product-performance definitions may use wider thresholds for abnormal values. These examples are not universal normal ranges. The correct reference is the patient’s lead model, device manual, polarity and established baseline. IMAGE 6.5-11   H4C4  Advantages of Impedance Monitoring • Lead-integrity surveillance: abrupt changes may suggest conductor, insulation, connector or electrode problems. • Implant assessment: impedance helps confirm an electrically connected and plausible circuit. • Trend monitoring: gradual changes may reveal evolving lead or interface behaviour. • Programming support: different vectors and polarities can be compared. • Battery and current assessment: unusually low impedance can increase current drain at a given voltage. • Procedure screening: stable lead parameters may form part of device-specific MRI or surgery checks. • Remote monitoring: threshold-crossing alerts can prompt earlier evaluation. H4C5  Interpreting Impedance Trends Figure 6.5-6. Illustrative impedance patterns. Real alert limits and trends are device- and lead-specific.   Pattern Possible interpretation Corroborating findings Action Stable near baseline Likely stable circuit Stable sensing and threshold; no noise or symptoms Continue routine trend review Abrupt high Open circuit, conductor fracture, connector or set-screw problem Noise, reduced capture or abrupt sensing change Urgent system evaluation and imaging as indicated Abrupt low Insulation breach, short circuit or alternate current path Increased drain, noise or threshold/sensing change Evaluate lead, pocket and polarity Intermittent spikes Mechanical conductor or connector intermittency Movement-related nonphysiologic EGM noise Treat as potentially significant despite a normal average Gradual rise Lead-tissue interface change, mineralization, fibrosis or chronic evolution Threshold may rise and sensing may change Trend closely and correlate clinically Gradual fall Maturation, configuration change or evolving insulation concern May be stable or accompanied by noise/drain Compare with baseline and other parameters   H4C6  Impedance and Lead Failure: Important Nuances Lead failure can be intermittent. A conductor fracture may produce brief noise during movement before the impedance trend becomes persistently high. Conversely, some impedance changes occur without clinically meaningful failure. Daily automatic values may also be obtained under different conditions from an office test. Review the raw trend rather than relying only on a single alert. • High impedance suggests reduced current flow through the intended circuit, but the cause may involve conductor, connector or measurement conditions. • Low impedance suggests an alternate current path or reduced opposition, commonly associated with insulation compromise, but correlation is essential. • Lead dislodgement may change threshold and sensing more dramatically than impedance. • Header or set-screw problems can resemble lead failure, especially after implant or generator replacement. • Noise plus symptoms plus an abrupt trend change is more concerning than any one finding alone. • Stable impedance does not exclude oversensing caused by EMI or a small intermittent conductor defect. IMAGE 6.5-12 .   H4C7  Impedance Clinical Pearls • Trend is usually more valuable than a single value. • Compare like with like: same chamber, vector, polarity and measurement method. • Abrupt high impedance raises concern for an open circuit; abrupt low impedance raises concern for a current leak or short circuit. • Displacement may cause major threshold and sensing changes with only a modest impedance change. • Intermittent fracture noise may precede a sustained impedance alert. • Low impedance can increase battery current for a given output. • Normal impedance does not prove normal sensing or capture. • Generator change is a key time to consider connector and set-screw problems. • Always correlate with EGMs and marker channels when noise is suspected. • Device-specific manuals and individual lead baselines take priority over memorized generic ranges.   H4C8  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Impedance Opposition of the selected pacing circuit to electrical current, reported in ohms. Ohm’s law Relationship among voltage, current and resistance or impedance; simplified as Z = V/I. Open circuit Path with very high opposition and little or no intended current flow. Short circuit Unintended low-opposition pathway allowing excessive or diverted current. Conductor fracture Break or intermittent disruption in the metallic conductor. Insulation breach Damage to insulation that permits unintended current leakage or signal entry. Bipolar impedance Impedance measured through a tip-to-ring circuit. Unipolar impedance Impedance measured through a tip-to-can circuit. Trend Sequence of measurements over time used to detect change. Lead integrity alert Device warning based on programmed or algorithmic evidence of possible lead abnormality.

Topic: Topic 6.5.4: Capture Threshold

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.4: Capture Threshold

Heading: Capture Threshold

Topic 6.5.4: Capture Threshold What it is, how it is measured, why amplitude and pulse width matter and how threshold supports safe programming H5C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define myocardial capture and capture threshold. • Differentiate measured threshold from programmed pacing output. • Explain how amplitude and pulse width interact through the strength–duration relationship. • Define rheobase and chronaxie at a practical learner level. • Describe a supervised threshold test and identify consistent capture and loss of capture. • List physiological, pharmacological, metabolic, lead and device factors that can alter threshold. • Explain the advantages of threshold monitoring and automatic capture-management algorithms. • Interpret threshold only after confirming chamber, polarity, pulse width and ECG/EGM evidence. H5C2  What Is Capture? Capture occurs when a pacing stimulus depolarizes enough excitable myocardium to produce the expected electrical activation of the paced chamber. Electrical capture is confirmed when an atrial pacing output is followed by an appropriate atrial depolarization, or when a ventricular pacing output is followed by an appropriate paced QRS complex. Mechanical contraction usually follows electrical capture, but electrical capture on ECG does not by itself prove adequate haemodynamic output. Capture must be distinguished from pacing output. A pacing spike or AP/VP marker shows that the device commanded a pulse. It does not prove that the myocardium responded. Loss of capture is present when a delivered stimulus is not followed by the expected chamber depolarization. Output is not capture The device can deliver a perfectly timed electrical pulse that fails to capture because the output is below threshold, the lead is displaced, the circuit is abnormal or the myocardium is temporarily less excitable.   IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.5-13 .   H5C3  What Is the Capture Threshold? The capture threshold is the lowest programmed stimulus strength that consistently produces myocardial capture under the stated test conditions. It is usually documented as voltage at a specified pulse width, for example “0.75 V at 0.4 ms.” A threshold value without pulse width is incomplete because the two variables jointly determine whether capture occurs. A practical test often begins at an output known to capture and then reduces amplitude, pulse width or both in controlled steps. The threshold is identified at the transition between consistent capture and loss of capture according to the device-specific test method. Because beat-to-beat variability may occur, several consecutive beats should be observed rather than relying on one isolated complex. Term Meaning Measured capture threshold Minimum output that captures during a supervised test under stated conditions Programmed output Routine amplitude and pulse width delivered by the device Safety margin Reserve programmed above threshold to accommodate variability Automatic capture threshold Threshold determined by a validated device algorithm Evoked response Electrical signal produced by the myocardium after a successful pacing stimulus Backup pulse Higher-output pulse delivered by some systems when capture is not confirmed   H5C4  Amplitude and Pulse Width Amplitude is commonly expressed in volts and represents the driving potential of the pacing pulse. Pulse width is expressed in milliseconds and represents how long the pulse is delivered. Increasing either variable can increase the probability of capture, but it also changes energy use. Threshold testing and programming therefore consider both dimensions. Figure 6.5-7. Conceptual strength–duration curve. The precise curve varies by lead, chamber and tissue. Programming change Likely effect on capture Energy implication Practical caution Increase amplitude Greater electrical field and capture probability Can substantially increase battery current High amplitude may mask a rising threshold if trends are ignored Increase pulse width Longer stimulus duration and capture probability Increases delivered charge and energy Very long pulse width is not always the most efficient solution Decrease amplitude Reduces reserve above threshold May improve longevity Can create intermittent loss of capture if margin is inadequate Decrease pulse width Reduces delivered duration May improve longevity Threshold voltage usually rises as pulse width becomes very short Change vector or polarity Changes current density and tissue stimulated May improve efficiency or avoid extracardiac stimulation Recheck threshold, impedance and sensing after any vector change   H5C5  Rheobase and Chronaxie Rheobase is the minimum current or voltage capable of producing excitation when pulse duration is very long. Chronaxie is the pulse duration required for capture at approximately twice rheobase. These concepts explain why extending pulse width helps most at short durations and produces progressively smaller benefit at longer durations. In clinical programming, they provide the physiological basis for choosing an efficient combination of amplitude and pulse width rather than maximizing both.   Practical interpretation The strength–duration curve is not a fixed patient constant. It can change with lead maturation, fibrosis, medications, electrolytes, ischaemia, lead movement, stimulation vector and measurement method.   IMAGE 6.5-14   H5C6  How a Manual Threshold Test Is Performed 1. Assess the patient, indication and pacemaker dependence. Ensure continuous rhythm monitoring and immediate backup support when required. 2. Select the correct chamber, lead vector, polarity and pulse width to be tested. 3. Confirm that the initial output produces stable capture and identify the expected ECG/EGM morphology. 4. Choose a test method that safely exposes the chamber response. Depending on the chamber and rhythm, the pacing rate may be set above the intrinsic rate or AV timing may be adjusted. 5. Reduce amplitude in controlled steps while observing surface ECG, EGM and marker annotations. 6. Identify the first output at which capture is lost or becomes inconsistent. 7. Increase one step or use the device-defined method to identify the lowest output producing consistent capture. 8. Repeat or verify the result when beat-to-beat variability, fusion, pseudofusion, ectopy or uncertain morphology is present. 9. Record threshold as voltage at the tested pulse width, together with polarity, chamber, rate and date. 10. Restore or program an appropriate safety margin and confirm stable capture before concluding the test. Threshold-test safety A threshold test intentionally approaches loss of capture. In a pacemaker-dependent patient, it must be brief, supervised and supported by a reliable escape rhythm, backup pacing strategy or other immediate rescue capability.   IMAGE 6.5-15 .   H5C7  How Capture Is Confirmed Chamber or situation Evidence of capture Common source of error Atrial pacing Pacing output followed by a consistent atrial depolarization or atrial EGM response Atrial signal may be hidden in the QRS or T wave; far-field activity may mislead Ventricular pacing Pacing output followed by a paced QRS morphology Fusion may alter QRS width and make capture appear intermittent His-bundle or conduction-system pacing Expected conduction-system or myocardial capture morphology according to implant criteria Selective, nonselective and myocardial capture may transition at different outputs CRT/LV pacing Expected ventricular activation with the selected LV vector RV fusion, anodal capture or phrenic stimulation may complicate assessment Automatic capture algorithm Device-detected evoked response after the pacing pulse Polarization artifact or algorithm limitations may affect classification   • Use more than one ECG lead when morphology is uncertain. • Inspect the EGM and marker channel but remember that a pacing marker confirms output, not capture. • Exclude fusion and pseudofusion by adjusting rate or timing when clinically safe. • Confirm that the expected chamber response occurs immediately after the pacing pulse. • When mechanical capture is clinically important, correlate with pulse, blood pressure, plethysmography or imaging as appropriate. IMAGE 6.5-16     H5C8  Why Threshold Changes Time or cause Mechanism Expected pattern Acute implant period Tissue injury, oedema and evolving electrode contact Threshold may change over hours to days Lead maturation Inflammation followed by fibrosis around the electrode Transient rise or gradual stabilization Lead displacement Reduced contact or change in stimulated tissue Abrupt threshold increase, possible sensing change Conductor or connector problem Reduced or intermittent delivery of current Loss of capture with high or unstable impedance and noise Insulation defect Current diverted away from intended electrode Low impedance, increased drain and possible threshold change Myocardial ischaemia or infarction Reduced excitability near the electrode Threshold rise and morphology change Electrolyte or acid–base disorder Altered membrane excitability Potential acute threshold increase Medication effect Some antiarrhythmics and other drugs alter excitability Threshold may rise or vary after treatment changes Fibrosis or calcification Chronic interface change Gradual threshold increase Vector change Different tissue and current density are stimulated Different threshold and extracardiac stimulation   H5C9  Advantages of Threshold Measurement • Confirms that the lead can reliably stimulate the intended chamber. • Supports safe output programming and avoids unnecessary excessive energy. • Provides an early clue to lead displacement, interface change or system abnormality. • Allows comparison of different pacing vectors, particularly for LV and multipolar systems. • Supports automatic capture-management algorithms and remote monitoring. • Helps estimate whether programmed output remains adequate as battery voltage changes. • Documents lead maturation and long-term stability. • Provides a baseline before MRI, surgery or other procedures when required by protocol. H5C10  Automatic Capture Management Many contemporary pacemakers include algorithms that periodically test capture, estimate threshold and adjust output. Some systems identify the evoked response after a paced beat; others use chamber-specific timing or confirmation methods. Automatic algorithms can provide continuous safety margins and reduce unnecessary output, but their operation, test timing, backup pulse and eligibility criteria are device-specific. • Confirm that the algorithm is appropriate for the lead, chamber and clinical situation. • Review whether the displayed threshold is a measured value, an algorithmic estimate or a programmed fallback value. • Inspect the threshold trend for abrupt changes or failed tests. • Do not assume automatic management can overcome lead dislodgement, intermittent fracture or severe interface abnormality. • Verify actual capture whenever symptoms, ECG findings or trends conflict with the algorithm result.
