Topic: Topic 6.5.5: Safety Margins

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.5: Safety Margins

Heading: Safety Margins

Topic 6.5.5: Safety Margins Programming reliable reserve above threshold while managing energy, longevity and patient risk H6C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define a pacing safety margin. • Explain why threshold variability requires programmed reserve. • Describe voltage-based, pulse-width-based and automatic safety-margin strategies. • Explain the trade-off between capture reliability and battery longevity. • Identify situations that justify a larger or more conservative margin. • Explain why generic multipliers must never replace device-specific instructions and clinical judgment. H6C2  What Is a Safety Margin? A pacing safety margin is the programmed reserve between the measured capture threshold and the routine pacing output. It protects against normal biological variability, measurement error, posture or rate effects, lead maturation, transient metabolic change and gradual threshold rise. Without a margin, an output programmed exactly at threshold may capture during the test yet fail intermittently later. Figure 6.5-8. Conceptual safety margin between measured threshold and programmed output.   Illustrative, not universal Some manufacturer manuals describe examples such as a two-times voltage margin or a three-times pulse-width margin. The appropriate strategy depends on the specific device, lead, chamber, automatic capture features, battery status, threshold stability and patient dependence.   H6C3  Ways to Create a Safety Margin   Strategy Example concept Advantages Limitations Increase amplitude Program voltage above the measured threshold Simple and widely used Energy increases rapidly with voltage; may cause extracardiac stimulation Increase pulse width Lengthen pulse duration above the threshold setting Can support capture when voltage reserve is limited Long pulse width also increases energy and may be inefficient Use both variables Moderate increase in amplitude and pulse width Flexible when threshold is high or variable Must be documented clearly and reassessed Automatic output adaptation Algorithm measures threshold and maintains programmed reserve May preserve capture while reducing unnecessary energy Device-specific eligibility, timing and fallback behaviour High fixed output Large reserve regardless of measured threshold Useful temporarily when threshold is uncertain Battery cost and potential masking of an evolving problem   H6C4  Why the Margin Must Be Individualized • Pacemaker dependence: consequences of intermittent loss of ventricular capture are greater. • Threshold stability: a stable chronic lead may require less reserve than an acutely changing lead. • Lead age and clinical history: displacement, revision, fracture concerns or interface abnormalities increase uncertainty. • Automatic capture function: validated beat-to-beat or periodic confirmation may permit lower routine output. • Chamber and vector: atrial, RV, conduction-system and LV thresholds behave differently. • Metabolic and medication factors: electrolyte disturbance, acidosis or drug changes can temporarily alter excitability. • Battery status: high output may materially shorten longevity, especially with frequent pacing. • Extracardiac stimulation: higher output may cause pectoral or phrenic nerve stimulation. • Upcoming procedure: MRI or surgery protocols may require verification of stable parameters and specific programming. IMAGE 6.5-18 .   H6C5  Energy and Battery Longevity Pacing energy depends on amplitude, pulse width, circuit impedance and pacing percentage. In a simplified resistive model, energy per pulse rises approximately with the square of voltage and directly with pulse width. Therefore, doubling voltage may have a greater battery effect than learners intuitively expect. The actual device current drain also depends on circuitry and waveform. Programming factor Effect on energy use Higher amplitude Usually increases energy substantially because voltage has a squared relationship in the simplified model Longer pulse width Increases delivered duration and energy approximately in direct proportion Lower impedance Allows more current at a given voltage and may increase battery drain Higher pacing percentage Multiplies the number of pulses delivered Higher paced rate Increases pulse frequency Multi-site pacing Adds output channels and can increase total current demand Automatic capture management May reduce output when thresholds are low and stable   H6C6  Safety-Margin Programming Workflow 1. Measure and verify threshold under reproducible conditions. 2. Review threshold trend, lead age, chamber, vector and recent clinical changes. 3. Determine pacemaker dependence and the consequence of potential loss of capture. 4. Confirm whether automatic capture management is active, validated and appropriate. 5. Select a device-specific margin using amplitude, pulse width or algorithmic reserve. 6. Check for extracardiac stimulation at the programmed output. 7. Estimate battery impact and confirm projected longevity is acceptable. 8. Verify stable capture over multiple beats and relevant positions or rates when indicated. 9. Document threshold, programmed output, pulse width, rationale and follow-up plan. H6C7  Safety-Margin Clinical Pearls • Programming at the exact measured threshold is not a safety strategy. • A margin protects against biological and measurement variability. • The required margin is larger when threshold is unstable or consequences of failure are severe. • Voltage and pulse width are interchangeable only in a limited physiological sense; energy cost differs. • Doubling voltage can have a disproportionately large battery effect. • High fixed output may be reasonable temporarily but should not replace investigation of a rising threshold. • Check for pectoral, diaphragmatic or phrenic stimulation at higher outputs. • Automatic capture features must be understood rather than merely enabled. • Record the threshold and programmed output together. • Reassess margins after lead revision, medication or electrolyte change, MRI, surgery or a significant trend change. H6C8  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Safety margin Reserve between measured capture threshold and programmed pacing output. Programmed output Routine amplitude and pulse width delivered by the device. Threshold variability Change in the minimum capture requirement over time or conditions. Battery longevity Estimated time remaining before elective generator replacement. Pacing percentage Proportion of cardiac cycles in which the device delivers pacing. Extracardiac stimulation Unintended stimulation of skeletal muscle, diaphragm or nerve. Phrenic stimulation Diaphragmatic activation from current reaching the phrenic nerve. Automatic output Device-adjusted pacing energy based on capture testing or algorithmic rules. Fixed output Programmed energy that does not automatically track threshold. Reserve Additional programmed energy intended to maintain capture under variability.

Topic: Topic 6.5.6: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI)

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.6: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI)

Heading: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI)

How external electromagnetic fields can enter the sensing system and alter pacemaker behaviour H7C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility in relation to pacemakers. • Explain how EMI can couple into the implanted system and be interpreted by sensing circuits. • Identify common hospital sources, with special focus on MRI and electrosurgery. • Describe possible EMI effects including oversensing, inhibition, noise response, mode change, magnet response and rare reset events. • Explain why pacemaker dependence, current path, distance, field strength and exposure duration change risk. • Apply a pre-procedure, intra-procedure and post-procedure device-management workflow. • Distinguish temporary device response from permanent reprogramming or damage. H7C2  What Is Electromagnetic Interference? Electromagnetic interference is an unwanted electrical or magnetic signal from an external source that affects, or has the potential to affect, the normal operation of an implanted pacemaker system. The interference may enter through the lead system, device can, body tissues or telemetry pathway. If its frequency, amplitude and timing resemble cardiac activity after filtering, the sensing channel may classify it as an intrinsic event. Electromagnetic compatibility is the ability of the device to function appropriately in its intended electromagnetic environment without producing or receiving unacceptable interference. Modern devices use shielding, filtering, bipolar sensing, noise-detection algorithms and protective modes, but no implanted system is immune to every source or exposure configuration.   Figure 6.5-9. Conceptual pathway from an EMI source to a device response.   IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 6.5-19 .   H7C3  What Determines EMI Risk? Risk factor Why it matters Pacemaker dependence Inhibition of ventricular pacing may have immediate haemodynamic consequences Source type and power Different sources produce different electric, magnetic and radiofrequency fields Distance from generator and leads Field strength and coupling generally decrease with greater separation Current path through the body A path crossing the generator or leads increases the chance of interaction Exposure duration and duty cycle Long or continuous exposure may be more consequential than brief intermittent exposure Sensing configuration Unipolar configurations create a larger antenna field than bipolar configurations Programmed sensitivity and filters A highly sensitive channel may accept smaller interference signals Device and lead model Shielding, algorithms and approved conditions differ by system Battery and lead status Abnormal system parameters may alter procedure planning Clinical environment Monitoring, resuscitation resources and trained personnel reduce procedural risk   Risk is system-specific The same equipment may be low risk for one patient and high risk for another because device type, lead configuration, programmed mode, dependence, distance and current path differ.   H7C4  Common Sources of EMI in Hospitals Source Possible interaction Key management concept MRI scanner Static magnetic field, gradient fields and radiofrequency energy may alter sensing, induce current, trigger mode response or cause heating Use only an approved device-specific workflow and conditions of use Monopolar electrosurgery High-frequency current may be sensed as rapid activity and inhibit pacing or trigger noise response Plan device mode, use short bursts and place current path away from the system Bipolar electrosurgery Current is concentrated between instrument tips and usually produces less widespread EMI Prefer when clinically suitable; monitoring is still required External defibrillation/cardioversion Large current may transiently affect sensing, threshold or device electronics Do not delay life-saving shock; optimize pad position and interrogate afterward when indicated Radiofrequency ablation RF current may produce oversensing, heating or electrical interaction Coordinate with the device team and control current path Therapeutic diathermy Strong electromagnetic energy may induce harmful current or heating Often contraindicated near implanted systems; follow manufacturer instructions Lithotripsy Mechanical and electrical energy may interact with sensors or device timing Use device-specific planning and avoid focal exposure to generator Radiation therapy Ionizing radiation may affect semiconductor electronics or cause reset Estimate dose, shield when useful, monitor and perform scheduled device checks Nerve stimulators/TENS Pulsed signals may be sensed, especially when near the device or lead path Evaluate current path and test under monitoring if use is necessary Telemetry and RFID systems Usually low risk at normal distances but can cause transient interaction when very close Follow device guidance on separation and avoid prolonged close contact   H7C5  MRI: Why It Requires a Controlled Workflow MRI exposes the implanted system to a strong static magnetic field, rapidly changing gradient fields and radiofrequency energy. Potential interactions include force or torque on components, induced voltage in the leads, inappropriate sensing, pacing inhibition, asynchronous or mode-related responses, heating at the electrode–tissue interface and device reset. Modern MR-conditional systems can be scanned safely only when the complete implanted system, scan parameters and patient conditions meet the manufacturer’s conditions of use. “MR conditional” does not mean MRI safe under all circumstances. The generator, every implanted lead, abandoned hardware, implant location, lead age, measured parameters, scanner strength, body position and programmed MRI mode may all matter. Institutional protocols should assign responsibility for device assessment, programming, monitoring and restoration. Figure 6.5-10. MRI requires system verification, prescribed programming, monitoring and post-scan restoration.   H7C6  Pre-MRI, During-MRI and Post-MRI Workflow Phase Essential actions Before the scan Identify generator and all leads; confirm MR status and conditions; assess dependence, battery, sensing, impedance and thresholds; determine the prescribed MRI mode; document baseline settings and emergency plan. Programming Activate the manufacturer-defined MRI mode. Depending on intrinsic rhythm and dependence, pacing may be disabled or programmed asynchronously. Disable features as required by the protocol. During the scan Use the permitted scanner and sequence conditions; maintain required physiological monitoring and communication; ensure trained personnel and emergency equipment are available outside the restricted field. Immediately after Exit MRI mode, restore intended programming, interrogate the system and compare battery, sensing, impedance and threshold with baseline. Follow-up Document the procedure and arrange additional review if parameters changed, symptoms occurred or the protocol requires delayed reassessment.   MRI safety rule Never rely on the generator label alone. MR eligibility applies to the complete system and the manufacturer’s specified conditions of use.   IMAGE 6.5-21   H7C7  Electrocautery and Electrosurgery Electrosurgery uses high-frequency current to cut tissue or achieve haemostasis. Monopolar electrosurgery sends current from the active electrode through the patient to a return electrode, creating a relatively large current path. Bipolar electrosurgery confines current mainly between two instrument tips and generally produces less widespread interference. The principal pacemaker concern is oversensing of electrosurgical energy. The device may interpret the signal as intrinsic activity, inhibit pacing or activate a noise response. Risk increases when surgery is near the generator or leads, the current path crosses the implanted system, long bursts are used, unipolar sensing is active or the patient is dependent. Figure 6.5-11. Electrosurgical current path should be planned away from the generator and leads whenever possible.   H7C8  Electrosurgery Risk-Reduction Principles • Determine device type, indication, programmed mode, magnet response and pacemaker dependence before the procedure. • Use bipolar electrosurgery when clinically suitable. • For monopolar use, choose the lowest effective energy and short, intermittent bursts. • Place the return electrode so the current path does not cross the generator or implanted leads. • Maximize practical distance between the active electrode and the pacemaker system. • Use continuous ECG plus a pulse-based monitor because electrical artifact can obscure the ECG. • Make external pacing and defibrillation capability immediately available when risk is meaningful. • Apply a magnet or reprogram only under an agreed plan; magnet behaviour is manufacturer- and programming-dependent. • After significant exposure or unexpected behaviour, interrogate the system and restore all intended settings. More commonly, it causes temporary sensing-related behaviour while the exposure is present, or it activates a designed noise, magnet or MRI response. However, sufficiently strong interference, ionizing radiation or an electrical event can rarely cause reset to a backup program. The distinction matters: temporary response ends when the source is removed or the special mode is exited, whereas reset or unintended persistent change requires interrogation and restoration.   Intervention or event What it does Caution Planned reprogramming Intentionally changes mode, rate, sensing or therapy for a procedure Must be documented and restored afterward Magnet application Activates the programmed/manufacturer magnet response without rewriting all parameters Response varies by device, battery state and programming; stable placement is essential MRI mode Applies a manufacturer-defined package of settings for scanning Must be deliberately activated and deactivated Noise response Temporary protective behaviour during repetitive detec

Topic: Topic 6.5.7: Integrated Electrical Troubleshooting

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.7: Integrated Electrical Troubleshooting

Heading: Integrated Electrical Troubleshooting

Topic 6.5.7: Integrated Electrical Troubleshooting Combining sensing, impedance, threshold, output, trends and patient condition into one safe workflow H8C1  Why Integration Matters Electrical measurements are interdependent. A rising threshold may reflect tissue change, lead movement or a circuit problem. An impedance alert may be clinically silent or may accompany noise oversensing and pacing inhibition. A sensing abnormality may arise from programming, timing windows, lead integrity, EMI or changing myocardial signal amplitude. The correct conclusion usually emerges from the pattern across several domains rather than from one number. The five-question framework 1) Is the patient stable? 2) Did the device deliver output when expected? 3) Did the myocardium capture? 4) Did the device sense true events and reject false ones? 5) Do sensing, threshold and impedance trends support a lead, tissue, programming or environmental explanation?   H8C2  Patient-First Troubleshooting Sequence 1. Assess symptoms, pulse, blood pressure and consciousness. Treat clinical instability before completing technical analysis. 2. Identify pacemaker dependence and the underlying rhythm. Arrange immediate backup pacing when loss of capture or inhibition could be dangerous. 3. Record a 12-lead ECG or rhythm strip that includes the suspicious event whenever possible. 4. Interrogate the device and display synchronized ECG, atrial EGM, ventricular EGM and marker channels. 5. Classify the primary observed behaviour: absent output, loss of capture, undersensing, oversensing, inappropriate timing or normal device response. 6. Review programmed mode, lower rate, AV delays, sensitivity, output, blanking, refractory periods and active algorithms. 7. Measure or review sensing amplitudes, lead impedance and capture thresholds in all relevant vectors. 8. Compare current findings with implant values, previous clinic checks and remote trends. 9. Search for triggers such as trauma, generator replacement, surgery, MRI, electrocautery, infection, medication change, electrolyte disturbance or new equipment. 10. Use imaging, laboratory testing, manufacturer technical support or specialist review when the pattern remains uncertain. 11. Implement a targeted correction, then repeat ECG/EGM review to confirm the problem is resolved and a new problem has not been created. 12. Document the event, evidence, intervention, final settings, patient status and follow-up plan. Findings Requiring Immediate Escalation • Loss of ventricular capture in a pacemaker-dependent patient. • Prolonged pauses caused by suspected ventricular oversensing or pacing inhibition. • New symptomatic bradycardia, syncope, presyncope, hypotension or altered mental status. • Abrupt major impedance change accompanied by noise, loss of capture or loss of sensing. • Evidence of lead displacement shortly after implant or revision. • Device reset, backup mode or inability to communicate after a procedure or electrical exposure. • Pocket infection, erosion, fever or bacteraemia with an implanted system. • Repeated phrenic or extracardiac stimulation that prevents effective CRT or safe programming. • Unexpected parameter changes after MRI, electrosurgery, external defibrillation or radiation therapy. • Any situation in which device behaviour cannot be safely reproduced or corrected with available support. Emergency priority Do not continue a detailed programmer investigation while the patient remains unstable. Establish circulation and a reliable rhythm first, using external pacing, temporary pacing, defibrillation or advanced resuscitation as clinically indicated.   H8C5  Worked Clinical Scenarios Scenario Key findings Interpretation pathway Priority action 1. Topic: Topic 6.5.8: Chapter Consolidation

Topic Description: Topic 6.5.8: Chapter Consolidation

Heading: Chapter Consolidation

Topic 6.5.8: Chapter Consolidation Clinical pearls, master vocabulary, image-production register and reference framework H9C1  Chapter Clinical Pearls • Sensing asks whether the pacemaker correctly hears intrinsic cardiac activity; threshold asks whether its output successfully activates myocardium. • Intrinsic amplitude and programmed sensitivity are both expressed in mV but describe different things. • In the common fixed-threshold convention, a lower mV sensitivity value makes the channel more sensitive. • Read surface ECG, EGM and marker channels vertically; no single row is sufficient. • A marker reflects device classification and may represent a true beat, far-field signal, T wave, noise or EMI. • Blanking and refractory periods can create intentional non-response that resembles undersensing. • Undersensing can produce inappropriate pacing; oversensing can produce inappropriate inhibition. • Ventricular oversensing is especially urgent when the patient is pacemaker-dependent. • Impedance is a circuit measurement and is most useful as a trend. • Abrupt high impedance suggests an open-circuit pattern; abrupt low impedance suggests an alternate low-resistance pathway, but neither is perfectly specific. • Normal impedance does not exclude intermittent lead noise, EMI or a sensing-programming problem. • Threshold must always be stated with pulse width. • A pacing spike or VP marker proves output, not capture. • Fusion and pseudofusion can make threshold testing appear inconsistent. • Safety margins protect against physiological and measurement variability. • Very high output improves reserve but may shorten longevity and cause extracardiac stimulation. • MRI safety depends on the complete implanted system and all specified conditions of use. • Electrosurgery risk is influenced by instrument type, distance, burst duration and current path. • EMI usually causes temporary sensing or protective behaviour; persistent reset is less common but requires interrogation. • Patient stability and a reliable rhythm take priority over detailed device diagnosis. H9C2  Master Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Intrinsic signal Electrical activity generated by the patient’s own myocardium. Sensing Detection and classification of intrinsic electrical activity by a device. Sensitivity threshold Signal criterion that must be crossed for detection. Electrogram (EGM) Electrical recording acquired from implanted electrodes. Near-field signal Local activity recorded close to the target electrode pair. Far-field signal Activity arising outside the intended local sensing region. Marker annotation Device-generated label for a sensed, paced, refractory or classified event. Undersensing Failure to recognize a genuine intrinsic event. Oversensing Recognition of an unwanted signal as a genuine event. Impedance Opposition of the selected pacing circuit to current. Threshold Minimum pacing stimulus that consistently captures. Capture Successful paced depolarization of myocardium. Loss of capture Output without the expected myocardial depolarization. Amplitude Magnitude of the pacing voltage or current. Pulse width Duration of the pacing pulse. Safety margin Programmed reserve above measured threshold. EMI External electromagnetic energy that interferes with device function. Noise response Protective device behaviour during repetitive nonphysiologic sensing. Asynchronous pacing Pacing that is not inhibited by intrinsic sensing. Pacemaker dependence Reliance on pacing to maintain an adequate rhythm or output. Current path Route followed by procedural electrical current through the body. Electrical reset Reversion to predefined backup settings after a major disturbance. Fusion Combined intrinsic and paced ventricular activation. Pseudofusion Pacing output coincident with an intrinsic beat without meaningful change in activation. Lead integrity Functional condition of conductor, insulation, connector and electrodes.       H9C3  Additional Image for Complete LMS Visual Coverage IMAGE  6.5-26 Learning purpose: Explain why polarity changes signal amplitude and susceptibility to distant signals.     IMAGE 6.5-27 . Learning purpose: Build pattern recognition for atrial sensing and false atrial detections.     IMAGE  6.5-28 Learning purpose: Build pattern recognition for ventricular sensing and oversensing. .   IMAGE  6.5-29 Learning purpose: Teach that apparent lead failure may originate at the connector, especially after implant or generator replacement. .   IMAGE  6.5-30 Learning purpose: Show that expected capture morphology depends on pacing site and technique.     IMAGE  6.5-31 Learning purpose: Explain why the highest output is not always clinically tolerable. .   IMAGE  6.5-32 Learning purpose: Demonstrate the programming trade-off while warning against reducing sensitivity without proving adequate intrinsic detection.     IMAGE  6.5-33 Learning purpose: Teach safe procedural planning without discouraging immediate lifesaving defibrillation. .   IMAGE  6.5-34 . Learning purpose: Introduce radiation as an electronic rather than sensing-only risk that requires multidisciplinary planning. .   IMAGE  6.5-35 Learning purpose: Support general patient counselling while directing users to device-specific instructions.       Final clinical disclaimer Electrical values, automatic algorithms, magnet behaviour, MRI eligibility, alert limits and recommended safety margins vary by manufacturer, model, lead, software version and clinical context. Topic: TOPIC 6.6.1: THE NBG CODE

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.6.1: THE NBG CODE

Heading: Pacemaker NBG Codes and Modes of Pacing

Decode the code, predict device behaviour, interpret the paced ECG and select the appropriate mode conceptually     Scope of this chapter This chapter provides a structured educational explanation of the NBG code and the requested pacing modes: VVI, VVIR, VOO, VDD, DDD, DDDR and DDIR. It connects each code to timing behaviour, ECG appearance, marker channels, clinical use, advantages, limitations and troubleshooting. Mode selection and programming must follow the patient’s rhythm, conduction, ventricular function, pacing burden, lead system, device manual and qualified clinical judgment.   Requested domain Learner outcome NBG code Translate each letter into a specific pacing function. Chamber paced Identify where an output can be delivered. Chamber sensed Identify which chamber can reset or influence timing. Response to sensing Predict inhibition, triggering, dual response or no response. Rate modulation Explain what the R adds and what it does not add. Pacing modes Predict VVI, VVIR, VOO, VDD, DDD, DDDR and DDIR behaviour. ECG and EGM Verify the predicted behaviour using pacing spikes, P waves, QRS complexes, EGMs and markers.   H1C1 Pacemaker NBG Codes and Modes of Pacing H1C2  Learning Objectives At the end of this chapter, the learner should be able to: • State the purpose of the NASPE/BPEG Generic (NBG) code and describe all five positions. • Decode the chamber paced, chamber sensed and response-to-sensing positions without memorizing each mode as an isolated word. • Explain O, A, V and D in the paced and sensed positions. • Explain O, I, T and D in the response position. • Explain the meaning of R in the fourth position and distinguish rate modulation from atrial tracking. • Describe the fifth-position multisite code and explain why it is often omitted in routine mode labels. • Decode VVI, VVIR, VOO, VDD, DDD, DDDR and DDIR letter by letter. • Predict what causes pacing to be inhibited, delivered or triggered in each requested mode. • Recognize expected ECG and marker-channel patterns for each mode. • Differentiate atrial tracking from rate-adaptive pacing. • Explain why VDD can sense but cannot pace the atrium. • Explain why DDIR senses both chambers but does not track sensed atrial events to the ventricle. • Identify the four normal event combinations possible in DDD pacing: AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS and AP–VP. • Explain major advantages, limitations and common clinical uses of each mode. • Recognize mode-related risks such as pacemaker syndrome, upper-rate behaviour, atrial tachyarrhythmia tracking and competitive asynchronous pacing. • Use a systematic ECG–EGM–marker workflow to determine whether observed pacing behaviour matches the programmed mode. • Select a conceptually appropriate mode for common clinical scenarios while recognizing when CRT, conduction-system pacing or specialist input is required. H1C3  Chapter Overview A pacing mode is a compact description of what the pacemaker is allowed to do. It does not identify the diagnosis, the number of implanted leads with complete certainty, the programmed rate, the AV delay, the upper tracking rate or every active algorithm. The mode tells the learner where the device can pace, where it can sense, how sensing changes pacing behaviour and whether rate modulation is active. The NBG code was developed to provide a common language across manufacturers and disciplines. The revised five-position code retains the familiar first three positions and adds rate modulation and multisite pacing. In routine clinical communication, three- or four-letter modes are common because the fifth position is often not required to describe standard single-site atrial and ventricular pacing. Core learning rule Do not memorize VVI, DDD or DDIR as unexplained abbreviations. Read every letter in order, convert each letter into a function, and then predict the timing response.       H1C4  Fundamentals: Code, Capability and Actual Behaviour The NBG code describes a programmed operating mode. The observed ECG is produced by the interaction of that mode with the patient’s intrinsic rhythm, the lower rate, sensor rate, AV delays, refractory periods, upper-rate limits, lead function and active algorithms. For example, a DDD pacemaker may show no pacing spikes when the patient has normal sinus rhythm and intact AV conduction. It remains DDD because it is capable of pacing and sensing both chambers even though intrinsic events are currently inhibiting output. • Code = the basic logic available in the programmed mode. • Timing settings = when the device will pace or respond. • Intrinsic rhythm = whether the capability is actually used on a given beat. • Leads and hardware = whether the required chambers can be paced and sensed. • Algorithms = additional rules such as mode switch, ventricular-pacing minimization, rate response or capture management. • ECG/EGM = the evidence used to confirm what actually happened. Figure 6.6-3. Decode the mode first and verify the prediction on ECG and marker channels.   IMAGE 6.6-02 Learning purpose: Prevent the error of naming the mode only from the spikes visible in one short ECG segment. .  

Heading: The NBG Code

A standardized language for antibradycardia pacing, rate modulation and multisite pacing H2C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Name and decode all five NBG positions. • Explain why the first three positions are sufficient for basic pacing logic. • Recognize that R is a modifier for rate response, not another chamber. • Recognize that an omitted position is usually not required for the stated mode, but must not be assumed when device details matter. • Translate code letters into a sentence describing device behaviour. H2C2  History and Purpose of the Code As pacing systems became more complex, a uniform naming system was needed so that clinicians, engineers, nurses, technicians and manufacturers could describe mode behaviour without relying on brand-specific terminology. The North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology and the British Pacing and Electrophysiology Group created the NBG code. The revised code published in 2002 uses five positions and was reaffirmed by the Heart Rhythm Society in 2023. The code is intentionally functional. It does not specify lead fixation, electrode location, battery chemistry, exact sensor type, pacing output or clinical indication. Two devices with different hardware can sometimes operate in the same NBG mode, while one dual-chamber device can be programmed into several different modes. NBG is a common language, not a complete prescription The code tells you the core logic. Safe programming still requires the full device settings, the patient’s physiology and device-specific instructions.   H2C3  The Five Positions Position Category Common letters Meaning I Chamber(s) paced O, A, V, D None, atrium, ventricle or both atrium and ventricle II Chamber(s) sensed O, A, V, D None, atrium, ventricle or both chambers III Response to sensing O, I, T, D None, inhibited, triggered or dual response IV Rate modulation O, R No rate modulation or rate modulation active V Multisite pacing O, A, V, D No multisite pacing, atrial, ventricular or both   The letters O and D are used in more than one position, but their meaning is determined by position. D in position I means both chambers can be paced. D in position II means both chambers can be sensed. D in position III means sensing can have both inhibited and triggered effects. D in position V means multisite pacing is available in both atrial and ventricular chambers. IMAGE 6.6-03     H2C4  Position I – Chamber Paced Letter Meaning What the device can do Example O None No pacing output is delivered by the stated mode ODO monitoring-only configurations in some devices; not a therapy mode A Atrium Deliver an atrial pacing stimulus AAI or AAIR V Ventricle Deliver a ventricular pacing stimulus VVI, VVIR, VOO or VDD D Dual Deliver both atrial and ventricular pacing stimuli DDD, DDDR or DDIR   Position I describes capability, not necessarily what appears on every beat. In VVI, the device may deliver no output for several seconds if intrinsic ventricular events repeatedly inhibit pacing. In DDD, atrial pacing may be absent when sinus activity is faster than the lower rate, while ventricular pacing may still occur because AV conduction is impaired.   Ask the learner A device is programmed VDD. Which chamber can it pace? Answer: the first letter is V, so it can pace the ventricle only. The D in the second position does not add atrial pacing.   IMAGE  6.6-04   H2C5  Position II – Chamber Sensed Letter Meaning What the device listens to Key consequence O None No intracardiac chamber is used to inhibit or trigger pacing Pacing proceeds asynchronously according to the programmed interval A Atrium Atrial electrical activity Atrial events may inhibit atrial pacing or trigger ventricular timing, depending on position III V Ventricle Ventricular electrical activity A sensed QRS may inhibit ventricular pacing D Dual Both atrial and ventricular activity The device can use events from both chambers in timing logic   Sensing capability does not guarantee that every true event will be recognized. The signal must reach the input circuit, cross the sensitivity criterion and occur outside blanking or relevant refractory windows. Conversely, the sensing channel may incorrectly detect T waves, far-field signals, lead noise or EMI. Therefore, the second letter identifies the channel used, while the EGM and marker channel verify what was actually classified. Ask the learner Compare VVI and VOO. Both pace the ventricle, but only VVI senses the ventricle. Therefore, only VVI can be inhibited by an intrinsic QRS.   IMAGE 6.6-05           H2C6  Position III – Response to Sensing Letter Response Meaning in timing logic Example concept O None Sensing does not alter pacing timing because no sensing response is used VOO asynchronous pacing I Inhibited A sensed event suppresses a scheduled pacing pulse or resets the relevant timer VVI: VS inhibits VP T Triggered A sensed event causes a pacing output or starts timing that leads to an output Atrial tracking can trigger a ventricular AV delay D Dual The device uses both inhibited and triggered responses, depending on chamber and event DDD: VS inhibits VP; AS triggers AV timing   Inhibited means the device withholds an output because intrinsic activity made it unnecessary. Triggered does not always mean an immediate pacing pulse. In dual-chamber pacing, an atrial sensed event commonly triggers an AV interval; ventricular pacing occurs only if no intrinsic ventricular event is sensed before the AV interval expires. Dual response combines these behaviours. • VVI: a ventricular sensed event inhibits the next ventricular output. • VDD: an atrial sensed event triggers an AV delay, while a ventricular sensed event inhibits the scheduled ventricular pulse. • DDD: sensed atrial and ventricular events interact with atrial and ventricular pacing timers. • DDI/DDIR: sensed events inhibit pacing in the corresponding chamber, but a sensed atrial event does not create atrial tracking to ventricular pacing. IMAGE 6.6-06   H2C7  Position IV – Rate Modulation R in the fourth position means a sensor can increase or otherwise modulate the pacing rate when the intrinsic rate does not meet the patient’s metabolic demand. Common sensors assess body motion, ventilation-related signals or combinations of variables. Topic: Topic 6.6.6: VVI Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.6: VVI Mode

Heading: VVI Mode

Ventricular demand pacing: pace the ventricle, sense the ventricle and inhibit output when an intrinsic ventricular event is detected Figure 6.6-4. VVI timing: VS resets the ventricular interval; VP occurs when the interval expires without a VS. H3C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode VVI letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in VVI. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of VVI. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of VVI. • Distinguish normal VVI behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems.   H3C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I V Ventricle paced The device can deliver ventricular pacing output. II V Ventricle sensed The ventricular channel detects intrinsic QRS/R-wave activity. III I Inhibited A sensed ventricular event inhibits the scheduled ventricular output.   H3C3  Core Operating Principle VVI is a single-chamber ventricular demand mode. The device continuously monitors the ventricular channel. If a ventricular event is sensed before the lower-rate interval expires, the ventricular timer is reset and no pacing pulse is delivered. If no event is sensed, the device delivers a ventricular pacing pulse. Atrial activity is neither paced nor used to coordinate ventricular timing. H3C4  Common Clinical Uses • Permanent atrial fibrillation or flutter with symptomatic slow ventricular response or AV block when atrial tracking is not useful. • Patients in whom a single ventricular lead is appropriate because atrial rhythm is chronically disorganized or atrial lead placement is not feasible. • Backup or simplified pacing in selected clinical situations. • Leadless ventricular pacemaker systems commonly use VVI/VVIR-type logic, depending on device capability. H3C5  Advantages • Simple pacing and sensing logic. • Avoids atrial lead and its associated implant and long-term complications. • Reliable ventricular support when atrial rhythm cannot be used. • Intrinsic ventricular events inhibit unnecessary output. H3C6  Limitations and Risks • No AV synchrony because atrial events do not coordinate ventricular pacing. • May produce pacemaker syndrome, particularly when sinus rhythm and retrograde VA conduction are present. • Cannot pace the atrium or correct sinus-node dysfunction directly. • Fixed lower-rate support may be inadequate during exertion when chronotropic incompetence is present. • Ventricular pacing burden and site may influence ventricular function; patients expected to require substantial pacing may need a more physiological strategy. H3C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Confirm that each intrinsic QRS has a corresponding VS marker and resets timing. • A VP marker or spike followed by no paced QRS indicates loss of capture, not a mode problem. • A VP near an intrinsic QRS may represent undersensing, fusion, pseudofusion or normal timing. • Repeated VS markers without true QRS complexes suggest ventricular oversensing and can inhibit pacing. • Retrograde P waves after VP may support a diagnosis of VA conduction and possible pacemaker syndrome. H3C8  Clinical Pearls • VVI is ventricular demand pacing, not continuous ventricular pacing. • A sensed QRS inhibits the next scheduled VP. • P waves may appear independently because the atrium is ignored by the mode. • Irregular P-to-QRS relationships are expected in atrial fibrillation. • VVI is often logical for permanent AF but may be poorly tolerated in sinus rhythm. • A normal short ECG may show only VS markers and no spikes even though the mode is VVI. • Ventricular oversensing is high risk in a dependent patient. • Rate support during activity requires VVIR rather than VVI. • Mode selection must consider pacing burden and ventricular function. • Leadless pacing does not automatically mean the patient’s complete physiological needs are met. H3C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition VVI Ventricle paced, ventricle sensed, inhibited response. VS Ventricular sensed event. VP Ventricular paced event. Ventricular demand pacing Output occurs only when no timely ventricular event is sensed. Pacemaker syndrome Symptoms caused by adverse AV timing or loss of synchrony. VA conduction Retrograde conduction from ventricle to atrium. Fusion Combined intrinsic and paced ventricular activation. Pseudofusion Pacing output coincident with an intrinsic QRS without meaningful activation change.   IMAGE 6.6-09 .   IMAGE 6.6-10   Ask the learner A patient in VVI has an intrinsic QRS before the lower-rate timer expires. What should happen? The device should mark VS, reset the ventricular timer and inhibit VP.

Topic: Topic 6.6.7: VVIR Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.7: VVIR Mode

Heading: VVIR Mode

VVI ventricular demand pacing with sensor-driven rate modulation Figure 6.6-5. VVIR can increase the ventricular pacing rate according to sensor input. H4C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode VVIR letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in VVIR. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of VVIR. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of VVIR. • Distinguish normal VVIR behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H4C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I V Ventricle paced Ventricular output is available. II V Ventricle sensed Intrinsic ventricular events are detected. III I Inhibited A VS inhibits scheduled VP. IV R Rate modulation A sensor can change the pacing rate within programmed limits.   H4C3  Core Operating Principle VVIR retains VVI demand logic but replaces a purely fixed lower-rate support pattern with a sensor-responsive pacing rate. When the sensor indicates activity or metabolic demand, the pacing interval shortens toward the programmed maximum sensor rate. Intrinsic ventricular events can still inhibit pacing. H4C4  Common Clinical Uses • Permanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia and chronotropic incompetence. • Ventricular-only pacing when activity-related rate support is required. • Selected leadless pacemakers with rate-responsive capability. • Patients who cannot provide a usable atrial signal for tracking but need exercise rate support. H4C5  Advantages • Provides activity-related rate increase without an atrial lead. • Retains simple ventricular demand inhibition. • May improve exercise tolerance compared with fixed-rate VVI in appropriate patients. • Sensor parameters can be tailored to activity pattern. H4C6  Limitations and Risks • Still lacks AV synchrony and atrial pacing. • Sensor response may be inadequate, excessive or triggered by nonmetabolic motion. • Activity sensors may respond poorly to cycling or static exercise; ventilation-based sensors may be influenced by respiratory conditions. • Maximum sensor rate, acceleration and recovery require individualized programming. • Sensor-driven rate cannot reproduce every aspect of normal sinus physiology. H4C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Compare paced rate with actual activity and symptoms. • Review activity histogram, sensor-indicated rate and maximum sensor rate. • A rapid paced rate without corresponding activity suggests inappropriate sensor response or another timing issue. • A flat paced rate during exercise suggests inactive or under-responsive sensor settings. • Intrinsic QRS complexes should still inhibit VP when sensed. H4C8  Clinical Pearls • R means sensor-driven rate modulation, not atrial tracking. • VVIR can raise ventricular rate even though the atrium is not sensed. • The sensor response should be evaluated during the patient’s real activities. • An accelerometer responds to movement, not metabolic demand directly. • Recovery time matters because an abruptly falling rate may cause symptoms. • The maximum sensor rate is different from an upper tracking rate. • Oversensing can inhibit VVIR just as it can inhibit VVI. • VVIR does not restore AV synchrony. • Rate-response programming should balance exertional support and inappropriate tachycardia. • A patient with sinus rhythm may still be better served by atrial-based or dual-chamber support when feasible.   H4C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition VVIR VVI mode with rate modulation. Rate-response sensor Device sensor used to estimate activity or metabolic demand. Sensor-indicated rate Pacing rate requested by the sensor algorithm. Maximum sensor rate Programmed upper limit for sensor-driven pacing. Reaction time Speed at which pacing rate rises after activity begins. Recovery time Speed at which pacing rate returns toward baseline. Chronotropic incompetence Inadequate heart-rate increase for physiological demand. Activity histogram Stored distribution of sensed and paced rates over time.   IMAGE 6.6-11 .   IMAGE  6.6-12   Ask the learner A patient with permanent AF has fatigue only during walking. VVI produces a fixed 60 bpm paced rate. Which requested mode adds activity-related rate support without atrial tracking? VVIR.

Topic: Topic 6.6.8 VOO Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.8 VOO Mode

Heading: Voo Mode

Asynchronous ventricular pacing with no sensing and no sensing response Figure 6.6-6. VOO ignores intrinsic activity and delivers ventricular output at fixed intervals. H5C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode VOO letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in VOO. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of VOO. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of VOO. • Distinguish normal VOO behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H5C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I V Ventricle paced A ventricular output is delivered at each programmed interval. II O No chamber sensed Intrinsic events do not reset or inhibit timing. III O No response to sensing Pacing continues asynchronously.   H5C3  Core Operating Principle VOO is an asynchronous ventricular mode. The pacing clock runs independently of intrinsic cardiac activity. Every programmed interval produces a ventricular output, whether an intrinsic QRS has occurred or not. Because sensing is disabled, EMI and intrinsic beats cannot inhibit pacing, but competitive pacing is possible. H5C4  Common Clinical Uses • Temporary procedural use when pacing inhibition from EMI would be unsafe in a pacemaker-dependent patient, under a defined protocol. • Magnet-related asynchronous pacing in some pacemakers, although the exact magnet response and rate vary by manufacturer and programming. • Emergency or testing situations in which sensing must be deliberately disabled for a short period. • Not generally intended as routine long-term pacing in a patient with competing intrinsic ventricular rhythm. H5C5  Advantages • Prevents inappropriate inhibition caused by oversensing or EMI. • Provides predictable fixed-rate output during a controlled procedure. • Useful when reliable sensing cannot be used temporarily and continuous support is required. H5C6  Limitations and Risks • Intrinsic ventricular activity is ignored, creating competitive pacing. • A pacing stimulus can fall during ventricular repolarization; the theoretical risk is greatest in vulnerable myocardium. • No demand inhibition, no atrial synchronization and no adaptation to intrinsic rhythm. • A magnet does not guarantee VOO in every device and may not provide a rate appropriate for every patient. • Failure to restore the intended mode after a procedure can expose the patient to unnecessary asynchronous pacing. H5C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Confirm that pacing outputs occur at a regular programmed interval independent of QRS timing. • Do not mistake absence of inhibition for ventricular undersensing; sensing is intentionally disabled. • Identify fusion or pseudofusion when an output coincides with an intrinsic QRS. • Verify capture and haemodynamic stability throughout the intended exposure. • Document activation and restoration of asynchronous mode. H5C8  Clinical Pearls • VOO means ventricular output with no sensing. • Asynchronous pacing is a deliberate mode, not a sensing failure. • It is usually a temporary procedural strategy rather than a chronic mode. • Competitive pacing is expected when intrinsic rhythm is present. • The procedural plan must consider dependence, underlying rate and EMI source. • Magnet response must be verified rather than assumed. • A magnet can move; reprogramming provides a more controlled response when appropriate. • Continuous ECG plus pulse monitoring is required during electrosurgery because artifact may obscure the ECG. • Remove the EMI source first if unexpected behaviour occurs and it is safe to do so. • Restore and verify the intended mode after the procedure. H5C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition VOO Ventricle paced, no chamber sensed, no sensing response. Asynchronous pacing Pacing delivered independently of intrinsic activity. Competitive pacing Pacing stimuli delivered while intrinsic activation is present. Magnet response Device behaviour produced by an applied magnet; model- and programming-specific. Fixed interval Constant time between programmed pacing outputs. R-on-T concern Potential pacing during ventricular repolarization when intrinsic activity is ignored. Fusion Combination of paced and intrinsic activation. Mode restoration Return to the intended therapeutic mode after temporary programming.   IMAGE  6.6-13   IMAGE 6.6-14   Ask the learner Why can VOO prevent electrosurgery-related inhibition? Because the second and third positions are O: the device does not sense or respond to the interference.

Topic: Topic 6.6.9: VDD Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.9: VDD Mode

Heading: VDD Mode

Topic 6.6.9: VDD Mode Atrial sensing and tracking with ventricular pacing, but no atrial pacing capability Figure 6.6-7. VDD: a sensed atrial event starts an AV delay; ventricular output follows if no VS occurs. H6C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode VDD letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in VDD. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of VDD. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of VDD. • Distinguish normal VDD behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H6C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I V Ventricle paced Only the ventricle can receive pacing output. II D Both chambers sensed Atrial and ventricular electrical activity can be detected. III D Dual response AS can trigger AV timing; VS inhibits VP.   H6C3  Core Operating Principle VDD provides atrial-synchronous ventricular pacing without atrial pacing. The device senses atrial depolarization, starts an AV delay and delivers ventricular pacing if no intrinsic ventricular event occurs. A sensed ventricular event inhibits the scheduled ventricular pulse. Because the first letter is V, sinus bradycardia cannot be corrected by atrial pacing. H6C4  Common Clinical Uses • High-grade or complete AV block with reliable sinus-node function and stable atrial signals. • Selected patients in whom a single-pass VDD lead can provide atrial sensing and ventricular pacing. • Situations in which AV synchrony is desired but an atrial pacing lead is not planned. • Patients with expected low need for atrial pacing and suitable atrial anatomy/signal stability. H6C5  Advantages • Preserves atrial tracking and AV synchrony in suitable sinus rhythm. • Can reduce the need for a separate atrial pacing electrode in a single-lead VDD system. • Ventricular sensing inhibits unnecessary ventricular output. • More physiological than ventricular-only pacing when atrial rhythm is reliable. H6C6  Limitations and Risks • Cannot pace the atrium; sinus-node dysfunction or chronotropic incompetence may cause inadequate rate support. • Atrial sensing may vary with posture, respiration or lead position, particularly in single-pass systems. • Atrial tachyarrhythmias can be tracked unless mode-switch or upper-rate protections intervene. • Loss of atrial sensing converts functional behaviour toward ventricular-only pacing. • An atrial leadless or single-lead configuration may limit future flexibility. H6C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Confirm each P wave or atrial EGM has an AS marker when tracking is expected. • After AS, verify that the AV delay begins and that VS inhibits VP when intrinsic conduction occurs. • A P wave without AS may indicate atrial undersensing, blanking or low atrial amplitude. • An AS marker aligned with QRS may indicate far-field R-wave sensing. • Slow sinus rhythm cannot be corrected with AP because VDD has no atrial pacing capability. H6C8  Clinical Pearls • The first V is the most important reminder: VDD cannot pace the atrium. • The second D allows atrial and ventricular sensing. • The third D allows atrial tracking plus ventricular inhibition. • VDD requires reliable sinus-node function. • Atrial sensing quality may determine whether VDD remains physiologically useful. • Upper-rate behaviour applies because atrial events can be tracked. • Mode switch is important when atrial tachyarrhythmias occur. • Atrial undersensing may produce unexpected ventricular pacing at the lower rate. • Far-field R-wave sensing can create false atrial events. • VDD and DDD can look identical during AS–VP, but only DDD can produce AP. H6C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition VDD Ventricle paced, both chambers sensed, dual response. Atrial tracking Use of AS events to time ventricular pacing. Single-pass VDD lead Ventricular lead with floating atrial sensing electrodes. AS–VP Atrial sensed followed by ventricular paced. AS–VS Atrial sensed followed by ventricular sensed. AV delay Interval from atrial event to expected ventricular event or pacing. Upper tracking rate Maximum rate at which AS events can drive ventricular pacing. Atrial undersensing Failure to detect genuine atrial activity.   IMAGE  6.6-15   IMAGE 6.6-16   Ask the learner A VDD patient develops sinus bradycardia at 40 bpm with complete AV block. Can the device pace the atrium? No. It can track atrial events only when they occur.

Topic: Topic 6.6.10: DDD Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.10: DDD Mode

Heading: DDD Mode

Dual-chamber pacing and sensing with both triggered and inhibited responses Figure 6.6-8. DDD may normally show AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS or AP–VP. H7C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode DDD letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in DDD. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of DDD. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of DDD. • Distinguish normal DDD behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H7C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I D Both chambers paced Atrial and ventricular output are available. II D Both chambers sensed Atrial and ventricular intrinsic activity is monitored. III D Dual response Atrial sensing can trigger AV timing; sensed events can inhibit unnecessary output.   H7C3  Core Operating Principle DDD is the classic dual-chamber tracking mode. It supports the atrium when the sinus rate falls below the lower rate, senses and tracks atrial activity when present, allows intrinsic AV conduction when ventricular activity occurs before the AV delay ends, and paces the ventricle when conduction fails. The result is beat-by-beat adaptation among four event combinations. H7C4  Common Clinical Uses • Symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction when atrial pacing is needed and AV conduction may be normal or impaired. • High-grade AV block in sinus rhythm when atrial synchrony and future atrial pacing capability are desired. • Combined sinus-node and AV-node disease. • Patients in whom dual-chamber timing can improve symptoms or haemodynamics compared with ventricular-only pacing. • A common base mode for algorithms that minimize unnecessary ventricular pacing or switch to nontracking behaviour during atrial tachyarrhythmias. H7C5  Advantages • Supports both atrial and ventricular bradycardia. • Preserves AV synchrony when atrial rhythm is usable. • Allows intrinsic atrial and ventricular activity to inhibit unnecessary pacing. • Can track physiological sinus acceleration up to the upper tracking limit. • Provides flexible timing and diagnostic information from both chambers. H7C6  Limitations and Risks • Requires more complex programming and interpretation. • Atrial tachyarrhythmias may be tracked without appropriate mode switching. • Upper-rate behaviour, pacemaker Wenckebach or 2:1 block can occur at fast atrial rates. • Unnecessary RV pacing may occur if AV delays or algorithms are not optimized. • Atrial lead complications and far-field sensing are possible. • Crosstalk and safety pacing must be understood. • DDD alone does not provide sensor-driven rate support if sinus-node chronotropic response is inadequate. H7C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Label every beat as AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS or AP–VP. • Measure the interval from AS or AP to VS or VP and compare with programmed AV delays. • Review lower-rate, upper-tracking and refractory timing before diagnosing malfunction. • Rapid atrial activity with controlled nontracking ventricular pacing may indicate automatic mode switch. • Progressive AV prolongation or dropped tracking at the upper rate may be normal pacemaker Wenckebach. • A VP soon after AP may be ventricular safety pacing rather than an abnormally short AV delay. H7C8  Clinical Pearls • DDD is a mode, not a promise that every beat will be dual-paced. • AS–VS is normal DDD behaviour when both chambers are intrinsic. • AS–VP indicates atrial tracking with ventricular support. • AP–VS indicates atrial support with preserved AV conduction. • AP–VP indicates support of both chambers. • The paced AV delay and sensed AV delay may be programmed differently. • PVARP and the upper tracking rate determine response to rapid atrial events. • Mode switch protects against sustained tracking of atrial tachyarrhythmias. • Minimizing unnecessary ventricular pacing may be desirable in selected patients. • Always evaluate ventricular function and expected pacing burden when choosing a long-term strategy. H7C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition DDD Both chambers paced and sensed with dual response. AS–VS Both atrial and ventricular events are intrinsic. AS–VP Intrinsic atrial event is tracked to ventricular pacing. AP–VS Atrial pacing followed by intrinsic ventricular conduction. AP–VP Atrial and ventricular pacing. Sensed AV delay Timing from AS to planned VP. Paced AV delay Timing from AP to planned VP. PVARP Post-ventricular atrial refractory period. Pacemaker Wenckebach Progressive AV timing behaviour at the upper tracking limit. Mode switch Automatic transition to nontracking behaviour during atrial tachyarrhythmia.   IMAGE  6.6-17   IMAGE 6.6-18   IMAGE 6.6-19 .   Ask the learner A DDD strip shows P waves with AS markers, followed by intrinsic QRS complexes with VS markers. Is the pacemaker inactive? No. It is appropriately sensing both chambers and inhibiting unnecessary pacing: AS–VS.

Topic: Topic 6.6.11: DDDR Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.11: DDDR Mode

Heading: DDDR Mode

Topic 6.6.11: DDDR Mode DDD dual-chamber tracking plus sensor-driven rate modulation   Figure 6.6-9. DDDR integrates atrial tracking and sensor-indicated rate support. H8C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode DDDR letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in DDDR. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of DDDR. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of DDDR. • Distinguish normal DDDR behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H8C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I D Both chambers paced Atrial and ventricular output are available. II D Both chambers sensed Both chambers contribute intrinsic timing information. III D Dual response Tracking and inhibition are available. IV R Rate modulation A sensor can support rate when intrinsic atrial response is inadequate.   H8C3  Core Operating Principle DDDR adds rate modulation to DDD. The device can still track sinus activity and preserve AV timing, but it can also increase atrial pacing and subsequent ventricular support according to sensor input when the sinus node does not accelerate adequately. Device logic blends intrinsic atrial rate, sensor-indicated rate, lower rate, upper tracking rate and maximum sensor rate. H8C4  Common Clinical Uses • Sinus-node dysfunction with chronotropic incompetence and a need for dual-chamber support. • Combined sinus-node and AV conduction disease. • Patients whose sinus rate does not reliably match activity despite otherwise usable atrial sensing. • Dual-chamber pacing when exertional symptoms persist because DDD without R provides insufficient rate support. H8C5  Advantages • Provides dual-chamber pacing, atrial tracking and sensor-driven rate support. • Can preserve AV synchrony during atrial pacing. • Supports activity even when sinus acceleration is inadequate. • Allows individual programming of sensor response and tracking limits. H8C6  Limitations and Risks • More settings can interact and create excessive or inadequate rates. • Atrial tracking and sensor response may compete or blend in device-specific ways. • Upper tracking rate and maximum sensor rate are distinct limits. • Atrial tachyarrhythmia still requires mode-switch protection. • Inappropriate sensor acceleration can cause palpitations or unnecessary pacing. • High atrial pacing rates may be limited by ventricular tracking and refractory timing. H8C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • Determine whether the paced rate is driven by sinus tracking or the sensor. • Review atrial markers, sensor-indicated rate, activity log and rate histograms. • During exercise, assess whether the rate rises soon enough, reaches an appropriate level and recovers smoothly. • Separate upper tracking behaviour from maximum sensor-rate limitation. • Confirm mode switch during atrial tachyarrhythmia and restoration afterward. H8C8  Clinical Pearls • DDDR is not simply “DDD but faster.” • The atrial channel can be intrinsic, paced by the sensor rate or affected by mode-switch logic. • Upper tracking rate limits AS-driven ventricular pacing. • Maximum sensor rate limits sensor-driven pacing. • Rate response should be tested during relevant activity. • Chronotropic incompetence can coexist with intermittent normal sinus acceleration. • An overactive sensor may mimic sinus tachycardia symptoms. • Mode switch prevents rapid ventricular tracking of atrial tachyarrhythmia. • Programming should consider AV timing at faster paced rates. • The best settings balance symptoms, haemodynamics, battery and pacing burden. H8C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition DDDR DDD mode with rate modulation. Sensor-indicated rate Rate requested by the rate-response algorithm. Maximum sensor rate Upper limit for sensor-driven pacing. Upper tracking rate Upper limit for ventricular tracking of atrial sensed events. Rate-adaptive AV delay AV timing adjusted as rate changes in some systems. Activity threshold Sensor input needed to begin rate acceleration. Blended rate Result of device logic combining intrinsic and sensor information. Mode switch Transition to nontracking behaviour during atrial tachyarrhythmia.   IMAGE 6.6-20   IMAGE 6.6-21   Ask the learner A DDDR patient has AP–VP at 110 bpm during walking even though no sinus P waves are present. What drives the rate? The R function can raise the atrial pacing rate, with ventricular pacing following through dual-chamber timing.

Topic: Topic 6.6.12: DDIR Mode

Topic Description: Topic 6.6.12: DDIR Mode

Heading: DDIR Mode

Topic 6.6.12: DDIR Mode Dual-chamber pacing and sensing with nontracking inhibited response and rate modulation Figure 6.6-10. DDIR senses atrial activity but does not track each sensed atrial event to ventricular pacing. H9C1  Mode Learning Objectives • Decode DDIR letter by letter. • Explain the timing logic and expected pacing response in DDIR. • Recognize the typical ECG and marker-channel pattern of DDIR. • Identify common clinical uses, advantages and limitations of DDIR. • Distinguish normal DDIR behaviour from sensing, capture or timing problems. H9C2  Letter-by-Letter Decoding Position Letter Meaning Functional consequence I D Both chambers paced Atrial and ventricular output are available. II D Both chambers sensed Both atrial and ventricular events can inhibit channel-specific pacing or influence timing. III I Inhibited response Sensed events inhibit pacing, but atrial sensed events are not tracked to the ventricle. IV R Rate modulation The sensor can determine an appropriate pacing rate within programmed limits.   H9C3  Core Operating Principle DDIR is a dual-chamber nontracking mode with rate modulation. A sensed atrial event can inhibit atrial pacing, and a sensed ventricular event can inhibit ventricular pacing, but a sensed atrial event does not trigger a ventricular AV delay in the way it does in DDD. When the device paces the atrium, an AV delay can coordinate a subsequent ventricular pace. The sensor provides rate support independent of atrial tracking. H9C4  Common Clinical Uses • Patients requiring dual-chamber pacing in whom atrial tachyarrhythmia tracking must be avoided. • Programmed destination of automatic mode switch in some dual-chamber systems. • Selected patients with frequent atrial arrhythmias and a need for atrial/ventricular bradycardia support. • Situations in which paced AV synchrony is desired during AP but sensed atrial activity should not drive the ventricle. H9C5  Advantages • Avoids tracking rapid atrial sensed events to the ventricle. • Can pace both chambers and coordinate ventricular pacing after AP. • Rate modulation provides activity support when atrial tracking is not used. • Useful as a protective nontracking mode during atrial tachyarrhythmia. H9C6  Limitations and Risks • Sensed sinus P waves do not trigger ventricular pacing, so AV synchrony may be less physiological when atrial events are intrinsic. • The difference between DDI/DDIR and DDD/DDDR is subtle and can be misinterpreted without markers. • Atrial undersensing or rapid arrhythmia may further reduce effective coordination. • Rate response settings become important because atrial sensed rate is not used for ventricular tracking. • Mode-switch entry and exit criteria can influence symptoms and pacing behaviour. H9C7  Troubleshooting and Interpretation • During AP, look for a programmed AV interval leading to VS or VP. • During AS, do not expect each atrial sensed event to trigger VP. • In atrial tachyarrhythmia, verify that ventricular rate follows lower/sensor timing rather than the atrial rate. • Review mode-switch markers and episode logs to determine whether DDIR is the programmed base mode or an automatic fallback. • Differentiate atrial nontracking from atrial undersensing by confirming AS markers are present. H9C8  Clinical Pearls • The third letter I is the key: DDIR is nontracking. • DDIR can sense atrial events without using them to trigger ventricular pacing. • Atrial pacing can still be followed by a coordinated ventricular response. • DDIR is often encountered as a mode-switch destination. • AS markers during atrial tachyarrhythmia do not imply ventricular tracking. • Rate modulation supplies activity support when tracking is absent. • DDIR is not equivalent to VVIR because atrial pacing and sensing remain available. • A patient may notice a haemodynamic change when switching from tracking DDDR to nontracking DDIR. • Mode-switch exit must be timely but should not repeatedly alternate during unstable atrial rhythm. • Always review actual manufacturer timing logic because DDI/DDIR details vary. H9C9  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition DDIR Both chambers paced and sensed, inhibited response, rate modulation. Nontracking mode Atrial sensed events do not drive ventricular pacing. Mode-switch destination Protective mode entered during atrial tachyarrhythmia. AP–VP coordination A paced atrial event starts AV timing for ventricular support. AS without tracking A sensed atrial event is recognized but does not trigger ventricular pacing. Sensor rate Activity-related pacing rate determined by the R function. Atrial tachyarrhythmia Rapid atrial rhythm that should not be tracked to the ventricle. Mode-switch exit Return to a tracking mode after atrial rhythm stabilizes.   IMAGE 6.6-22   IMAGE 6.6-23   Ask the learner A DDIR strip shows rapid AS markers at 180 bpm but VP remains near 70 bpm. Is the device failing to track? No. Nontracking is the intended response because the third letter is I.

Topic 6.6.13: Mode Comparison and Clinical Selection Mode Use rhythm, sinus-node function, AV conduction, activity needs and procedural context to interpret or choose a mode conceptually Figure 6.6-11. Rate response Typical conceptual use VVI No Yes No Yes No No Permanent AF with bradycardia; simple ventricular demand support VVIR No Yes No Yes No Yes VVI indication plus chronotropic support VOO No Yes No No No No Temporary asynchronous procedural support VDD No Yes Yes Yes Yes No AV block with reliable sinus-node function DDD Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes No Sinus-node and/or AV conduction disease with dual-chamber support DDDR Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes DDD indication plus chronotropic incompetence DDIR Yes Yes Yes Yes No Yes Dual-chamber nontracking support; mode switch or atrial arrhythmia context   H10C2  Conceptual Clinical Selection Questions 1. Is the atrial rhythm organized, stable and useful for timing? 2. Does the patient require atrial pacing because of sinus-node dysfunction? 3. Is AV conduction intact, intermittent or absent? 4. Is atrial tracking desirable, or would it transmit atrial tachyarrhythmia to the ventricle? 5. Does the patient need sensor-driven rate support during activity? 6. How dependent is the patient on pacing, and what are the consequences of inhibition or loss of capture? 7. What ventricular pacing burden is expected, and is conventional RV pacing appropriate for the patient’s ventricular function? 8. Does the patient need CRT, conduction-system pacing or another strategy beyond the basic requested modes? 9. What lead system and sensing quality are available? 10. Is the mode chronic therapy, temporary testing or a procedural protection strategy? Figure 6.6-12. Conceptual mode-selection pathway. Final choice requires individualized clinical assessment. ventricular demand support is required Assess symptoms, ventricular function and pacing burden Permanent AF, complete AV block, exertional fatigue VVIR Ventricular demand support plus sensor-driven rate increase Optimize sensor response and maximum rate Pacemaker-dependent patient undergoing high-EMI surgery VOO temporarily Asynchronous output prevents EMI-related inhibition Use only under a procedural plan and restore afterward Normal sinus node, complete AV block, stable atrial sensing VDD or DDD Atrial tracking preserves AV synchrony; VDD is possible if atrial pacing is not needed VDD fails to support future sinus bradycardia Sinus-node dysfunction with intact AV conduction DDD or DDDR Atrial pacing is required; intrinsic ventricular conduction may be preserved Program to minimize unnecessary ventricular pacing when appropriate Sinus-node dysfunction plus complete AV block DDD or DDDR Both chambers require pacing support Assess chronotropic competence and ventricular pacing strategy Frequent atrial tachyarrhythmia with dual-chamber pacing need DDIR or automatic mode-switch destination Prevents tracking of rapid atrial sensed events Loss of atrial tracking can alter haemodynamics AV block with chronotropic incompetence DDDR Atrial/ventricular support plus sensor-driven rate response Upper tracking and sensor limits must be coordinated Normal sinus rhythm and intact AV conduction, no bradycardia No pacing mode indicated from these facts alone A mode is selected only after a pacing indication is established Avoid treating a code rather than a patient Reduced LVEF with expected high ventricular pacing burden Basic DDD code is insufficient to decide strategy CRT or conduction-system pacing may be more appropriate Use current guidelines and specialist assessment   H10C4  Do Not Choose a Mode by Diagnosis Alone A diagnosis such as AV block does not automatically select VDD or DDD. The decision also depends on sinus-node function, atrial rhythm, expected progression, age, activity, ventricular function, pacing burden, comorbidities, venous access, lead strategy and patient preference. Similarly, permanent AF often points toward ventricular-only pacing, but rate response, ventricular function and the need for CRT or conduction-system pacing may change the final system. High pacing-burden caution In a patient with reduced ventricular function or an expected high burden of ventricular pacing, conventional RV pacing mode selection should not be considered in isolation. The pacing site and resynchronization or conduction-system strategy may be as important as the NBG letters.   H10C5  Mode Comparison Clinical Pearls • VVI and VVIR ignore atrial timing; VVIR adds only sensor-driven rate response. • VOO is asynchronous and usually temporary. • VDD can track the atrium but cannot pace it. • DDD can support both chambers and track atrial activity. • DDDR adds rate modulation to DDD. • DDIR senses both chambers but is nontracking because the third letter is I. • Atrial tracking and rate modulation solve different physiological problems. • The best mode is not always the mode with the most letters. • A patient can have the correct NBG mode but poor results because of unsuitable timing or sensor settings. • Pacing mode, lead strategy and pacing site must be considered together.

Verify the programmed mode using pacing spikes, chamber events, marker channels and timing intervals H11C1  A Seven-Step Mode-Recognition Method 1. Identify P waves, QRS complexes and pacing spikes on the surface ECG. 2. Determine whether atrial spikes, ventricular spikes or both are present. 3. Look for intrinsic events that inhibit pacing. 4. Use marker channels to label AS, AP, VS and VP. 5. Determine whether AS events trigger an AV delay and possible VP. 6. Assess whether paced rate changes with activity or sensor markers. 7. Compare the observed behaviour with the displayed programmed mode and timing values. Do not infer the full mode from one beat AS–VP can occur in both VDD and DDD. Only evidence of atrial pacing, the programmed mode or lead/system information distinguishes them.   IMAGE 6.6-25   H11C2  Expected Marker Patterns by Mode Mode Expected marker patterns Pattern that requires explanation VVI VS or VP Atrial markers should not control timing; extra VS without QRS suggests oversensing VVIR VS or VP plus sensor-driven rate information Paced rate that does not match activity or exceeds programmed sensor limits VOO Regular VP markers independent of intrinsic rhythm Any apparent inhibition suggests the actual mode is not VOO or output was interrupted VDD AS–VS or AS–VP; VS may occur without prior AS AP should not occur in true VDD DDD AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS or AP–VP Unexpected timing must be checked against lower/upper rate, AV delays and refractory periods DDDR DDD patterns plus sensor-driven AP/VP support Separate AS tracking from R-driven AP DDIR AS may inhibit AP, but AS is not followed by tracked VP; AP may initiate AV timing Rapid AS followed by equally rapid VP suggests tracking mode or inappropriate behaviour   H11C3  Interactive: Decode the Mode For each code, ask the learner to complete the four prompts before revealing the answer. VVIR: V, V, inhibited, R. VOO: V, none, none, no R. VDD: V, dual, dual, no R. DDD: dual, dual, dual, no R. DDDR: dual, dual, dual, R. VP is inhibited and the ventricular timer resets. VOO: intrinsic QRS occurs Does pacing timer reset? No. The next VP occurs at the fixed interval. VDD: AS occurs and no VS follows What occurs after AV delay? VP is delivered. DDD: AP occurs and intrinsic VS appears before paced AV delay ends Is VP delivered? No. VS inhibits VP.
