DDIR: rapid AS events occur Does every AS trigger VP? No. AS is not tracked in the inhibited-response mode.   IMAGE 6.6-26   H11C5  Interactive: Label a DDD ECG Label number Feature to identify 1 Atrial sensed event / P wave 2 AS marker 3 Sensed AV delay 4 Ventricular paced spike 5 Paced QRS 6 T wave 7 Atrial paced spike 8 Atrial capture 9 Paced AV delay 10 Intrinsic QRS / VS 11 VS marker 12 Inhibited ventricular output   IMAGE 6.6-27   H11C6  Common Mode-Identification Errors Error Why it occurs Correction Calling every ventricular-paced rhythm VVI Only ventricular spikes are noticed Check P waves, atrial markers, AV relationship and programmed mode. Calling AS–VP VDD VDD is associated with atrial tracking DDD can also produce AS–VP; look for AP capability and device programming. Calling VOO undersensing Intrinsic QRS does not inhibit pacing VOO intentionally has no sensing; confirm the programmed mode. Calling DDIR atrial undersensing AS does not trigger VP AS may be sensed normally but nontracked because the third letter is I. Confusing R with atrial tracking Rate rises with activity R is sensor driven; tracking requires atrial sensing and a triggered/dual response. Calling upper-rate behaviour malfunction Every P wave is not followed by VP at high atrial rates Review upper tracking rate and refractory timing. Equating spike with capture Pacing marker is present Confirm P wave or QRS after the spike.   H11C7  ECG/EGM Clinical Pearls • Start with P waves, QRS complexes and pacing spikes before reading markers. • Markers show device interpretation and must be checked against the ECG/EGM. • VDD and DDD can look identical during AS–VP. • VOO is diagnosed from programmed no-sensing behaviour, not from apparent failure to inhibit alone. • DDIR may show many AS markers without ventricular tracking. • The R function is best recognized from rate behaviour and programmer data rather than one resting ECG. • Upper-rate responses can be normal in tracking modes. • A pacing spike without capture is a threshold/output problem, not a different NBG mode. • Undersensing and oversensing can make any inhibited mode appear to behave incorrectly. • Always correlate mode, timing settings, EGMs and the patient’s rhythm.

Topic 6.6.15: Chapter Consolidation Mode Clinical pearls, master vocabulary, assessments and image-production register H12C1   Clinical Pearls • Read the NBG code from left to right: pace, sense, respond, rate, multisite. • The first letter identifies output capability; the second identifies input capability. • The third letter predicts the timing response and is essential for distinguishing DDD from DDIR. • R means sensor-driven rate modulation and is independent of atrial tracking. • VVI is ventricular demand pacing; VVIR adds activity-related rate support. • VOO is asynchronous and usually temporary. • VDD tracks atrial activity but cannot pace the atrium. • DDD can produce AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS and AP–VP. • DDDR adds rate response to DDD. • DDIR senses both chambers but does not track sensed atrial events to the ventricle. • A code describes core logic, not all timing settings or algorithms. • A short ECG may not reveal the full programmed capability. • Atrial tracking and rate response solve different problems. • Upper tracking rate and maximum sensor rate are different limits. • Mode switch commonly moves a tracking mode to a nontracking mode during atrial tachyarrhythmia. • Pacing spikes prove output, not capture. • Sensed markers prove classification, not that the signal was physiologically appropriate. • Mode selection requires rhythm, conduction, activity, ventricular function and pacing-burden assessment. • More complex mode is not automatically better. • Patient stability and appropriate pacing strategy are more important than code memorization. H12C2  Master Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition NBG NASPE/BPEG Generic code for pacing functions. Position I Chamber or chambers paced. Position II Chamber or chambers sensed. Position III Response to sensing. Position IV Rate modulation. Position V Multisite pacing. O None in the stated position. A Atrium. V Ventricle. D in position I/II Both atrium and ventricle. I Inhibited response. T Triggered response. D in position III Dual inhibited and triggered response. R Rate modulation. VVI Ventricular paced, ventricular sensed, inhibited. VVIR VVI with rate response. VOO Asynchronous ventricular pacing without sensing. VDD Ventricular paced, dual sensed, dual response. DDD Dual paced, dual sensed, dual response. DDDR DDD with rate response. DDIR Dual paced, dual sensed, inhibited response, rate modulation. Atrial tracking AS event initiates ventricular timing in a tracking mode. Nontracking Atrial sensed events do not drive ventricular pacing. AS Atrial sensed marker. AP Atrial paced marker. VS Ventricular sensed marker. VP Ventricular paced marker. AV delay Timing interval from atrial event to ventricular event or pacing. Lower rate Minimum pacing support rate under the programmed timing logic. Upper tracking rate Maximum ventricular rate driven by AS tracking. Maximum sensor rate Maximum rate driven by rate-response sensor. Mode switch Automatic transition to nontracking behaviour during atrial tachyarrhythmia. Pacemaker Wenckebach Upper-rate tracking pattern with progressive AV delay. Pacemaker syndrome Symptoms from adverse AV timing or loss of synchrony. Asynchronous pacing Pacing independent of intrinsic sensing. Chronotropic incompetence Inadequate intrinsic rate increase with demand.   H12C3  Knowledge Check – Mode Decoding Question Answer What does the first V in VDD mean? Only the ventricle can be paced. What does the second D in VDD mean? Both atrium and ventricle can be sensed. What does the third D in DDD mean? Dual response: triggered and inhibited actions. What does R add to VVIR? Sensor-driven rate modulation. Why is VOO not inhibited by a QRS? It has no sensing and no sensing response. Can VDD pace sinus bradycardia in the atrium? No. What four event combinations may appear in DDD? AS–VS, AS–VP, AP–VS and AP–VP. Does DDIR track AS events to VP? No; it is a nontracking inhibited-response mode. What is the difference between upper tracking rate and maximum sensor rate? One limits AS-driven tracking; the other limits sensor-driven pacing. Can one short ECG prove the complete mode? Not always; programmer mode and marker evidence are required.   H12C5  Additional Images   Final clinical disclaimer The NBG code provides a universal foundation, but manufacturers implement timing cycles, sensors, mode switching, pacing-minimization algorithms, magnet behaviour and marker nomenclature differently. Use current device-specific instructions and qualified clinical judgment for programming and patient care.

Chapter: CHAPTER 6.7: PACEMAKER FEATURES

Topic: TOPIC 6.7.1: RATE-RESPONSIVE PACING

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.7.1: RATE-RESPONSIVE PACING

Heading: Pacemaker Features

Rate-responsive pacing, activity-based pacing and piezoelectric sensor technology   Figure 6.7-1. Rate-responsive pacing converts a sensor signal into a patient-specific pacing-rate response.   Scope of this chapter This chapter explains the principles and practical interpretation of rate-responsive pacing, with special emphasis on activity-based sensors and piezoelectric technology. It is intended for LMS education of service engineers, clinical support staff, field application specialists and healthcare learners. Device-specific names, ranges and algorithms vary; current technical manuals and qualified clinical judgment remain essential.   H1C1  Pacemaker Features H1C2  Learning Objectives At the end of this chapter, the learner should be able to: • Define rate-responsive pacing and explain the meaning of the fourth-position letter R in the NBG code. • Explain the physiological relationship among exercise, metabolic demand, autonomic activation, stroke volume and heart rate. • Define chronotropic incompetence and explain why resting pacemaker function may appear normal despite exertional symptoms. • Differentiate atrial tracking from sensor-driven rate modulation. • Describe the signal pathway from body motion to a sensor-indicated pacing rate. • Explain activity-based pacing and distinguish piezoelectric crystal sensors from integrated-circuit accelerometers. • Explain how a piezoelectric element converts mechanical stress, vibration and pressure waves into an electrical signal. • Describe the strengths and limitations of activity sensors, including rapid onset, low power use, vibration susceptibility and under-response during low-torso-motion exercise. • Explain the purpose of lower rate, maximum sensor rate, activity threshold, response factor, reaction time and recovery time. • Explain rate-profile optimization, sensor trending and passive sensor collection as manufacturer-specific concepts. • Identify expected paced-rate changes at rest, activity onset, sustained activity and recovery. • Interpret rate response in VVIR, DDDR, DDIR and AAIR modes. • Use walking, stair, treadmill, bicycle, six-minute walk and cardiopulmonary exercise testing to evaluate response in context. • Troubleshoot insufficient, excessive, delayed or prolonged sensor-driven pacing. • Recognize procedure and environmental situations in which vibration or motion may produce an inappropriate activity-sensor response. • Document a rate-response assessment and programming rationale in a reproducible clinical format. H1C3  Chapter Overview A fixed-rate pacemaker can prevent bradycardia at rest, yet it may not reproduce the normal increase in heart rate required during walking, climbing stairs, household work, exercise or emotional stress. Rate-responsive pacing adds a sensor and algorithm that increase the pacing rate when the patient’s own sinus node cannot produce an adequate chronotropic response. The feature is represented by the letter R in the fourth position of the NBG code, as in VVIR, DDDR, DDIR or AAIR. The sensor does not directly know how much cardiac output the patient needs. Instead, it measures a surrogate of demand. An activity sensor measures motion, acceleration, vibration or mechanical stress. A minute-ventilation sensor measures changes related to respiration. Other systems may use contractility or impedance-derived signals. The algorithm converts the measured surrogate into a sensor-indicated rate bounded by programmed limits. Correct rate-response therapy is therefore not achieved merely by turning the sensor on. The clinician must decide whether rate modulation is indicated, choose an appropriate mode, set the minimum and maximum rates, determine how easily the sensor activates, select the slope of rate increase, and shape the onset and recovery. The response must then be tested using activities that resemble the patient’s actual symptoms and daily life. Central concept The sensor detects a surrogate of effort. The algorithm interprets that surrogate. Programming determines the rate response. Patient testing determines whether the final response is clinically appropriate.   H1C4  Fundamentals: Normal Chronotropic Response During exercise, oxygen demand rises. Venous return, sympathetic activation, myocardial contractility and heart rate increase, while vagal influence decreases. Stroke volume contributes substantially at lower workloads, but the ability to increase heart rate becomes increasingly important as demand rises. The normal sinus node accelerates rapidly at activity onset, continues to increase with workload and then decelerates gradually during recovery. The appropriate response is not a single target rate. It depends on age, fitness, medications, autonomic function, cardiac disease, exercise type, posture, temperature and emotional state. A healthy response during brisk walking differs from the response during cycling, resistance exercise or arm work. For this reason, device optimization should focus on symptoms, workload and rate trajectory rather than a memorized universal number. Figure 6.7-2. Chronotropic incompetence produces an inadequate heart-rate rise relative to activity demand. IMAGE 6.7-01 Learning purpose: Connect rate-responsive pacing to the normal physiology it is designed to approximate.     H1C5  Chronotropic Incompetence Chronotropic incompetence is the inability of the heart to increase its rate appropriately for the patient’s metabolic demand. It may result from sinus-node dysfunction, autonomic disease, medication effects, surgical injury, transplanted-heart physiology or a combination of factors. The patient may have an acceptable resting rate yet develop fatigue, dyspnoea, exercise intolerance, dizziness or reduced functional capacity because the rate fails to rise adequately. Diagnostic criteria vary. Exercise testing may examine peak heart rate, heart-rate reserve, metabolic equivalents, oxygen consumption, symptoms and medication context. A single age-predicted formula is not sufficient for every patient. In device follow-up, the practical question is whether the intrinsic or paced heart-rate profile is appropriate for the activity performed and the patient’s clinical goals.       Finding Possible interpretation Important caution Resting rate is normal but remains nearly fixed during walking Possible chronotropic incompetence or sensor not contributing Confirm that the patient is actually pacing and that medications are considered Rate rises but plateaus early Upper sensor rate or response factor may limit response The plateau may also reflect patient physiology or test intensity Rate rises slowly after activity starts Reaction time or activity threshold may be too conservative Gradual onset may be intentional for some patients Rate rises adequately but symptoms persist Symptoms may not be rate-related Assess rhythm, AV timing, ventricular function, ischaemia, pulmonary and non-cardiac causes Intrinsic sinus rate rises normally Sensor-driven pacing may be unnecessary in a tracking mode Avoid attributing all rate increase to the sensor   IMAGE 6.7-02 . Learning purpose: Show why a normal resting device check may not explain exertional symptoms. .   H1C6  Rate Response in the NBG Code   Figure 6.7-3. The fourth-position R indicates rate modulation.   The first three letters of the NBG code describe the chamber paced, chamber sensed and response to sensing. The fourth position describes rate modulation. When R is present, a sensor can modify the pacing rate according to the programmed algorithm. R does not specify the type of sensor, the programmed limits or whether the feature is clinically appropriate. Mode Rate-response interpretation Typical functional concept VVIR Ventricular demand pacing with rate modulation Sensor raises ventricular pacing rate when intrinsic ventricular activity is too slow DDDR Dual-chamber pacing and sensing with dual response plus rate modulation Atrial tracking and/or sensor response can support rate; timing rules decide the final rate DDIR Dual-chamber pacing and sensing, nontracking inhibited response plus rate modulation Sensor supports rate without beat-to-beat atrial tracking AAIR Atrial demand pacing with rate modulation Sensor increases atrial pacing rate when sinus rate is inadequate and AV conduction is suitable   Figure 6.7-4. Rate modulation changes timing within the mode defined by the first three NBG positions.   Tracking is not the same as rate response In DDD or DDDR, a faster ventricular rate may result from tracking a faster intrinsic atrial rate, from sensor-driven pacing, or from both. Always review atrial events, sensor status, markers and programmed limits before deciding which mechanism produced the rate.    

Heading: Rate-Responsive Pacing

Topic 6.7.1: Rate-Responsive Pacing Definition, physiological purpose, indications, benefits and limitations H2C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Define rate-responsive pacing. • Explain why a fixed lower rate may be insufficient during activity. • Identify patients who may benefit from rate modulation. • Distinguish sensor-indicated rate, lower rate, upper sensor rate and tracked rate. • Explain advantages, limitations and cautions. H2C2  What Is Rate-Responsive Pacing? Rate-responsive pacing, also called rate-adaptive pacing, is a feature that varies the pacing rate in response to activity or a measured physiological surrogate. In a mode ending with R, the device calculates a sensor-indicated rate and uses it to modify pacing timing within the limits of the programmed mode. The rate generally rises when sensed activity or demand increases and declines when the signal falls. The purpose is not to force every patient to a high rate. The purpose is to provide a rate appropriate to the patient’s activity when the intrinsic sinus response is inadequate. The system should remain near the lower rate during rest, rise promptly enough for ordinary movement, provide an adequate sustained rate for meaningful exertion and return smoothly after activity ends. Figure 6.7-5. Sensor, algorithm and pacing mode function as a controlled rate-response system. IMAGE 6.7-03   H2C3  Why Rate Response Is Needed •           Prevents a fixed bradycardic pacing rate from limiting cardiac output during activity. •           May improve walking tolerance, exercise duration, perceived energy and ability to perform daily activities in appropriately selected patients. •           Provides chronotropic support when the sinus node is diseased, surgically injured, pharmacologically suppressed or unable to respond adequately. •           Allows ventricular rate support in patients with atrial fibrillation and bradycardia when atrial tracking is unavailable. •           Can support rate during atrial arrhythmia mode switch when the fallback mode is rate-adaptive. •           Can provide a more gradual transition between rest and exertion than a single fixed rate.     H2C4  Clinical Situations in Which Rate Response May Be Considered Clinical situation Why rate response may help Assessment required Sinus-node dysfunction with chronotropic incompetence Intrinsic atrial rate does not rise sufficiently during activity Symptoms, exercise response, medications and AV conduction Permanent atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response or AV block No organized atrial rhythm is available for tracking VVIR response, ventricular function and acceptable upper rate Post-AV-node ablation Ventricular rate is fully device-dependent Gradual rate plan, activity tolerance and ventricula

Topic: Topic 6.7.2: Activity-Based Pacing

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.2: Activity-Based Pacing

Heading: Learning Objectives

How motion becomes a sensor-indicated pacing rate H3C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Describe the activity-sensor signal chain. • Explain frequency and amplitude components of motion. • Explain activity threshold, response factor, reaction time and recovery time. • Identify strengths and blind spots of motion-based pacing. • Use sensor trends and patient activity testing to assess performance. H3C2  What Is Activity-Based Pacing? Activity-based pacing uses a mechanical sensor within the pulse generator to detect motion associated with physical activity. The sensor produces an electrical signal whose amplitude and frequency vary with movement. Signal processing rejects low-level or irrelevant components, and a rate-response algorithm maps the remaining signal to a pacing rate above the lower rate. Activity sensing is attractive because body movement usually begins immediately when activity starts. It is therefore well suited to the onset of walking, standing and many daily tasks. However, body motion and metabolic demand are not identical. A bumpy vehicle can produce motion without exercise, while cycling can create significant metabolic demand with limited upper-body acceleration. Figure 6.7-6. Activity-based pacing requires both mechanical sensing and programmed algorithmic interpretation. IMAGE  6.7-05 Learning purpose: Show where the feature physically resides and how it connects to pacing control.     H3C3  Motion Frequency and Amplitude The frequency component reflects how often motion occurs, such as step cadence. The amplitude component reflects the magnitude or force of motion. An algorithm may combine both. Slow gentle movement may produce a small signal; brisk walking may produce a larger and more frequent signal. The mapping from signal to pacing rate is not a direct step counter and varies among device families.   Motion pattern Sensor signal Possible rate-response implication Gentle walking Low-to-moderate repetitive signal Should usually exceed an appropriately programmed activity threshold Brisk walking or jogging Higher frequency and amplitude Higher sensor-indicated rate until limited by response factor or maximum sensor rate Cycling Potentially limited torso motion despite high workload Activity sensor may under-respond Vehicle vibration Repetitive mechanical vibration without exercise May produce an inappropriate response in susceptible sensors/settings Upper-body tool use Localized repetitive movement May produce a rate disproportionate to whole-body demand Tremor Persistent low-amplitude repetitive motion May cross a very sensitive activity threshold   IMAGE 6.7-06 Learning purpose: Teach that the sensor evaluates motion characteristics rather than simply detecting movement or no movement.     H3C4  Activity Threshold The activity threshold is the amount of processed sensor signal that must be exceeded before the rate begins to rise above the lower rate. A more sensitive threshold requires less motion. A less sensitive threshold requires more motion. The correct setting should permit a response to ordinary activities such as walking while preventing an inappropriate rate increase at rest. Figure 6.7-7. A lower activity threshold can initiate rate response earlier but may accept unwanted motion.       Threshold setting direction Expected effect Potential benefit Potential problem More sensitive / lower activity requirement Rate response begins with smaller movements May improve onset during gentle walking or frailty May respond to tremor, respiration, heartbeat, handling or vibration Less sensitive / higher activity requirement More motion is required before rate rises Reduces inappropriate activation at rest May fail to respond during light activity or low-impact movement   Do not confuse two different sensitivities Activity threshold controls response to mechanical motion. Cardiac sensing sensitivity controls detection of intracardiac electrical signals. Changing one does not directly change the other.   H3C5  Response Factor, Sensor Gain or Slope The response factor determines how much the pacing rate rises for a given level of activity above threshold. A higher response factor generally produces a higher rate at the same activity level or allows the rate to approach the maximum sensor rate with less activity. A lower response factor produces a more conservative rate increase. Figure 6.7-8. Response factor changes the relationship between activity and sensor-indicated rate. IMAGE 6.7-07 Learning purpose: Allow learners to predict how slope changes alter the steady-state rate.     H3C6  Reaction Time Reaction time determines how quickly the pacing rate rises after activity is detected. A short reaction time produces a rapid acceleration. A long reaction time produces a gradual increase. Reaction time changes the onset dynamics but does not necessarily determine the final steady-state rate at a sustained activity level. The ideal onset depends on the patient. A person who becomes symptomatic during the first minute of walking may need a faster response. A patient who experiences palpitations with sudden acceleration may benefit from a slower onset, provided exercise support remains adequate. H3C7  Recovery Time Recovery time determines how quickly the pacing rate declines after activity stops or decreases. A short recovery time returns the rate toward the lower rate quickly. A long recovery time produces a gradual deceleration. Recovery prevents an abrupt drop immediately after exercise, when venous return, temperature and metabolic demand may remain elevated. Figure 6.7-9. Reaction time shapes acceleration; recovery time shapes deceleration. IMAGE  6.7-08 . Learning purpose: Relate abstract timing settings to activities that patients recognise. .   H3C8 Lower Rate and Maximum Sensor Rate The lower rate provides the resting pacing floor when neither intrinsic rhythm nor another device timing rule produces a faster rate. The maximum sensor rate is the highest rate the sensor is allowed to command. It is a safety and haemodynamic limit, not a target that every patient must reach. The maximum sensor rate must be considered with upper tracking behaviour, refractory periods, AV delays, ventricular function and the patient’s ability to tolerate faster rates. In dual-chamber devices, the final paced ventricular rate may be limited by the sensor, atrial tracking limit or another timing rule depending on the event sequence.         Parameter Primary role Common error in interpretation Lower rate limit Defines the pacing floor at rest Assuming that increasing it improves exercise response without assessing slope Maximum sensor rate Defines the sensor-driven ceiling Assuming the patient will automatically reach it Upper tracking rate Defines atrial-tracked ventricular limit Confusing it with maximum sensor rate Maximum pacing rate Device-specific combined limit in some systems Ignoring manufacturer-specific hierarchy   IMAGE 6.7-09 Learning purpose: Clarify why several rate limits can interact in a dual-chamber pacemaker.     H3C9 Sensor Trending and Passive Data Collection Some devices can collect activity-sensor information even when the sensor is not actively controlling the pacing rate. This may be called passive sensor operation or sensor trending. The stored data can be compared with the patient’s rate histogram and symptoms before rate-adaptive programming is enabled or changed. Rate-profile optimization algorithms may analyse daily sensor-rate distributions and adjust response curves toward a programmed target. The principle is useful, but automatic optimization remains device-specific. Learners must distinguish a manually programmed setting, an automatically adapted setting and a diagnostic trend that does not influence pacing. IMAGE 6.7-10 Learning purpose: Show how sensor data can be reviewed before and after activation.     H3C10 Strengths of Activity-Based Pacing • Rapid response to the onset of body motion. • Simple signal acquisition with low computational and energy requirements. • Independent of atrial rhythm and atrial sensing. • Useful during walking and many daily activities. • Programmable activation threshold, slope, onset and recovery. • Ability to generate activity diagnostics and trends. • Applicable to transvenous and leadless pacemaker designs. H3C11 Limitations and Blind Spots Limitation Example Possible management Motion is not metabolic demand Riding over bumps produces vibration Raise activity threshold or use a different/blended sensor when available Low torso motion despite exertion Stationary bicycle or some resistance exercises Use activity-specific testing; consider physiologic or blended sensor Pocket pressure or case vibration External manipulation or tools Review sensor type and environmental history Movement disorder Tremor or repetitive involuntary motion Assess at rest and during symptoms; avoid overly sensitive threshold Orientation dependence in some piezoelectric systems Sensor coupling differs with generator position Test actual response after implant and during follow-up Response depends on programming Sensor is on but rate remains too low Review threshold, response factor and limits rather than assuming sensor failure   IMAGE 6.7-11 Learning purpose: Make the surrogate nature of activity sensing memorable.     H3C12  Topic Clinical Pearls •           Activity threshold controls when response starts; response factor controls how much rate is produced. •           Reaction time changes onset speed; recovery time changes offset speed. •           A patient can have an appropriate threshold but an inadequate response factor. •           A high maximum sensor rate cannot compensate for a low response factor. •           Cycling may produce only a moderate accelerometer response because torso motion is limited. •           Vibration can create rate response without metabolic demand. •           A sensor may collect trends without actively controlling pacing. •           Always test the patient’s real symptom-producing activity. •           Cardiac sensing sensitivity and activity-sensor threshold are different parameters. •           Parameter names and directions must be confirmed in the device-specific manual.   H3C13  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Activity sensor Mechanical sensor that detects body motion associated with activity. Activity threshold Minimum processed motion signal required to initiate a rate response. Response factor Setting that determines rate increase for a given activity level. Reaction time Time course of pacing-rate rise after activity begins. Recovery time Time course of pacing-rate decline after activity falls. Maximum sensor rate Highest pacing rate the sensor may command. Sensor trending Storage and display of sensor activity or sensor-indicated rate over time. Passive sensor Sensor collecting diagnostic data without controlling the pacing rate. Rate profile Distribution of sensor or paced rates over time. Motion artifact Mechanical signal not proportional to metabolic demand.

Topic: Topic 6.7.3: Piezoelectric Sensors

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.3: Piezoelectric Sensors

Heading: Piezoelectric Sensors

How mechanical stress and vibration are converted into a pacing-rate signal H4C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Explain the direct piezoelectric effect. • Describe how a crystal can function as an activity sensor inside a pacemaker. • Identify mechanical inputs that influence the sensor. • Compare piezoelectric and accelerometer technology. • Explain orientation, vibration and pocket-pressure limitations. • Recognize inappropriate sensor activation in clinical and procedural settings. H4C2  The Piezoelectric Effect Certain crystalline or ceramic materials develop an electrical charge when they are mechanically stressed, bent, compressed or vibrated. This is the direct piezoelectric effect. In a rate-responsive pacemaker, a piezoelectric element can be mechanically coupled to the pulse-generator case. Body motion, muscle contraction and pressure waves deform the element and generate an electrical signal. The generated charge is very small. It is amplified, filtered and processed before it is useful. The device analyses characteristics such as signal frequency, amplitude and persistence, then applies the programmed activity threshold and rate-response curve. The crystal does not directly measure heart rate, oxygen consumption or blood flow. Figure 6.7-10. Piezoelectric material converts mechanical stress into an electrical signal. IMAGE 6.7-12 Learning purpose: Explain the physical transduction principle without requiring advanced materials science. .   H4C3  Piezoelectric Sensor Construction in a Pacemaker 1.       Traditional activity-responsive systems placed a piezoelectric crystal or piezo-quartz element in mechanical contact with the generator case. The titanium can transmitted movement, vibration and pressure to the sensor. Because mechanical coupling is part of the signal path, generator orientation, pocket location, surrounding tissue and case pressure can influence the response. 2.       Patient movement creates acceleration, vibration or muscular pressure around the generator. 3.       The titanium can transmits part of the mechanical energy to the piezoelectric element. 4.       The element deforms and generates a small electrical potential. 5.       An amplifier increases the signal to a measurable level. 6.       Filters select the range considered compatible with activity and reject low-level or unwanted components. 7.       The signal is compared with the programmed activity threshold. 8.       The rate-response algorithm maps the accepted signal to a sensor-indicated rate. 9.       Reaction, recovery and maximum-rate settings shape the final pacing interval.   IMAGE 6.7-13 Learning purpose: Show the complete physical path from case vibration to algorithm input.     H4C4  What the Piezoelectric Sensor Detects Mechanical input Why it produces a signal Clinical implication Walking and running Repeated body acceleration and muscle pressure waves Usually produces a prompt rate increase Arm and shoulder movement Movement transmitted through the pectoral pocket May contribute strongly even when whole-body demand is modest External vibration Mechanical energy deforms the crystal May cause inappropriate rate acceleration Pocket pressure or manipulation Direct case stress can deform a case-coupled sensor Historical systems may respond to pressure or handling Tremor Repeated low-amplitude mechanical stress May activate a sensitive threshold Cycling with stable torso Less generator movement despite substantial effort May under-estimate demand   IMAGE 6.7-14 Learning purpose: Demonstrate which mechanical inputs may be physiologic or misleading.     H4C5  Piezoelectric Sensor Signal Characteristics The crystal output reflects both the magnitude and pattern of mechanical deformation. A brief tap may create a high-amplitude transient. Repeated walking creates a rhythmic signal. Sustained static pressure produces less useful dynamic information than changing pressure, although case-coupled designs may still respond to manipulation. The algorithm must distinguish meaningful activity from noise and prevent one short impulse from causing a prolonged high pacing rate. Because mechanical energy can travel through tissue and the pulse-generator case, the signal may depend on implant depth, pocket fibrosis, generator fixation and orientation. Follow-up testing after implantation is therefore essential; nominal programming cannot predict every patient’s motion-to-rate relationship. IMAGE 6.7-15 Learning purpose: Build visual recognition of different mechanical signal patterns.   H4C6 Piezoelectric Crystal versus Accelerometer Figure 6.7-11. Piezoelectric and accelerometer sensors both measure activity but use different transduction and mechanical coupling. Current implanted devices commonly use solid-state integrated-circuit accelerometers, while piezoelectric crystal systems remain important historically and conceptually. Both are activity-based sensors. A piezoelectric crystal generates charge when mechanically stressed. An accelerometer measures acceleration along one or more axes and produces an electronic signal related to motion. Accelerometers can be isolated from direct static case pressure and can analyse motion frequency and amplitude. Piezoelectric case-coupled sensors may be more influenced by pressure, orientation and external vibration. Neither technology directly measures metabolic demand, so both require careful programming and real-world testing.               Feature Piezoelectric crystal Integrated-circuit accelerometer Physical principle Mechanical stress generates electrical charge Acceleration is measured electronically Mechanical coupling Often coupled to generator case Internal solid-state component Common signal Vibration, pressure waves, muscle tension and movement Acceleration frequency and amplitude Orientation effect Can be important in case-coupled systems Axis and device orientation may still influence response Static case pressure May influence some designs Modern isolated designs are less responsive to simple static pressure Current use Historically important; selected or emerging designs may use piezoelectric elements Common in contemporary rate-responsive pacemakers Shared limitation Activity surrogate can mismatch metabolic demand Activity surrogate can mismatch metabolic demand   IMAGE 6.7-16 Learning purpose: Prevent the terms piezoelectric and accelerometer from being treated as exact synonyms. .   H4C7  Sensor Orientation and Pocket Factors The response of a mechanically coupled sensor can vary with generator orientation. A crystal facing toward or away from the chest wall may receive different mechanical energy. Pocket depth, fixation, surrounding tissue and patient body habitus also influence coupling. Published experience with piezoelectric systems demonstrated that adequate response could be achieved in different orientations, but programming requirements could differ. The practical lesson is not to memorize one orientation rule. It is to test the implanted system after healing and during the activities the patient performs. If a generator is revised or moved, sensor behaviour should be reassessed. IMAGE 6.7-17 . Learning purpose: Explain why orientation can alter the effective sensor signal and programming needs.     H4C8  Advantages of Piezoelectric Activity Sensors • Simple direct conversion of mechanical energy to an electrical signal. • Rapid response to movement onset. • Low power consumption and compact construction. • Independent of atrial electrical rhythm. • Useful for walking and movement-dominant daily activities. • Can provide activity diagnostics as well as rate modulation. H4C9  Limitations and Sources of Inappropriate Response • External vibration may be interpreted as activity. • Movement intensity may not equal metabolic demand. • Generator orientation and pocket mechanics can affect signal amplitude. • Cycling or static exercise may produce inadequate response. • Tremor, shoulder movement or repetitive tools may increase rate disproportionately. • Very sensitive settings may respond to low-level non-exercise motion. • A technically functioning sensor may still provide clinically unsuitable chronotropy.   Operating-room awareness Mechanical vibration from patient movement or powered equipment can activate an activity sensor as part of normal sensor function. A peri-procedural device plan should consider the programmed rate-responsive feature as well as EMI and pacing dependence.   IMAGE 6.7-18 Learning purpose: Teach that an unexpected rate increase may represent normal sensor response to abnormal mechanical input, not device failure.     H4C10  Topic Clinical Pearls • Piezoelectric sensors convert mechanical stress into electrical charge. • They measure motion-related mechanical energy, not oxygen demand directly. • Mechanical coupling to the pulse-generator case can make orientation and pocket factors important. • Walking usually produces a strong signal; cycling may not. • Vibration can increase the pacing rate without true exertion. • A rate increase during pocket manipulation can be sensor-mediated. • A modern accelerometer is related to, but not identical to, a piezoelectric crystal sensor. • The algorithm and programming settings determine the clinical response more than the sensor element alone. • Reassess sensor behaviour after generator revision or relocation. • Confirm unexpected rate acceleration with markers, sensor status and exposure history.   H4C11  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Piezoelectric effect Generation of electrical charge when a material is mechanically stressed. Piezoelectric crystal Material used to convert deformation or vibration into an electrical signal. Mechanical coupling Transfer of movement or pressure from the generator case to the sensor. Transduction Conversion of one form of energy into another. Accelerometer Sensor that measures acceleration along one or more axes. Vibration artifact Mechanical signal that activates the sensor without equivalent physiological demand. Pocket manipulation External pressure or movement applied to the implanted generator area. Sensor orientation Direction of the sensor or generator relative to the body and motion vectors. Signal conditioning Amplification and filtering that make the sensor output usable by the algorithm. Surrogate sensor Sensor measuring a variable correlated with, but not identical to, metabolic demand.

Topic: Topic 6.7.4: Programming Rate Response

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.4: Programming Rate Response

Heading: Programming Rate Response

Patient-specific selection of threshold, slope, limits, onset and recovery H5C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Perform a structured pre-programming assessment. • Explain each major rate-response parameter. • Use exercise and daily-activity testing to optimize settings. • Differentiate parameter problems that produce similar symptoms. • Document rationale and post-programming verification. H5C2  Programming Philosophy Rate-response programming should reproduce the patient’s functional needs without creating unnecessary high rates. It is a process of hypothesis, controlled testing and verification. The programmer settings are not ends in themselves. Each setting should be linked to an observed problem: no response to light activity, excessive acceleration, early plateau, slow onset or prolonged recovery. Nominal settings may be a safe starting point, but they are not automatically optimal. Age, mobility, frailty, fitness, medications, ventricular function, AV conduction, activity type and symptom goals should influence the final profile. Programming sequence First decide whether rate response is indicated. Then confirm the pacing mode. Next set safe rate limits. After that adjust activation, slope, onset and recovery. Finally test the complete system during relevant activity.   H5C3  Pre-Programming Assessment 1. Confirm the pacemaker indication, programmed mode and degree of pacing dependence. 2. Review symptoms at rest and during specific activities. 3. Assess intrinsic sinus and ventricular rate behaviour from ECG, histograms and stored data. 4. Review medications that alter chronotropy or exercise tolerance. 5. Check battery, lead integrity, sensing, capture and programmed AV timing. 6. Determine whether rate increase currently comes from atrial tracking, the sensor or both. 7. Identify the activity that best reproduces symptoms: level walking, stairs, cycling, arm work or sustained exercise. 8. Define the clinical goal and a safe upper-rate range with the treating team. 9. Document baseline rate, blood pressure, symptoms and sensor settings. IMAGE  6.7-19 Learning purpose: Provide a reproducible assessment before any sensor parameter is changed.     H5C4  Core Programming Parameters Parameter Question answered If increased or made more aggressive If decreased or made more conservative Lower rate What rate is maintained at rest? Higher resting pacing floor Lower resting pacing floor Activity threshold How much motion starts the response? Direction depends on manufacturer terminology; more sensitive means less motion required Less sensitive means more motion required Response factor / slope How much rate is produced for a given activity? Higher sustained sensor rate Lower sustained sensor rate Reaction time How quickly does the rate rise? Faster if programmed toward short/rapid response Slower if programmed toward long/gradual response Recovery time How quickly does the rate fall? Direction depends on parameter representation; clinically a shorter recovery means faster fall Longer recovery means slower fall Maximum sensor rate How high can sensor-driven pacing go? Higher allowed ceiling Lower allowed ceiling ADL rate / response where available How is ordinary daily activity separated from higher exertion? More support for daily activity depending on device design More conservative daily-activity support       IMAGE 6.7-20 . Learning purpose: Support an LMS slider interaction linking each parameter to the response curve.     H5C5  Parameter Interactions Different parameter combinations can produce a similar rate at one moment but different behaviour over time. For example, a sensitive activity threshold with a low response factor may create an early but modest rate rise. A less sensitive threshold with a high response factor may create delayed onset followed by a steep increase. Reaction time can hide an otherwise adequate slope during a short corridor walk. Maximum sensor rate can create a plateau even when the response factor is high.   Observed pattern Possible parameter combination Early small increase that remains too low Sensitive threshold + low response factor Delayed but steep increase Insensitive threshold + high response factor Appropriate final rate but symptoms at activity onset Adequate slope + long reaction time Good exercise rate but palpitations with gentle movement Threshold too sensitive and/or response factor too high Rate remains high after stopping Long recovery time or persistent sensed motion Rate plateaus despite greater effort Maximum sensor rate or another upper-rate limit reached   IMAGE 6.7-21 . Learning purpose: Teach that similar symptoms may arise from different parameter interactions.     H5C6  Testing Methods Test What it assesses Strength Limitation Corridor walk Onset during ordinary ambulation Simple and realistic May be too short to assess steady-state rate Stair climbing Rapid increase in demand Reproduces daily symptoms Safety and orthopedic limitations Six-minute walk Functional endurance and rate trajectory Standardized and repeatable Submaximal and influenced by motivation Treadmill Progressive workload with ECG monitoring Good control of speed and grade May not match daily movement or balance ability Stationary bicycle Metabolic demand with low torso motion Reveals activity-sensor under-response Not suitable for all patients Arm ergometry or upper-body task Response to arm-dominant work Useful for occupation-specific symptoms May overemphasize pectoral motion Cardiopulmonary exercise testing Heart rate related to oxygen consumption and ventilatory data Most detailed physiological assessment Resource-intensive and specialist-led   IMAGE 6.7-22 Learning purpose: Show comprehensive testing and the link between rate, workload and symptoms. .   H5C7  Stepwise Optimization Workflow 1. Select a monitored activity that reproduces the patient’s complaint. 2. Record baseline paced rate, intrinsic rate, symptoms and sensor markers. 3. If there is no response, confirm that a rate-adaptive mode is programmed and the sensor is active rather than passive. 4. If activation is delayed, review activity threshold and reaction time separately. 5. If the rate rises but remains inadequate, review response factor and maximum sensor rate. 6. If the rate is excessive during mild activity, reduce sensor sensitivity or slope as appropriate to the device. 7. If the rate falls too quickly or too slowly after exercise, adjust recovery behaviour. 8. Repeat the same activity after each meaningful change rather than changing several settings at once. 9. Confirm that the new rate does not cause symptoms, ischaemia, loss of AV synchrony or undesirable ventricular pacing behaviour. 10. Review histograms and remote trends after the patient resumes normal life.   IMAGE 6.7-23 . Learning purpose: Provide a safe repeatable optimization sequence.     H5C8  Programming in VVIR, DDDR and DDIR Mode Sensor role Key programming focus Common interpretation challenge VVIR Primary source of rate increase when ventricular intrinsic rate is slow Lower rate, sensor slope and maximum sensor rate Distinguishing sensor pacing from intermittent intrinsic ventricular rhythm DDDR Complements atrial tracking and supports rate when sinus response is insufficient Sensor/tracking interaction, upper rates, AV timing and ventricular pacing strategy Determining whether rate is atrial-tracked or sensor-driven DDIR Provides rate support without atrial tracking Sensor response during atrial tachyarrhythmia or nontracking strategy Atrial events may be sensed but not tracked AAIR Raises atrial pacing rate and relies on AV conduction AV conduction at higher paced rates and atrial response Risk of inadequate ventricular support if AV conduction deteriorates   H5C9  Documentation Template Field Record Clinical indication Reason rate response is needed and activity-related symptoms Baseline mode and rates Mode, lower rate, upper tracking rate and maximum sensor rate Sensor status Off, passive, active, blended or manufacturer-specific state Baseline parameters Activity threshold, response factor, reaction and recovery Test activity Walk, stairs, bicycle, treadmill or CPET protocol Observed response Rest rate, onset time, steady rate, peak rate and recovery Symptoms and haemodynamics Dyspnoea, fatigue, palpitations, blood pressure and oxygenation where relevant Programming change One or more parameters changed with rationale Verification Post-change ECG/EGM and repeat activity response Follow-up Histogram, remote monitoring or clinic reassessment plan   H5C10  Programming Clinical Pearls • Change one programming domain at a time whenever possible. • Use the same activity before and after a programming change. • No response may reflect sensor off/passive, intrinsic rate above the pacing rate or an insensitive activity threshold. • A low exercise rate may reflect response factor or maximum sensor rate rather than threshold. • A fast onset with excessive rate suggests threshold and slope should both be reviewed. • Reaction time and response factor are not interchangeable. • Test cycling if cycling is the patient’s main activity. • Review AV timing and ventricular pacing burden when increasing rates in a dual-chamber system. • Confirm that rate increase does not provoke angina, hypotension or intolerable palpitations. • Document the full parameter set because manufacturer names and scales differ.   H5C11 Vocabulary and Definitions   Term Definition Programming goal Patient-specific functional outcome the rate response is intended to achieve. Upper sensor limit Programmed ceiling for sensor-driven rate. Rate plateau Failure of the rate to increase further despite greater workload. ADL rate Device-specific target or transition rate associated with ordinary daily activity. Exercise protocol Standardized activity used to test sensor response. Rate trajectory Pattern of rate change from rest through exercise and recovery. Rate profile optimization Device-specific automatic adjustment based on stored rate patterns. Sensor blend Combination of two sensor inputs to determine rate. Post-programming verification Repeat assessment confirming intended response and absence of adverse effects. Functional endpoint Patient-centred outcome such as walking distance, symptoms or exercise capacity.

Topic: Topic 6.7.5: ECG, EGM and Exercise Interpretation

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.5: ECG, EGM and Exercise Interpretation

Heading: ECG, EGM and Exercise Interpretation

Recognising rest, onset, sustained response, plateau and recovery H6C1 Topic Learning Objectives • Identify sensor-driven rate response on a paced ECG. • Differentiate paced rate increase from intrinsic atrial tracking. • Interpret rate acceleration, plateau and recovery. • Use marker channels and sensor trends. • Recognize inadequate or inappropriate response patterns. H6C2 What to Look for on the ECG • Pacing rate near the lower rate at rest when intrinsic rhythm is slower. • Progressive shortening of paced cycle length after activity begins. • A paced rate that stabilizes at a sensor-indicated level during sustained activity. • A ceiling when the maximum sensor rate or another upper limit is reached. • Gradual lengthening of cycle length during recovery. • Preserved capture and appropriate chamber sequence at faster rates. • Symptoms or haemodynamic changes despite an apparently smooth rate curve. Figure 6.7-12. Typical sensor-driven rate pattern across rest, onset, sustained activity and recovery. IMAGE 6.7-24 Learning purpose: a paced-ECG labelling activity .   H6C3 Surface ECG, EGM and Marker Alignment The surface ECG shows the actual cardiac rhythm. The EGM shows local intracardiac activity. The marker channel shows how the device classified sensed and paced events. The sensor trend or sensor-indicated rate shows the output of the rate-response algorithm. These rows answer different questions and should be reviewed together.   Display row Question answered Surface ECG What electrical activation actually occurred? Atrial EGM Was atrial activity intrinsic or paced and what was its timing? Ventricular EGM Was ventricular activity intrinsic or paced and was capture present? Marker channel What did the device sense, pace or classify? Sensor-indicated rate What rate did the activity algorithm request? Programmed rates Which lower and upper limits constrained the result?   IMAGE 6.7-25 Learning purpose: Teach vertical interpretation and the distinction between device classification and actual rhythm.       H6C4  Distinguishing Sensor-Driven Rate from Atrial Tracking Finding Sensor-driven explanation Atrial-tracking explanation Atrial pace markers increase with rate Sensor raises atrial pacing rate Not applicable because atrial events are paced Intrinsic AS markers precede VP beats Sensor may be inactive or acting as a lower timing floor Ventricular rate may be driven by tracked sinus P waves Sensor-indicated rate rises but intrinsic atrial rate is faster Sensor is not the limiting mechanism Intrinsic atrial tracking dominates Mode is DDIR Sensor can raise pacing rate Atrial events are sensed but not tracked beat-to-beat Mode is VVIR Sensor or intrinsic ventricular rhythm determines rate Atrial tracking is unavailable   Interpretation rule A paced rate increase in DDDR is not proof of rate-response pacing. Look for AP versus AS markers and compare the sensor-indicated rate with the intrinsic atrial rate.   H6C5  Expected Rest-to-Exercise Pattern by Mode Mode Rest Activity onset Sustained activity Recovery VVIR VP near lower rate if no faster VS VP intervals shorten as sensor rate rises VP at sensor-indicated rate unless intrinsic ventricular events inhibit VP intervals lengthen according to recovery DDDR with sinus-node dysfunction AP-VP or AP-VS near lower rate AP rate increases; ventricular response follows AV conduction or pacing AP-driven dual-chamber sequence at sensor rate AP rate gradually falls DDDR with intact sinus acceleration AS-VS or AS-VP depending conduction Sinus AS rate increases and may dominate sensor Tracked rate within upper limits Sinus rate and/or sensor rate fall DDIR AP/VP or sensed events without tracking Sensor raises paced rate independently of atrial tracking Nontracking rate-adaptive pacing Sensor-driven rate declines   IMAGE 6.7-26 Learning purpose: Train learners to recognise how rate response appears in different pacing modes. .   H6C6  Upper-Rate Plateau When the paced rate reaches the maximum sensor rate, additional activity may not produce a further sensor-driven increase. In dual-chamber pacing, an upper tracking rate or total device timing limit may create a different plateau. The patient may describe a sudden ceiling, exertional fatigue or abrupt loss of performance at a reproducible workload. A plateau is not automatically a programming error. It may be a deliberate safety limit. Before increasing it, evaluate symptoms, age, ventricular function, ischaemia risk, AV timing, refractory periods and the reason the existing limit was selected. IMAGE 6.7-27 Learning purpose: Explain the difference between inadequate slope and an upper-rate ceiling. .   H6C7  Inadequate Response Patterns Pattern ECG / trend clue Possible explanation No rise Rate remains at lower rate throughout activity Sensor off/passive, threshold too high, intrinsic inhibition or mode not rate-adaptive Late rise Long delay before cycle length shortens Threshold too high or reaction time too long Shallow rise Rate increases but remains low at sustained workload Response factor too low Early plateau Rate stops increasing at modest workload Maximum sensor rate too low or another upper limit Abrupt fall after activity Rapid return toward lower rate Recovery too short for patient needs Prolonged high rate Rate remains elevated after activity ends Recovery too long or continuing vibration/motion   H6C8 Inappropriate Response Patterns • Rate rises while the patient is resting in a vibrating vehicle. • Rate rises during tremor or repetitive shoulder movement. • Rate accelerates during pocket manipulation. • Pacing rate is disproportionate to low-level activity. • Rate remains near the maximum sensor rate during mild effort. • A very fast onset produces palpitations or dyspnoea. • The rate increase is technically smooth but causes angina or hypotension. • Atrial tracking rather than the sensor is misidentified as the source of the high rate.   IMAGE 6.7-28 .     H6C9  Exercise-Test Interpretation Checklist 1. Confirm the programmed mode and whether the sensor is active. 2. Record resting rate, rhythm, blood pressure and symptoms. 3. Mark the exact time activity starts. 4. Observe time to first rate increase. 5. Measure rate at a defined low workload. 6. Observe the slope as workload rises. 7. Identify the peak rate and whether a programmed limit is reached. 8. Confirm capture, AV timing and rhythm stability at peak rate. 9. Mark the exact time activity stops. 10. Observe recovery time and symptoms. 11. Compare sensor-indicated rate, paced rate and intrinsic rate. 12. Document whether the response met the patient-specific goal. H6C10  Topic Clinical Pearls • Interpret the rate curve over time, not from one heart-rate value. • Mark activity onset and cessation precisely during testing. • A paced rate increase in DDDR may be atrial-tracked rather than sensor-driven. • The sensor-indicated rate is not always the actual paced rate. • An early plateau can reflect a limit even when the sensor signal continues to rise. • Check capture and AV sequence at faster rates. • A short corridor walk may not reveal the steady-state response. • Cycling is a useful challenge test for an activity sensor. • Symptoms with an apparently normal rate require a wider clinical evaluation. • Post-exercise recovery is part of the therapy and should be tested. H6C11  Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Rate acceleration Shortening of pacing cycle length as the sensor-indicated rate rises. Steady-state rate Stable rate reached during sustained activity. Rate deceleration Lengthening of pacing cycle length during recovery. Upper-rate plateau Ceiling beyond which the paced rate does not rise further. Sensor-indicated rate Algorithm-calculated target rate from sensor input. Actual paced rate Rate at which pacing pulses are delivered after all timing rules are applied. Tracked rate Ventricular rate driven by sensed atrial events. AP-VP Atrial paced followed by ventricular paced event sequence. AS-VP Atrial sensed followed by ventricular paced event sequence. Chronotropic profile Complete heart-rate pattern across rest, exercise and recovery.

Topic: Topic 6.7.6: Troubleshooting and Optimization

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.6: Troubleshooting and Optimization

Heading: Troubleshooting and Optimization

From symptom pattern to parameter, sensor, mode or clinical cause H7C1  Topic Learning Objectives • Classify the observed response pattern before programming. • Identify common causes of insufficient and excessive response. • Distinguish sensor failure from inactive settings or mode interactions. • Recognize environmental and procedural mechanical triggers. • Use a patient-first troubleshooting workflow. H7C2  Troubleshooting Principle A rate-response complaint should be translated into an observable pattern: no activation, delayed activation, inadequate slope, early plateau, excessive response, overly rapid onset or prolonged recovery. Each pattern points toward a different programming domain. Randomly increasing or decreasing the sensor is unsafe because one change may correct one symptom while producing another. Figure 6.7-13. Match the observed pattern to the relevant programming domain before changing settings.     H7C3  Insufficient Rate Response Possible cause Evidence Next assessment Non-rate-adaptive mode Mode does not end in R Confirm mode and indication before enabling rate response Sensor off or passive Programmer status and absent sensor-driven rate Determine whether diagnostic-only operation was intentional Activity threshold too insensitive No activation during gentle or moderate movement Review live sensor signal and lower threshold cautiously Response factor too low Sensor activates but rate increase is shallow Increase slope within clinical limits Reaction time too long Rate eventually becomes adequate but onset is delayed Shorten onset after reproducing the complaint Maximum sensor rate too low Rate plateaus at programmed ceiling Assess safe upper rate and other timing limits Low torso motion Cycling or static exercise with little generator acceleration Use activity-specific testing or another sensor strategy Intrinsic events inhibit pacing Patient’s own rate is above the device timing rate Determine whether symptoms are unrelated to pacing rate Device or lead problem Unexpected pacing/capture abnormality Complete standard pacemaker electrical evaluation   IMAGE 6.7-29 . Learning purpose: Provide a rapid troubleshooting path for insufficient chronotropic support.     H7C4  Excessive or Inappropriate Rate Response Possible cause Evidence Possible direction Activity threshold too sensitive Rate rises with minimal movement or at rest Require more activity before activation Response factor too high Rate becomes excessive at ordinary walking Reduce rate gain or slope Reaction time too short Abrupt rate acceleration causes palpitations Program a more gradual onset Maximum sensor rate too high for tolerance Rate reaches a clinically unsuitable ceiling Reassess the safe upper sensor limit Vibration or vehicle motion Rate correlates with external mechanical exposure Modify settings or exposure; confirm sensor type Tremor or repetitive movement Rate correlates with involuntary or localized motion Adjust threshold after monitored reproduction Atrial tracking misidentified as sensor response AS markers drive VP at fast rate Evaluate atrial rhythm and tracking behaviour Sensor blend interaction Second sensor sustains or augments rate Review each sensor and blend algorithm   IMAGE 6.7-30 Learning purpose: Help learners identify when the sensor response is disproportionate to demand.     H7C5  Delayed Onset Delayed onset means the rate response begins too late for the patient’s activity. The main programming possibilities are an insensitive activity threshold and a long reaction time. They can be distinguished by examining the sensor signal. If the signal does not cross threshold until vigorous movement, activation is the problem. If it crosses promptly but the rate rises slowly, reaction time is the problem. IMAGE  6.7-31 Learning purpose: How to separate two commonly confused causes of delayed chronotropy.     H7C6 Slow or Fast Recovery A patient may feel that the heart continues racing after activity or drops too quickly after stopping. Confirm whether the sensor signal itself remains elevated due to continued movement, vibration or posture. If the signal falls but the pacing rate remains high, recovery programming is the likely domain. If the rate falls quickly and symptoms occur during cool-down, a longer recovery may be considered after clinical assessment. IMAGE 6.7-32 Learning purpose: Make recovery time a visible and testable programming variable.     H7C7  Mechanical Triggers and Procedure Environments • Transport trolley vibration or rough vehicle travel. • Powered surgical or orthopedic equipment transmitting vibration. • External chest percussion or vigorous physiotherapy. • Pocket manipulation during examination or surgery. • Repetitive shoulder or arm movement. • Tremor, shivering or seizure-related movement. • Mechanical ventilation is more directly relevant to minute-ventilation sensors, but patient movement and vibration can still activate an activity sensor. • Electromagnetic interference and activity-sensor activation are different mechanisms and may coexist in procedural environments. IMAGE 6.7-33 Learning purpose: Prevent learners from confusing sensor-driven rate increase with EMI oversensing. .   H7C8 Patient-First Troubleshooting Workflow 1. Assess symptoms, pulse, blood pressure and rhythm stability. 2. Confirm that the observed rate is paced rather than intrinsic. 3. Identify AP, AS, VP and VS markers and the programmed mode. 4. Check whether the sensor is off, passive, active or blended. 5. Reproduce the symptom using a safe monitored activity. 6. Review the sensor signal, sensor-indicated rate and actual paced rate. 7. Classify the pattern: no activation, delayed onset, low slope, plateau, excessive response or abnormal recovery. 8. Review the parameter associated with that pattern. 9. Exclude lead, capture, AV timing, arrhythmia, ischaemia and non-cardiac causes. 10. Change the minimum number of settings needed to test the hypothesis. 11. Repeat the identical activity and verify the complete response. 12. Document final settings and arrange follow-up trends or remote review. IMAGE 6.7-34 . Learning purpose: Train learners to build an evidence chain instead of changing settings by trial and error. .   H7C9  Red Flags for Immediate Clinical Review • Angina, syncope, hypotension or severe dyspnoea during sensor-driven rate increase. • Very rapid paced rate that is not explained by programmed sensor limits. • Loss of capture or unstable pacing at higher rates. • New atrial or ventricular tachyarrhythmia. • Unexpected mode change or device reset. • Rate-response behaviour following generator migration, trauma or revision. • Symptoms that persist despite an apparently appropriate rate profile. • Any uncertainty in a pacemaker-dependent patient during exercise testing. H7C10  Clinical Pearls • First describe the pattern; then choose the parameter domain. • Threshold controls activation, response factor controls slope, reaction controls onset and recovery controls offset. • Check mode and sensor status before assuming sensor failure. • A rate plateau may be an upper-rate limit, not a weak sensor. • Atrial tracking may mimic sensor-driven rate in DDDR. • Vibration-related rate increase can be normal sensor function in an abnormal environment. • Cycling is a useful test for motion-sensor under-response. • Do not correct exercise symptoms without confirming capture and AV timing at faster rates. • Change one domain at a time and repeat the same activity. • Urgent symptoms take priority over programmer optimization.   H7C11  Vocabulary and Definitions   Term Definition Insufficient response Sensor-driven rate lower or slower than required for the activity. Excessive response Sensor-driven rate disproportionate to activity or patient tolerance. Delayed activation Late onset of rate increase after activity begins. Early plateau Rate reaches a ceiling at a workload below the desired level. Prolonged recovery Sensor-driven rate remains elevated too long after activity stops. Vibration response Rate increase caused by mechanical vibration rather than exercise demand. Sensor status Programmed state such as off, passive, active or blended. Hypothesis-driven programming Changing a parameter to test a defined suspected mechanism. Reproducibility Ability to produce the same rate pattern during the same activity. Red flag Finding requiring urgent clinical evaluation rather than routine optimization.

Topic: Topic 6.7.8: Chapter Consolidation

Topic Description: Topic 6.7.8: Chapter Consolidation

Heading: Chapter Consolidation

Clinical pearls, master vocabulary, image register and reference framework H9C1  Chapter Clinical Pearls • Rate-responsive pacing is designed to support chronotropy, not simply to produce a faster heart rate. • The letter R identifies rate modulation but not the sensor type or programming quality. • Activity sensors measure a surrogate of metabolic demand. • Piezoelectric crystals generate electrical charge when mechanically stressed. • Accelerometers and piezoelectric sensors are related activity-sensor technologies but are not identical. • Activity threshold controls when the response starts. • Response factor controls how much rate is produced for a given activity. • Reaction time controls acceleration and recovery time controls deceleration. • Maximum sensor rate is a ceiling, not a mandatory target. • Atrial tracking and sensor-driven rate must be distinguished in DDDR. • Walking generally activates an activity sensor well; cycling may not. • Vibration, tremor, repetitive arm movement and pocket manipulation can produce inappropriate activity-sensor response. • An active sensor can be clinically inadequate; a passive sensor can collect data without controlling the rate. • The sensor-indicated rate may differ from the actual paced rate because intrinsic events and timing limits intervene. • Exercise testing should reproduce the patient’s real complaint. • Rate-response programming must be integrated with AV timing, ventricular pacing strategy and cardiac function. • A smooth rate curve is not necessarily a haemodynamically appropriate curve. • Change one programming domain at a time whenever possible. • Verify capture and rhythm stability at the higher paced rates. • Patient symptoms and safety take priority over achieving a programmed numerical target. H9C2 Master Vocabulary and Definitions Term Definition Rate-responsive pacing Sensor-controlled variation of pacing rate according to activity or physiological demand. Chronotropic incompetence Inadequate heart-rate increase relative to metabolic need. Activity sensor Implanted sensor detecting motion, acceleration, vibration or mechanical stress. Piezoelectric effect Electrical charge generated by mechanical deformation of a material. Accelerometer Solid-state sensor measuring acceleration. Sensor-indicated rate Rate requested by the sensor algorithm. Actual paced rate Rate delivered after intrinsic events and timing limits are applied. Activity threshold Minimum activity signal required to activate rate response. Response factor Gain or slope translating activity into rate increase. Reaction time Time course of rate increase after activity begins. Recovery time Time course of rate decrease after activity falls. Lower rate limit Minimum pacing floor. Maximum sensor rate Highest sensor-driven pacing rate allowed. Upper tracking rate Highest ventricular tracking rate for atrial sensed events. Sensor trending Stored activity or sensor-rate data. Passive sensor Diagnostic sensor operation without active rate control. Rate histogram Distribution of sensed and paced rates over time. Rate plateau Ceiling reached despite increasing workload. Mechanical coupling Transfer of motion from generator case or tissue to sensor. Vibration artifact Mechanical stimulus unrelated to metabolic demand. Atrial tracking Ventricular timing driven by sensed atrial events. Sensor blend Combination of activity and another physiologic sensor. Rate-profile optimization Device-specific automatic adaptation of rate-response curves. Chronotropic profile Rate pattern from rest through activity and recovery. Functional testing Activity assessment used to determine whether programmed response meets clinical goals.   H9C3 Additional Images for Complete LMS Coverage         Clinical and technical disclaimer Rate-response algorithms, parameter names, directions, ranges, sensor designs and automatic optimization differ among manufacturers and models. The chapter teaches transferable principles. Patient programming must use current device-specific documentation, monitored testing and qualified clinical judgment.
