Chapter: Chapter 6.8: Pacemaker Functions & Programming

Topic: TOPIC 6.8: PACEMAKER FUNCTIONS AND PROGRAMMING

Topic Description: TOPIC 6.8: PACEMAKER FUNCTIONS AND PROGRAMMING

Heading: PACEMAKER FUNCTIONS AND PROGRAMMING

Defining programming requirements and applying the PBLSTOP workflow safely Figure 6.8-1. PBLSTOP provides a repeatable sequence for programming and follow-up.   Chapter scope This chapter explains a structured educational workflow for interrogation, testing, programming, verification and documentation. It does not replace manufacturer-specific manuals, institutional protocols or decisions by trained clinicians. Programming should be performed only by qualified personnel with appropriate monitoring and emergency support.     6.8.H1C1 Learning Objectives At the end of this chapter, the learner should be able to: • Define pacemaker interrogation and programming and distinguish observation from active parameter change. • Explain why programming must balance accurate functioning, haemodynamic benefit, symptom control, patient safety and battery longevity. • Describe the clinical and technical requirements that should be reviewed before any programming change. • Apply the PBLSTOP sequence: Pacing, Battery, Lead parameters, Sensing, Threshold, Observation and Print. • Review programmed mode, lower and upper rates, AV timing, rate response, output, sensitivity and major algorithms in a logical order. • Interpret battery status, projected longevity and replacement indicators using model-specific terminology and trends. • Review lead configuration, impedance, pacing burden, sensing amplitude and capture threshold as an integrated system. • Perform or describe supervised sensing and threshold tests while protecting pacemaker-dependent patients. • Compare baseline and post-programming ECG, EGM and marker-channel behaviour. • Recognize programming changes that may improve function but create a new risk, such as oversensing, loss of capture or excessive rate response. • Use patient symptoms, activity level and clinical goals to assess whether nominal settings are appropriate. • Document every meaningful change, the reason for the change, verification evidence and follow-up plan. • Recognize red flags requiring immediate escalation rather than routine optimization. • Use a structured printout or electronic report to communicate findings to the responsible clinical team. 6.8.H1C2  Chapter Overview Pacemaker programming is the process of selecting and adjusting device parameters so the implanted system delivers the intended therapy for a specific patient. It is not simply changing numbers on a programmer screen. A complete programming session begins with a clinical question, collects baseline evidence, evaluates battery and leads, tests sensing and capture, makes a targeted change, observes the patient and device response, and preserves a report that allows future comparison. The same numerical setting can be appropriate for one patient and unsafe for another. A lower rate of 60 beats per minute may be satisfactory for a sedentary patient with intermittent AV block but may be insufficient for a symptomatic patient with sinus-node dysfunction. A long AV delay may reduce unnecessary ventricular pacing in one patient but permit symptomatic first-degree AV delay or pacemaker syndrome in another. A very high output may protect capture but shorten longevity or cause extracardiac stimulation. Programming therefore requires interpretation, not memorization. Figure 6.8-2. Pacemaker programming is a closed loop of need, measurement, intervention and verification. IMAGE 6.8-01 Learning purpose: Establish the full session workflow before learners study individual checks.     6.8.H1C3  Fundamentals: Interrogation, Testing and Programming Activity Definition Does it alter chronic settings? Example Interrogation Communication with the implanted device to read current settings, diagnostics, measurements, episodes and trends No, unless followed by an active command Read battery longevity, pacing percentages and stored EGMs Temporary test Short controlled change used to measure sensing, threshold or rhythm response Usually returns to prior settings when ended, but behaviour is device-specific Lower-rate sensing test or threshold decrement test Programming Deliberate transmission of new persistent parameters to the device Yes Change mode, lower rate, sensitivity, output or AV delay Emergency programming Rapid change to protect a patient during instability or a procedure Yes, often temporary until the situation ends Asynchronous pacing during a defined procedure Remote interrogation Transmission of device data without the patient being physically in the clinic Usually read-only; remote reprogramming availability is system- and jurisdiction-specific Battery, lead alerts and arrhythmia review Observation Assessment of ECG, EGM, markers, symptoms and haemodynamics before or after a change No Confirm capture and appropriate inhibition   Programming principle The programmer display is a user interface to an implanted therapy system. Always distinguish what is being displayed, what is being tested temporarily and what will remain programmed after telemetry ends.   6.8.H1C4  Defining the Requirements of Programming The programming requirement is the set of clinical and technical outcomes that the device must achieve for the patient. It should be defined before changing parameters. The requirement is broader than “maintain a minimum heart rate.” It includes safe sensing, reliable capture, appropriate chamber coordination, adequate rate during activity, avoidance of unnecessary pacing, management of atrial arrhythmias, diagnostic quality, procedural readiness and acceptable battery use . Requirement domain Questions to define before programming Indication and rhythm Why was the pacemaker implanted? Is the problem sinus-node dysfunction, AV block, atrial fibrillation with bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence or another condition? Dependence What happens if pacing is inhibited or capture is lost? Is a reliable intrinsic escape rhythm present? Symptoms and goals Is the patient experiencing fatigue, dyspnoea, presyncope, palpitations, exercise limitation or pacemaker-syndrome symptoms? Mode and synchrony Which chambers need pacing and sensing? Should atrial events be tracked? Is AV synchrony clinically valuable? Rate behaviour What resting, sleep, activity and upper rates are appropriate? Is rate response required? Electrical safety Are sensing amplitudes, impedance, thresholds and output margins stable? Battery and longevity What is the projected service life, and can energy be reduced without compromising safety? Arrhythmia behaviour Are mode switch, PMT prevention, atrial arrhythmia detection and diagnostics appropriate? Follow-up and monitoring Which alerts and remote-monitoring parameters are needed, and when should the next review occur?   IMAGE 6.8-02 Learning purpose: Show that programming is individualized across clinical and technical domains.     6.8.H1C5  Battery Life and Accurate Functioning: The Central Trade-off Battery conservation is important, but the first duty of programming is accurate and safe therapy. Longevity should be optimized only after sensing, capture, rate support and clinical goals are protected. Energy is consumed by pacing pulses, background circuitry, telemetry, diagnostics, sensors and algorithms. Pacing output, pulse width, pacing percentage, rate and the number of active channels are major contributors. Figure 6.8-3. Conceptual balance between reserve and longevity; the optimal setting is patient-specific.   Programming choice Potential benefit Potential battery cost or clinical risk Higher pacing amplitude Greater capture reserve Higher energy use; may hide a rising threshold; possible extracardiac stimulation Longer pulse width Improves capture probability Higher energy use; may be inefficient at very long durations Lower sensitivity mV value Detects smaller intrinsic signals May oversense noise, T waves, myopotentials or far-field activity Higher lower rate Prevents bradycardia and may improve symptoms More pacing, higher average rate and greater energy use Rate response enabled Improves activity-related rate support May cause inappropriate acceleration or additional sensor use Shorter AV delay May improve ventricular support and AV timing May increase ventricular pacing burden Longer AV delay or conduction-search algorithm May reduce unnecessary RV pacing May cause long PR/AV intervals, symptoms or upper-rate interactions Automatic capture management Can maintain reserve while reducing output Algorithm eligibility and measurement accuracy are device-specific Extensive diagnostics/remote alerts Earlier detection and richer follow-up information Data interpretation and workflow burden; small device energy cost   Never optimize longevity in isolation A lower-output or lower-rate setting is not “better” if it causes loss of capture, symptoms, inadequate rate support or reduced diagnostic safety.   IMAGE 6.8-03 . Learning purpose: Make the trade-off visible without implying that battery life has priority over safety. .   6.8.H1C6  Core Programming Parameter Map Figure 6.8-4. Major pacemaker parameters interact and should not be adjusted independently of the whole system.     Parameter family Examples What the learner must verify Pacing mode VVI, VVIR, DDD, DDDR, DDIR and others Correct chamber support, sensing response, tracking and rate-response status Rate limits Lower rate, sleep/rest rate, maximum tracking rate, maximum sensor rate Adequate resting and activity support without unsafe or symptomatic rates Timing Paced/sensed AV delay, PVARP, blanking, refractory intervals AV synchrony, upper-rate behaviour, sensing protection and PMT prevention Output Amplitude, pulse width, polarity, vector Reliable capture with an appropriate margin and no extracardiac stimulation Sensing Sensitivity, polarity, filters and automatic sensing Reliable intrinsic detection without oversensing Rate response Sensor status, threshold, response factor, reaction and recovery Appropriate activity-related rate curve Algorithms Mode switch, AV search, hysteresis, PMT intervention, capture management Correct indication, trigger and safe fallback behaviour Diagnostics Episode storage, histograms, alerts and remote-monitoring settings Useful data without misleading classification or missed alerts   IMAGE 6.8-04 Learning purpose: Orient learners to the main parameter families without copying a proprietary interface. .   6.8.H1C7  The PBLSTOP Programming Framework PBLSTOP is a practical educational sequence for ensuring that no major programming domain is omitted. It does not replace a manufacturer workflow, and the order may be modified in an emergency. Its value is consistency: learners begin with therapy delivery, review battery and lead integrity, confirm sensing and capture, observe the real response and finish with a permanent record. Figure 6.8-5. PBLSTOP sequence.   Letter Domain Minimum review P Pacing Presenting rhythm, programmed mode, rate limits, AV timing, pacing burden, rate response and active algorithms B Battery Battery status, voltage/indicator, longevity estimate, ERI/RRT/EOL terminology and trend L Lead parameters Lead identity, polarity/vector, impedance, alerts, trend and pacing percentages S Sensing P/R amplitude, sensitivity, EGMs, marker alignment, undersensing and oversensing T Threshold Capture test, amplitude at pulse width, output margin, automatic capture and extracardiac stimulation O Observation Surface ECG, EGM, markers, symptoms, haemodynamics, activity response and post-change behaviour P Print Baseline and final settings, test values, strips, episodes, changes, rationale, verification and follow
